Vipulena hi me mahaggatena cetasā viharato abhibhuyya lokaṃ adhiṭṭhāya manasā ye pāpakā akusalā mānasā abhijjhāpi byāpādāpi sārambhāpi te na bhavissanti. Tesaṃ pahānā aparittañca me cittaṃ bhavissati appamāṇaṃ subhāvita’nti. Tassa evaṃpaṭipannassa tabbahulavihārino āyatane cittaṃ pasīdati. Sampasāde sati etarahi vā āneñjaṃ samāpajjati paññāya vā adhimuccati kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati yaṃ taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa āneñjūpagaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamā āneñjasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyati’’.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard.

On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Kurus, at a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!" "Venerable sir," those monks replied.

The Blessed One said this: "Impermanent, monks, are sensual pleasures, hollow, false, deceptive. They are illusory, monks, the prattle of fools.

Sensual pleasures here and now and sensual pleasures in lives to come, sensual perceptions here and now and sensual perceptions in lives to come - both alike are Māra’s realm, Māra’s domain, Māra’s bait, Māra’s hunting ground. On account of them, these evil unwholesome mental states such as covetousness ( *abhijjhā*), ill will (*byāpāda*), and presumption (*sārambhāpi*) arise, and they constitute an obstruction to a noble disciple in training here.

Therein, monks, a noble disciple considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures here and now and sensual pleasures in lives to come, sensual perceptions here and now and sensual perceptions in lives to come - both alike are Māra’s realm, Māra’s domain, Māra’s bait, Māra’s hunting ground. On account of them, these evil unwholesome mental states such as covetousness (*abhijjhā*), ill will (*byāpāda*), and presumption (*sārambhāpi*) arise, and they constitute an obstruction to a noble disciple in training here.

Suppose I were to abide with a mind abundant and exalted, having transcended the world and made a firm resolution with the mind. When I do so, there will be no more evil unwholesome mental states such as covetousness (*abhijjhā*), ill will (*byāpāda*), and presumption (*sārambhāpi*) in me. And with the abandoning of them my mind will be unlimited, immeasurable, and well developed.’

When he practises in this way and frequently abides thus, his mind acquires confidence in this base. Once there is full confidence, he either attains to the imperturbable (*āneñja*) now or else he decides upon perfecting wisdom. On the dissolution of the body, after death, it is possible that this consciousness of his, leading to rebirth, may pass on to rebirth in the imperturbable (*āneñjūpagaṃ*).

This, monks, is declared to be the first way directed to the imperturbable (*āneñjasappāyā*).
commentary_pali:
66.Evaṃme sutanti āneñjasappāyasuttaṃ. Tattha aniccāti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā. Kāmāti vatthukāmāpi kilesakāmāpi. Tucchāti niccasāradhuvasāraattasāravirahitattā rittā, na pana natthīti gahetabbā. Na hi tucchamuṭṭhīti vutte muṭṭhi nāma natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yassa pana abbhantare kiñci natthi, so vuccati tuccho. Musāti nāsanakā. Mosadhammāti nassanasabhāvā, khettaṃ viya vatthu viya hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ viya ca na paññāyittha, katipāheneva supinake diṭṭhā viya nassanti na paññāyanti. Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘mosadhammā’’ti, māyākatametanti yathā māyāya udakaṃ maṇīti katvā dassitaṃ, badaripaṇṇaṃ kahāpaṇoti katvā dassitaṃ, aññaṃ vā pana evarūpaṃ dassanūpacāre ṭhitasseva tathā paññāyati, upacārātikkamato paṭṭhāya pākatikameva paññāyati. Evaṃ kāmāpi ittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ‘‘māyākata’’nti vuttā. Yathā ca māyākāro udakādīni maṇiādīnaṃ vasena dassento vañceti, evaṃ kāmāpi aniccādīni niccādisabhāvaṃ dassentā vañcentīti vañcanakaṭṭhenapi ‘‘māyākata’’nti vuttā. Bālalāpananti mayhaṃ putto, mayhaṃ dhītā, mayhaṃ hiraññaṃ mayhaṃ suvaṇṇanti evaṃ bālānaṃ lāpanato bālalāpanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammikā kāmāti mānusakā pañca kāmaguṇā. Samparāyikāti te ṭhapetvā avasesā. Diṭṭhadhammikā. Kāmasaññāti mānusake kāme ārabbha uppannasaññā. Ubhayametaṃ māradheyyanti ete kāmā ca kāmasaññā ca ubhayampi māradheyyaṃ. Yehi ubhayametaṃ gahitaṃ, tesañhi upari māro vasaṃ vatteti. Taṃ sandhāya ‘‘ubhayametaṃ māradheyya’’nti vuttaṃ.

Mārassesa visayotiādīsupi yathā coḷassa visayo coḷavisayo, paṇḍassa visayo paṇḍavisayo, saṃvarānaṃ visayo saṃvaravisayoti pavattanaṭṭhānaṃ visayoti vuccati, evaṃ yehi ete kāmā gahitā, tesaṃ upari māro vasaṃ vatteti. Taṃ sandhāya mārassesa visayoti vuttaṃ. Pañca pana kāmaguṇe nivāpabījaṃ viya vippakiranto māro gacchati. Yehi pana te gahitā, tesaṃ upari māro vasaṃ vatteti. Taṃ sandhāya mārassesa nivāpoti vuttaṃ. Yathā ca yattha hatthiādayo vasaṃ vattenti, so hatthigocaro assagocaro ajagocaroti vuccati, evaṃ yehi ete kāmā gahitā, tesu māro vasaṃ vatteti. Taṃ sandhāya mārassesa gocaroti vuttaṃ.

Mārassesa visayo mārassesa visayo mārassesa nivāpo mārassesa gocaro

Etthāti etesu kāmesu. Mānasāti cittasambhūtā. Tattha siyā – duvidhe tāva kāme ārabbha abhijjhānalakkhaṇā abhijjhā, karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo sārambho ca uppajjatu, byāpādo kathaṃ uppajjatīti? Mamāyite vatthusmiṃ acchinnepi socanti, acchijjantepi socanti, acchinnasaṅkinopi socanti, yo evarūpo cittassa āghātoti evaṃ uppajjati. Teva ariyasāvakassāti te ariyasāvakassa. Vakāro āgamasandhimattaṃ hoti. Idha manusikkhatoti imasmiṃ sāsane sikkhantassa te tayopi kilesā antarāyakarā honti. Abhibhuyya lokanti kāmalokaṃ abhibhavitvā. Adhiṭṭhāya manasāti jhānārammaṇacittena adhiṭṭhahitvā. Aparittanti kāmāvacaracittaṃ parittaṃ nāma, tassa paṭikkhepena mahaggataṃ aparittaṃ nāma. Pamāṇantipi kāmāvacarameva, rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ appamāṇaṃ. Subhāvitanti pana etaṃ kāmāvacarādīnaṃ nāmaṃ na hoti, lokuttarassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā etassa vasena aparittaṃ appamāṇaṃ subhāvitanti sabbaṃ lokuttarameva vaṭṭati.

Etthā Mānasā Teva ariyasāvakassā Idha manusikkhato Abhibhuyya loka Adhiṭṭhāya manasā Aparitta Pamāṇa appamāṇaṃ. Subhāvita

Tabbahulavihārinoti kāmapaṭibāhanena tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Āyatane cittaṃ pasīdatīti kāraṇe cittaṃ pasīdati. Kiṃ panettha kāraṇaṃ? Arahattaṃ vā, arahattassa vipassanaṃ vā, catutthajjhānaṃ vā, catutthajjhānassa upacāraṃ vā. Sampasāde satīti ettha duvidho sampasādo adhimokkhasampasādo ca paṭilābhasampasādo ca. Arahattassa hi vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā viharato mahābhūtādīsu upaṭṭhahantesu yenime nīhārena mahābhūtā upaṭṭhahanti, upādārūpā upaṭṭhahanti nāmarūpā upaṭṭhahanti, paccayā sabbathā upaṭṭhahanti, lakkhaṇārammaṇā vipassanā upaṭṭhahati, ajjeva arahattaṃ gaṇhissāmīti appaṭiladdheyeva āsā santiṭṭhati, adhimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Tatiyajjhānaṃ vā pādakaṃ katvā catutthajjhānatthāya kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontassa nīvaraṇavikkhambhanādīni samanupassato yenime nīhārena nīvaraṇā vikkhambhanti, kilesā sannisīdanti, sati santiṭṭhati, saṅkhāragataṃ vā vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ hutvā dibbacakkhukassa paraloko viya upaṭṭhāti , cittuppādo lepapiṇḍe laggamāno viya upacārena samādhiyati, ajjeva catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattessāmīti apaṭiladdheyeva āsā santiṭṭhati, adhimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati . Ayaṃ adhimokkhasampasādo nāma. Tasmiṃ sampasāde sati. Yo pana arahattaṃ vā paṭilabhati catutthajjhānaṃ vā, tassa cittaṃ vippasannaṃ hotiyeva. Idha pana ‘‘āyatane cittaṃ pasīdatī’’ti vacanato arahattavipassanāya ceva catutthajjhānūpacārassa ca paṭilābho paṭilābhasampasādoti veditabbo. Vipassanā hi paññāya adhimuccanassa kāraṇaṃ, upacāraṃ āneñjasamāpattiyā.

Tabbahulavihārino Āyatane cittaṃ pasīdatī Sampasāde satī adhimokkhasampasādo paṭilābhasampasādo

Etarahi vā āneñjaṃ samāpajjati. Paññāya vā adhimuccatīti ettha etarahi vā paññāya adhimuccati, āneñjaṃ vā samāpajjatīti evaṃ padaparivattanaṃ katvā attho veditabbo. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – tasmiṃ sampasāde sati etarahi vā paññāya adhimuccati, arahattaṃ sacchikarotīti attho. Taṃ anabhisambhuṇanto āneñjaṃ vā samāpajjati, atha vā paññāya vā adhimuccatīti arahattamaggaṃ bhāveti, taṃ anabhisambhuṇanto āneñjaṃ vā samāpajjati. Arahattamaggaṃ bhāvetuṃ asakkonto etarahi catusaccaṃ vā sacchikaroti. Taṃ anabhisambhuṇanto āneñjaṃ vā samāpajjatīti.

Etarahi vā āneñjaṃ samāpajjati. Paññāya vā adhimuccatī paññāya vā adhimuccatī

Tatrāyaṃ nayo – idha bhikkhu tatiyajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā catutthajjhānassa kasiṇaparikammaṃ karoti. Tassa nīvaraṇā vikkhambhanti, sati santiṭṭhati, upacārena cittaṃ samādhiyati. So rūpārūpaṃ parigaṇhāti, paccayaṃ pariggaṇhāti, lakkhaṇārammaṇikaṃ vipassanaṃ vavatthapeti, tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘‘upacārena me jhānaṃ visesabhāgiyaṃ bhaveyya, tiṭṭhatu visesabhāgiyatā, nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ naṃ karissāmī’’ti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ sacchikaroti. Ettakenassa kiccaṃ kataṃ nāma hoti. Arahattaṃ sacchikātuṃ asakkonto pana tato osakkitamānaso antarā na tiṭṭhati, catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjatiyeva. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā puriso ‘‘vanamahiṃsaṃ ghātessāmī’’ti sattiṃ gahetvā anubandhanto sace taṃ ghāteti, sakalagāmavāsino tosessati, asakkonto pana antarāmagge sasagodhādayo khuddakamige ghātetvā kājaṃ pūretvā etiyeva.

Tattha purisassa sattiṃ gahetvā vanamahiṃsānubandhanaṃ viya imassa bhikkhuno tatiyajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā catutthajjhānassa parikammakaraṇaṃ, vanamahiṃsaghātanaṃ viya – ‘‘nīvaraṇavikkhambhanādīni samanupassato visesabhāgiyaṃ bhaveyya, tiṭṭhatu visesabhāgiyatā, nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ naṃ karissāmī’’ti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattassa sacchikaraṇaṃ, mahiṃsaṃ ghātetuṃ asakkontassa antarāmagge sasagodhādayo khuddakamige ghātetvā kājaṃ pūretvā gamanaṃ viya arahattaṃ sacchikātuṃ asakkontassa, tato osakkitvā catutthajjhānasamāpajjanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Maggabhāvanā catusaccasacchikiriyāyojanāsupi eseva nayo.

Idāni arahattaṃ sacchikātuṃ asakkontassa nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ dassento kāyassa bhedātiādimāha. Tattha yanti yena kāraṇena taṃ saṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa āneñjūpagaṃ, taṃ kāraṇaṃ vijjatīti attho. Ettha ca taṃsaṃvattanikanti tassa bhikkhuno saṃvattanikaṃ. Yena vipākaviññāṇena so bhikkhu saṃvattati nibbattati, taṃ viññāṇaṃ. Āneñjūpaganti kusalāneñjasabhāvūpagataṃ assa, tādisameva bhaveyyāti attho. Keci kusalaviññāṇaṃ vadanti. Yaṃ tassa bhikkhuno saṃvattanikaṃ upapattihetubhūtaṃ kusalaviññāṇaṃ āneñjūpagataṃ assa, vipākakālepi tannāmakameva assāti attho. So panāyamattho – ‘‘puññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Apuññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāroti, apuññupagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Āneñjaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, āneñjūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇa’’nti (saṃ. ni. 2.51) iminā nayena veditabbo. Āneñjasappāyāti āneñjassa catutthajjhānassa sappāyā. Na kevalañca sā āneñjasseva, upari arahattassāpi sappāyāva upakārabhūtāyevāti veditabbā. Iti imasmiṃ paṭhamakaāneñje samādhivasena osakkanā kathitā.

kāyassa bhedā ya taṃsaṃvattanika Āneñjūpaga Āneñjasappāyā
commentary_english:
66. Thus have I heard. This is the Āneñjasappāyasutta.

There, *aniccā* means impermanent due to being the opposite of permanence.

*Kāmā* means both the *vatthukāmā* (desires for objects) and the *kilesakāmā* (desires that are defilements).

*Tucchā* means empty because it is devoid of permanence, essence, lasting essence, and self essence; it is hollow. But it is not to be taken as non-existent.

For if it is said "empty fist," it is not said that there is no fist.

But if there is nothing inside, it is called empty.

*Musā* means destructive.

*Mosadhammā* means of a nature to vanish. Like a field, like an object, like gold and silver, it cannot be perceived. Even in a short time, like things seen in a dream, they vanish and are not perceived.

Therefore it was said, "Mosadhammā." *Māyākatameta* means just as water is shown as a jewel by means of illusion, or a jujube leaf is shown as a coin, or anything else of this kind is perceived as such only as long as one is in the sphere of illusion; from the moment one transcends that sphere, it is perceived as its natural self.

Thus, *kāmāpi* is said to be *‘‘māyākata’’* because of their fleeting nature.

And just as an illusionist deceives by showing water and other things as jewels and so on, so also, the *kāmāpi* deceive by showing impermanent things and so on as having a permanent nature and so on; therefore, they are said to be *‘‘māyākata’’* even in the sense of being deceptive.

*Bālalāpana* means the babbling of fools, such as "my son, my daughter, my gold, my silver"; thus, *bālalāpanaṃ* is the babbling of fools.

*Diṭṭhadhammikā kāmā* means the five human sensual qualities.

*Samparāyikā* means the remaining ones, having set those aside.

*Diṭṭhadhammikā. Kāmasaññā* means the perception that arises in connection with human sense pleasures.

*Ubhayameṭaṃ māradheyya* means both these, namely the sense pleasures and the perception of sense pleasures, are the domain of Māra.

Those by whom both of these are grasped—over them Māra wields his power.

With reference to that, it was said, *‘‘Ubhayameṭaṃ māradheyya.’’*

*Mārassesa visayo* etc. Just as the territory of the Cholas is the Chola territory, the territory of a eunuch is the eunuch territory, the territory of restraints is the territory of restraints, so the sphere of activity is called territory; likewise, those by whom these sense pleasures are grasped—over them Māra wields his power.

With reference to that, it was said, *Mārassesa visayo*.

But scattering the seed of craving in the five sensual qualities, Māra departs.

Those by whom those are grasped—over them Māra wields his power.

With reference to that, it was said, *Mārassesa nivāpo*.

And just as where elephants and so on dwell, that is called elephant pasture, horse pasture, goat pasture, so likewise, those by whom these sense pleasures are grasped—in them Māra wields his power.

With reference to that, it was said, *Mārassesa gocaro*.

The territory of Māra. The territory of Māra. The oblation to Māra.

The territory of Māra.

*Etthā* means in these sense pleasures.

*Mānasā* means born of the mind.

There, it may be asked: since craving, characterized by covetousness, and violence, characterized by aggressiveness, arise in connection with the two kinds of sense pleasures, how does ill will arise? They grieve even when the thing they consider theirs is not lost, they grieve even when it is being lost, they grieve even when they suspect it might be lost; thus, ill will arises, being an affliction of the mind of this kind.

*Teva ariyasāvakassā* means to that noble disciple.
The letter *va* has only the function of euphonic combination (*āgamasandhi*).

"Here, for one training" means that for one training in this teaching, those three defilements are obstacles.

"Having overcome the world" means having overcome the world of desire ( *kāmaloka*).

"Having resolved with the mind" means having resolved with a mind focused on the object of *jhāna*.

"Limited" (*aparitta*) means that a mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-citta*) is called limited (*paritta*); by rejecting that, the exalted (*mahaggata*) is called unlimited (*aparitta*).

"Boundless" (*pramāṇa*) also refers to only the desire realm; the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) and formless realm (*arūpāvacara*) are "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*).

"Well developed" means that this term is not a designation for the desire realm etc.; this term is only for the supramundane (*lokuttara*).

Therefore, based on that, "limited," "immeasurable," and "well developed" all apply only to the supramundane.

Here, "mental," "truly," "for the noble disciple," "here, for one training," "having overcome the world," "having resolved with the mind," "limited," "measurable," "immeasurable," "well developed..."

"Habitually dwelling thus" means for one dwelling habitually, having made that very practice the constant one, by rejecting desire.

"The mind is calmed in the base" means the mind is calmed by the cause.

What is the cause here? Either *arhatship*, or insight (*vipaśyanā*) into *arhatship*, or the fourth *jhāna*, or access (*upacāra*) to the fourth *jhāna*.

"When there is serenity" means that here there are two kinds of serenity: serenity of conviction (*adhimokkha-sampasāda*) and serenity of attainment (*paṭilābha-sampasāda*).

Indeed, for one dwelling, having established insight into *arhatship*, when the great elements etc. are present, the great elements are present by means of that outflow; the appropriated form is present, name and form are present, the conditions are present in every way, insight with characteristic objects is present, and the hope stands, "Today I will attain *arhatship*," even without attainment, he obtains conviction.

Or, for one making the third *jhāna* the basis and performing the preliminary work (*kasiṇa-parikamma*) for the sake of the fourth *jhāna*, for one contemplating the suppression of the hindrances etc., by means of that outflow, the hindrances are suppressed, the defilements subside, mindfulness stands firm, or the formations (*saṅkhāra*) having become distinct and manifest, appear like the other world to one with divine vision; the arising of the mind, like sticking to a lump of clay, is concentrated by access; the hope stands, "Today I will generate the fourth *jhāna*," even without attainment, he obtains conviction.

This is called serenity of conviction (*adhimokkha-sampasāda*).

When there is that serenity.

But whoever attains *arhatship* or the fourth *jhāna*, his mind is indeed very clear.

Here, however, because of the saying "the mind is calmed in the base," one should understand that the attainment of insight into *arhatship* and also access to the fourth *jhāna* is serenity of attainment (*paṭilābha-sampasāda*).

Indeed, insight is the cause of conviction in wisdom, and access [is the cause] of imperturbable attainment.

Habitually dwelling thus, the mind is calmed in the base, when there is serenity.

Serenity of conviction, serenity of attainment. He attains imperturbability right now, or else he is convinced by wisdom.

"Or he attains imperturbability right now, or he is convinced by wisdom": here, having made a word-permutation in this way, the meaning should be understood.

For this is said: "When there is that serenity, either he is convinced by wisdom right now, or he realizes *arhatship*."

Not fully comprehending that, either he attains imperturbability, or else "he is convinced by wisdom," he cultivates the path of *arhatship*; not fully comprehending that, either he attains imperturbability.

Not being able to cultivate the path of *arhatship*, either he realizes the Four Noble Truths right now.

Not fully comprehending that, either he attains imperturbability.

Either he attains imperturbability right now.

Or he is convinced by wisdom, or he is convinced by wisdom. In that case, this is the method: here, a monk makes the third *jhāna* the basis and performs the preliminary work for the fourth *jhāna*.

His hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness stands firm, the mind is concentrated by access.

He grasps form and the formless, he grasps the condition, he determines insight with characteristic objects; it occurs to him thus: "By access, may my *jhāna* have a superior share; let the having a superior share stand firm, I will make it have a penetrating share," having increased insight, he realizes *arhatship*.

By this much, the task is said to be done.

But not being able to realize *arhatship*, then, with a mind that has drawn back from that, he does not stand in between; he attains the fourth *jhāna* itself.
Just as what? Just as a man, thinking "I will kill a wild buffalo," takes a knife and follows it.
If he kills it, he will please all the villagers. But if he is unable, he kills rabbits, lizards, and other small animals along the way, and fills up his hand.

There, just as the act of a man taking a knife and following a wild buffalo is like a foundation for this monk's third *jhāna* and preparation for the fourth *jhāna*, the act of killing the wild buffalo is like—"For one who contemplates the hindrances being removed, there will be a special state. Let the special state remain; I will perform the state of penetration"—developing insight and realizing *arhatship*. Just as the act of one unable to kill a buffalo killing rabbits, lizards and the like along the way, filling up his hand, and going is like one unable to realize *arhatship*, and then withdrawing, the attainment of the fourth *jhāna* should be understood.
The same method applies to the cultivation of the path and the application of the four noble truths.

Now, showing the place of arising for one unable to realize *arhatship*, [he] says, "*kāyassa bhedā*, etc."
There, "*ya*," means: The meaning is that the cause by which that consciousness, which is subject to change, becomes imperturbable exists.
And here, "*taṃsaṃvattanika*," means that which is subject to change for that monk.
That consciousness by which that monk changes and arises is that consciousness.
"*āneñjūpaga*," means: it becomes possessed of the nature of wholesome imperturbability. It means that it would be just like that.
Some say it is wholesome consciousness.
The meaning is: the wholesome consciousness which is subject to change for that monk, which is the cause of rebirth, and which is possessed of imperturbability, would have just that name even at the time of its fruition.
But this is the meaning: "If he generates a meritorious volitional formation, consciousness fares on to the meritorious; if he generates a demeritorious volitional formation, consciousness fares on to the demeritorious; if he generates an imperturbable volitional formation, consciousness fares on to the imperturbable" (Saṃ.
Ni.
2.51) should be understood in this way.
"*āneñjasappāyā*" means the suitable conditions (*sappāya*) for the fourth *jhāna* of imperturbability (*āneñja*).
And it should be understood that it is not only the suitable condition for imperturbability, but it is also helpful as the suitable condition for *arhatship*.
Thus, in this first imperturbable state, the falling away due to *samādhi* has been spoken.
*kāyassa bhedā* *ya* *taṃsaṃvattanika* *āneñjūpaga* *āneñjasappāyā*

mula_pali:
67. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmā, ye ca samparāyikā kāmā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmasaññā , yā ca samparāyikā kāmasaññā; yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ (sabbaṃ rūpaṃ) ( ) natthi sī. pī. potthakesu cattāri ca mahābhūtāni, catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpa’nti. Tassa evaṃpaṭipannassa tabbahulavihārino āyatane cittaṃ pasīdati. Sampasāde sati etarahi vā āneñjaṃ samāpajjati paññāya vā adhimuccati kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati yaṃ taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa āneñjūpagaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, dutiyā āneñjasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmā, ye ca samparāyikā kāmā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmasaññā, yā ca samparāyikā kāmasaññā; ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā rūpā, ye ca samparāyikā rūpā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā rūpasaññā, yā ca samparāyikā rūpasaññā – ubhayametaṃ aniccaṃ. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ nālaṃ abhinandituṃ, nālaṃ abhivadituṃ, nālaṃ ajjhositu’nti. Tassa evaṃpaṭipannassa tabbahulavihārino āyatane cittaṃ pasīdati. Sampasāde sati etarahi vā āneñjaṃ samāpajjati paññāya vā adhimuccati kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati yaṃ taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa āneñjūpagaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, tatiyā āneñjasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyati.
mula_english:
67. Again, monks, a noble disciple considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures here and now and sensual pleasures in lives to come, sensual perceptions here and now, and sensual perceptions in lives to come; whatever form there is (all form) Cattāri and the great elements, and the form derived from the four great elements.’

When he practises in this way and frequently abides thus, his mind acquires confidence in this base (āyatana). When there is full confidence (sampasāde sati), he either attains to the imperturbable (āneñjaṃ samāpajjati) now or else he decides upon perfecting wisdom (paññāya). On the dissolution of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), it is possible that this consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) of his, leading to rebirth (taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ), may pass on to rebirth in the imperturbable (āneñjūpagaṃ). This, monks, is declared to be the second way directed to the imperturbable (āneñjasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyati).

Again, monks, a noble disciple considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures here and now and sensual pleasures in lives to come, sensual perceptions here and now and sensual perceptions in lives to come, material forms here and now and material forms in lives to come, perceptions of forms here and now and perceptions of forms in lives to come - both alike are impermanent (aniccaṃ). What is impermanent (yadaniccaṃ) is not worth delighting in (abhinandituṃ), not worth welcoming (abhivadituṃ), not worth holding to (ajjhosituṃ).’

When he practises in this way and frequently abides thus, his mind acquires confidence in this base (āyatane cittaṃ pasīdati). When there is full confidence, he either attains to the imperturbable (āneñjaṃ samāpajjati) now or else he decides upon perfecting wisdom. On the dissolution of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death, it is possible that this consciousness of his, leading to rebirth, may pass on to rebirth in the imperturbable. This, monks, is declared to be the third way directed to the imperturbable (āneñjasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyati).
commentary_pali:
67.Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti catutthajjhānaṃ patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi bhikkhu heṭṭhimena bhikkhunā paññavantataro tassa ca bhikkhuno attano cāti dvinnampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Tabbahulavihārinoti rūpapaṭibāhanena tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Āneñjaṃ samāpajjatīti ākāsānañcāyatānāneñjaṃ samāpajjati. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha visesamattameva pana vakkhāma. Iti imasmiṃ dutiyaāneñje vipassanāvasena osakkanā kathitā, ‘‘yaṃkiñci rūpa’’nti evaṃ vipassanāmaggaṃ dassentena kathitāti attho.

Itipaṭisañcikkhatīti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā dvīhi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti tiṇṇampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Ubhayametaṃ aniccanti ettha aṭṭha ekekakoṭṭhāsā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikavasena pana saṅkhipitvā ubhayanti vuttaṃ. Nālaṃ abhinanditunti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinandituṃ na yuttaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Tabbahulavihārinoti kāmapaṭibāhanena ca rūpapaṭibāhanena ca tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Āneñjaṃ samāpajjatīti viññāṇañcāyatanāneñjaṃ samāpajjati. Imasmiṃ tatiyaāneñje vipassanāvasena osakkanā kathitā.

Iti paṭisañcikkhatī Ubhayametaṃ anicca Nālaṃ abhinanditu
commentary_english:
"Thus, he reflects," having attained the fourth *jhāna*, he reflects thus. For this *bhikkhu* is more wise than the *bhikkhu* below, and he combines and considers the meditation subject of that *bhikkhu* and of himself, even the two. "He dwells abounding in that," for one dwelling abounding in that same practice, having warded off form. "He attains the imperturbable," he attains the imperturbable of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*). The rest is the same as before. And as here, so everywhere, but we will speak only of the distinction. Thus, in this second imperturbable, decline by way of insight is spoken of, "Whatever is form," thus the meaning is, it is spoken of by one showing the path of insight.

"Thus, he reflects," having attained the sphere of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*), he reflects thus. For this one is more wise than the two *bhikkhus* below, and he combines and considers the meditation subject of those *bhikkhus* and of himself, even the three. "Both of these are impermanent," here, eight individual sections are mentioned, but contracting them in terms of what is visible in this life and the next, it is said "both." "It is not fit to delight in," it is not proper to delight in by way of craving and views. The same rule applies in the case of the two remaining terms. "He dwells abounding in that," for one dwelling abounding in that same practice, having warded off desire and having warded off form. "He attains the imperturbable," he attains the imperturbable of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). In this third imperturbable, decline by way of insight is spoken of.

Thus, he reflects, both of these are impermanent, it is not fit to delight in.

mula_pali: 68. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmā, ye ca samparāyikā kāmā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmasaññā, yā ca samparāyikā kāmasaññā; ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā rūpā, ye ca samparāyikā rūpā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā rūpasaññā, yā ca samparāyikā rūpasaññā; yā ca āneñjasaññā – sabbā saññā. Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhanti etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītaṃ – yadidaṃ ākiñcaññāyatana’nti. Tassa evaṃpaṭipannassa tabbahulavihārino āyatane cittaṃ pasīdati. Sampasāde sati etarahi vā ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjati paññāya vā adhimuccati kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati yaṃ taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa ākiñcaññāyatanūpagaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamā ākiñcaññāyatanasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyati.
mula_english:
“Again, O bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures here and now and sensual pleasures in lives to come, sensual perceptions here and now and sensual perceptions in lives to come, material forms here and now and material forms in lives to come, perceptions of forms here and now and perceptions of forms in lives to come, and perceptions of the imperturbable - all are perceptions (saññā).

Where these perceptions cease without remainder, that is the peaceful, that is the sublime, namely, the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana).’

When he practises in this way and frequently abides thus, his mind acquires confidence in this base (āyatana).

Once there is full confidence (sampasāde sati), he either attains to the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjati) now or else he decides upon perfecting wisdom (paññāya). On the dissolution of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā),

it is possible that this consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) of his, leading to rebirth, may pass on to rebirth in the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatanūpagaṃ).

This, O bhikkhus, is the first practice (paṭipadā) that conduces to the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatanasappāyā) and is proclaimed as such.”
commentary_pali:
68.Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā tīhi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti catunnampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhantīti yaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ patvā etā heṭṭhā vuttā sabbasaññā nirujjhanti. Etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītanti etaṃ aṅgasantatāya ārammaṇasantatāya ca santaṃ, atappakaṭṭhena paṇītaṃ. Tabbahulavihārinoti tāsaṃ saññānaṃ paṭibāhanena tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Imasmiṃ paṭhamākiñcaññāyatane samādhivasena osakkanā kathitā.

Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti viññāṇañcāyatanameva patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā catūhi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti pañcannampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Attena vā attaniyena vāti ahaṃ mamāti gahetabbena suññaṃ tucchaṃ rittaṃ. Evamettha dvikoṭikā suññatā dassitā. Tabbahulavihārinoti heṭṭhā vuttapaṭipadañca imañca suññatapaṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Imasmiṃ dutiyākiñcaññāyatane vipassanāvasena osakkanā kathitā.

Attena vā attaniyena vā Tabbahulavihārino
commentary_english:
68.
"Thus, he contemplates," that is, having reached the base of boundless consciousness, thus he contemplates.

For indeed, he is more wise than three monks below, and he reflects on the meditation subject by combining into one the fourfold meditation subjects of those monks and of himself.

"Where these cease without remainder," that is, having reached the base of nothingness, these perceptions, previously mentioned, cease without remainder.

"This is peaceful, this is excellent," that is, this is peaceful through the continuity of the parts [of consciousness] and the continuity of the object, and excellent through the intensity of non-attachment.

"Abiding frequently in that," that is, for one who dwells having frequently cultivated that same practice by repelling those perceptions.

In this first base of nothingness, the decline through the force of concentration is described.

"Thus, he contemplates," that is, having reached the base of boundless consciousness itself, thus he contemplates.

For indeed, he is more wise than four monks below, and he reflects on the meditation subject by combining into one the fivefold meditation subjects of those monks and of himself.

"By self or by what belongs to self," that is, empty, void, and vacant of what should be grasped as "I" or "mine."

Thus, here the twofold emptiness is shown.

"Abiding frequently in that," that is, for one who dwells having frequently cultivated both the practice previously mentioned and this practice of emptiness.

In this second base of nothingness, the decline through the force of insight is described.

By self or by what belongs to self. Abiding frequently in that.

mula_pali: 69. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘suññamidaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā’ti. Tassa evaṃpaṭipannassa tabbahulavihārino āyatane cittaṃ pasīdati. Sampasāde sati etarahi vā ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjati paññāya vā adhimuccati kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati yaṃ taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa ākiñcaññāyatanūpagaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, dutiyā ākiñcaññāyatanasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyati.
mula_english:
“Again, *bhikkhus*, a noble disciple, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, considers thus: ‘This is void of a self (*ātman*) or of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).’
When he practises in this way and frequently abides thus, his mind acquires confidence in this base (*āyatana*).
Once there is full confidence (*samprasāda*), he either attains to the base of nothingness (*ākiṃcaññāyatanaṃ*) now or else he decides upon perfecting wisdom (*prajñā*). On the dissolution of the body (*kāya*), after death (*maraṇā*),
it is possible that this consciousness (*vijñāṇa*) of his, leading to rebirth, may pass on to rebirth in the base of nothingness (*ākiṃcaññāyatanūpagaṃ*).
This, *bhikkhus*, is declared to be the second way directed to the base of nothingness (*ākiṃcaññāyatanasappāyā pratipadā*).

mula_pali:
70. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘nāhaṃ kvacani kvacini (syā. kaṃ. sī. aṭṭha.) kassaci kiñcanatasmiṃ kiñcanatasmi (?), na ca mama kvacani kismiñci kiñcanaṃ natthī’ti. Tassa evaṃpaṭipannassa tabbahulavihārino āyatane cittaṃ pasīdati. Sampasāde sati etarahi vā ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjati paññāya vā adhimuccati kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati yaṃ taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa ākiñcaññāyatanūpagaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, tatiyā ākiñcaññāyatanasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmā, ye ca samparāyikā kāmā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmasaññā, yā ca samparāyikā kāmasaññā; ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā rūpā, ye ca samparāyikā rūpā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā rūpasaññā, yā ca samparāyikā rūpasaññā ; yā ca āneñjasaññā, yā ca ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā – sabbā saññā. Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhanti etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītaṃ – yadidaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatana’nti. Tassa evaṃpaṭipannassa tabbahulavihārino āyatane cittaṃ pasīdati. Sampasāde sati etarahi vā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjati paññāya vā adhimuccati kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati yaṃ taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ viññāṇaṃ assa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpagaṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasappāyā paṭipadā akkhāyatī’’ti.
mula_english:
‘‘Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus: ‘I am not anything belonging to anyone anywhere, nor is there anything belonging to me in anyone anywhere.’ When he practises in this way and frequently abides thus, his mind acquires confidence in this base (āyatana). Once there is full confidence (sampasāde sati), he either attains to the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ) now or else he decides upon perfecting wisdom (paññāya). On the dissolution of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), it is possible that this consciousness of his (viññāṇaṃ), leading to rebirth, may pass on to rebirth in the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). This, bhikkhus, is declared to be the third way (tatiyā paṭipadā) directed to the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana).

‘‘Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures here and now (diṭṭhadhammikā kāmā) and sensual pleasures in lives to come (samparāyikā kāmā), sensual perceptions here and now (diṭṭhadhammikā kāmasaññā) and sensual perceptions in lives to come (samparāyikā kāmasaññā), material forms here and now (diṭṭhadhammikā rūpā) and material forms in lives to come (samparāyikā rūpā), perceptions of forms here and now (diṭṭhadhammikā rūpasaññā) and perceptions of forms in lives to come (samparāyikā rūpasaññā); and the perception of imperturbability (āneñjasaññā), and the perception of the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā)—all perceptions (sabbā saññā). Where these perceptions cease without remainder (aparisesā nirujjhanti), that is the peaceful (santaṃ), that is the sublime (paṇītaṃ), namely, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).’ When he practises in this way (evaṃpaṭipannassa) and frequently abides thus (tabbahulavihārino), his mind (cittaṃ) acquires confidence in this base (āyatana). Once there is full confidence (sampasāde sati), he either attains to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ) now or else he decides upon perfecting wisdom (paññāya). On the dissolution of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), it is possible that this consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) of his, leading to rebirth (taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ), may pass on to rebirth in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). This, bhikkhus, is declared to be the way (paṭipadā) directed to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).’’
commentary_pali:
70.Itipaṭisañcikkhatīti viññāṇañcāyatanameva patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā pañcahi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti channampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Nāhaṃ kvacani kassaci kiñcanatasmiṃ, na ca mama kvacani kismiñcikiñcanaṃ natthīti ettha pana catukoṭikā suññatā kathitā. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi nāhaṃ kvacanīti kvaci attānaṃ na passati, kassaci kiñcanatasminti attano attānaṃ kassaci parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ na passati, attano bhātiṭṭhāne bhātaraṃ sahāyaṭṭhāne sahāyaṃ parikkhāraṭṭhāne vā parikkhāraṃ maññitvā upagantvā upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Na ca mama kvacanīti ettha mama – saddaṃ tāva ṭhapetvā na ca kvacani parassa ca attānaṃ kvaci na passatīti ayamattho. Idāni mama – saddaṃ āharitvā mama kismiñci kiñcanaṃ natthīti so parassa attā mama kismiñci kiñcanabhāve atthīti na passati. Attano bhātiṭṭhāne bhātaraṃ sahāyaṭṭhāne sahāyaṃ parikkhāraṭṭhāne vā parikkhāranti kismiñci ṭhāne parassa attānaṃ iminā kiñcanabhāvena upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Evamayaṃ yasmā neva katthaci attānaṃ passati, na taṃ parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ attano kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati, tasmā ayaṃ suññatā catukoṭikāti veditabbā. Tabbahulavihārinoti heṭṭhā vuttappaṭipadaṃ imaṃ catukoṭisuññatañca bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Imasmiṃ tatiyākiñcaññāyatanepi vipassanāvaseneva osakkanā kathitā.

Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ patvā evaṃ paṭisañcikkhati. Ayañhi heṭṭhā chahi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti sattannampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhantīti yaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ patvā ettha etā heṭṭhā vuttā sabbasaññā nirujjhanti. Tabbahulavihārinoti tāsaṃ saññānaṃ paṭibāhanena tameva paṭipadaṃ bahulaṃ katvā viharantassa. Imasmiṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatane samādhivasena osakkanā kathitā.

Iti paṭisañcikkhatī Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhantī
commentary_english:
70. "Thus, he reflects," meaning having attained the sphere of nothingness, thus he reflects.

Indeed, he is more wise than the five monks below, and he contemplates by combining into one the meditation subject of those monks and himself, even six in all.

"<hi rend="bold">I have no 'mine' anywhere in anything, nor is there any 'mine' in anything anywhere,</hi>" meaning, in this context, emptiness (śūnyatā) with its four extremes (catukoṭikā) is discussed.

How [is this]? Indeed, "<hi rend="bold">I am not anywhere</hi>" means he does not see a self (ātman) anywhere. "<hi rend="bold">There is no 'mine' in anything belonging to anyone</hi>" means he does not see his own self as deducible in the fact of anyone else's owning it; meaning, he does not see it as deducible, imagining and approaching a brother in the place of a brother in his own property, a friend in the place of a friend, or chattel in the place of chattel.

"<hi rend="bold">Nor is there any 'mine' anywhere</hi>" means, in this [phrase], setting aside the word "mine" for the moment, the words "nor anywhere" mean that he does not see another's self anywhere; this is the meaning.

Now, bringing in the word "mine," "<hi rend="bold">there is no 'mine' in anything anywhere</hi>" means that he does not see thus, "Another's self exists owing to some state of my owning of it."

He does not see in any instance another’s self deducible owing to this fact of his owning a brother in the case of a brother in his own property, a friend in the case of a friend, or chattel in the case of chattel; this is the meaning.

So he sees no self anywhere of his own; nor does he see it as deducible in the fact of another's owning; nor does he see another's self; nor does he see that as deducible in the fact of his own owning. Therefore, this emptiness is to be understood as having four extremes.

"<hi rend="bold">One who dwells abiding much in that</hi>" means one who dwells making much of this practice described below and the emptiness with its four extremes.

In this third sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) also, cessation (osakkanā) is described by way of insight (vipaśyanā).

"Thus, he reflects," meaning having attained the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), thus he reflects.

Indeed, he is more wise than the six monks below, and he contemplates by combining into one the meditation subject of those monks and himself, even seven in all.

"<hi rend="bold">Where these cease without remainder</hi>" means, having attained the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), here these perceptions (saññā) described below cease.

"<hi rend="bold">One who dwells abiding much in that</hi>" means one who dwells making much of that very practice through the repelling of those perceptions.

In this sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, cessation is described by way of concentration (samādhi).

Thus, he reflects; where these cease without remainder.

mula_pali: 71. Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘idha, bhante, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – ‘no cassa, no ca me siyā; na bhavissati, na me bhavissati; yadatthi yaṃ, bhūtaṃ – taṃ pajahāmī’ti. Evaṃ upekkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Parinibbāyeyya nu kho so, bhante, bhikkhu na vā parinibbāyeyyā’’ti? ‘‘Apetthekacco, ānanda, bhikkhu parinibbāyeyya, apetthekacco bhikkhu na parinibbāyeyyā’’ti. ‘‘Ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo yenapetthekacco bhikkhu parinibbāyeyya, apetthekacco bhikkhu na parinibbāyeyyā’’ti? ‘‘Idhānanda, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – ‘no cassa, no ca me siyā; na bhavissati, na me bhavissati; yadatthi, yaṃ bhūtaṃ – taṃ pajahāmī’ti. Evaṃ upekkhaṃ paṭilabhati. So taṃ upekkhaṃ abhinandati, abhivadati, ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ upekkhaṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato tannissitaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ tadupādānaṃ. Saupādāno, ānanda, bhikkhu na parinibbāyatī’’ti. ‘‘Kahaṃ pana so, bhante, bhikkhu upādiyamāno upādiyatī’’ti? ‘‘Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ, ānandā’’ti. ‘‘Upādānaseṭṭhaṃ kira so, bhante, bhikkhu upādiyamāno upādiyatī’’ti? ‘‘Upādānaseṭṭhañhi so, ānanda, bhikkhu upādiyamāno upādiyati. Upādānaseṭṭhañhetaṃ, ānanda, yadidaṃ – nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ’’.
mula_english:
71. When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Here, venerable sir, a *bhikkhu* is practicing thus: ‘If it were not, it would not be mine; it will not be and it will not be mine. What exists, what has come to be, that I am abandoning.’
Thus he obtains equanimity (*upekkhā*).
Venerable sir, does such a *bhikkhu* attain *Nibbāna*?”
“Here, Ānanda, a *bhikkhu* may attain *Nibbāna*, or a *bhikkhu* may not attain *Nibbāna*.”
“What is the cause and reason, venerable sir, why one *bhikkhu* here might attain *Nibbāna*, while another *bhikkhu* here might not attain *Nibbāna*?”
“Here, Ānanda, a *bhikkhu* is practicing thus: ‘If it were not, it would not be mine; it will not be and it will not be mine. What exists, what has come to be, that I am abandoning.’
Thus he obtains equanimity (*upekkhā*).
He delights in that equanimity (*upekkhā*), welcomes it, and remains holding to it.
As he delights in that equanimity (*upekkhā*), welcomes it, and remains holding to it, his consciousness (*vijñāṇa*) becomes dependent on it and clings to it (*upādāna*).
This *bhikkhu* is clinging (*saupādāno*), Ānanda, and does not attain *Nibbāna*.”
“But, venerable sir, when that *bhikkhu* clings, what does he cling to (*upādiyatī*)?”
“The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*), Ānanda.”
“When that *bhikkhu* clings, venerable sir, it seems he clings to the best object of clinging (*upādāna*)”.
“When that *bhikkhu* clings, Ānanda, he clings to the best object of clinging (*upādāna*);
for this is the best object of clinging (*upādāna*), namely, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*).”
commentary_pali:
71.No cassa no ca me siyāti sace mayhaṃ pubbe pañcavidhaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ na āyūhitaṃ assa, yaṃ me idaṃ etarahi evaṃ pañcavidhaṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ etaṃ me na siyā nappavatteyyāti attho. Na bhavissatīti sace etarahi pañcavidhaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ āyūhitaṃ na bhavissati. Na me bhavissatīti tasmiṃ asati anāgate me pañcavidhaṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ na bhavissati. Yadatthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ taṃ pajahāmīti yaṃ atthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ etarahi khandhapañcakaṃ, taṃ pajahāmi. Evaṃupekkhaṃ paṭilabhatīti so bhikkhu evaṃ vipassanupekkhaṃ labhatīti attho.

Parinibbāyeyya nu kho so, bhante, bhikkhu na vā parinibbāyeyyāti kiṃ pucchāmīti pucchati, tatiyajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa arahattampi osakkanāpi paṭipadāpi paṭisandhipi kathitā, tathā catutthajjhānādīni pādakāni katvā ṭhitānaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa na kiñci kathitaṃ, taṃ pucchāmīti pucchati. Apetthāti api ettha. So taṃ upekkhaṃ abhinandatīti so taṃ vipassanupekkhaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhiabhinandanāhi abhinandati. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Tannissitaṃ hoti viññāṇanti viññāṇaṃ vipassanānissitaṃ hoti. Tadupādānanti yaṃ nikantiviññāṇaṃ, taṃ tassa upādānaṃ nāma gahaṇaṃ nāma hoti. Saupādānoti sagahaṇo. Na parinibbāyatīti vipassanāya sālayo bhikkhu mama sāsane na parinibbāyati. Yo pana vihārapariveṇaupaṭṭhākādīsu sālayo, tasmiṃ vattabbameva natthīti dasseti. Kahaṃ panāti? Kattha pana? Upādiyamānoupādiyatīti paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhamāno gaṇhāti. Upādānaseṭṭhaṃ kira so, bhanteti, bhante, so kira bhikkhu gahetabbaṭṭhānaṃ seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ bhavaṃ upādiyati, seṭṭhabhave paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhātīti attho. Iminā tassa bhikkhuno paṭisandhi kathitā. Idānissa arahattaṃ kathetuṃ idhānandātiādimāha.

Parinibbāyeyya nu kho so, bhante, bhikkhu na vā parinibbāyeyyā Apetthā So taṃ upekkhaṃ abhinandatī Tannissitaṃ hoti viññāṇa Tadupādāna Saupādāno Na parinibbāyatī Kahaṃ panā Upādiyamāno upādiyatī Upādānaseṭṭhaṃ kira so, bhante idhānandā
commentary_english:
71. “'It would not be his, and it would not be mine' (no cassa no ca me siyā)": if previously a fivefold cycle of action (pañcavidhaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ) had not been accumulated by me, then this present fivefold cycle of result (pañcavidhaṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ) would not be mine. That is the meaning.

"'It will not be' (na bhavissati)": if now a fivefold cycle of action is not accumulated.

"'It will not be mine' (na me bhavissati)": in that non-existent future, a fivefold cycle of result will not be mine.

"'Whatever exists, whatever has come to be, that I abandon' (yadatthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ taṃ pajahāmī)": whatever exists, whatever has come to be, now, the aggregate of five (*khandhapañcakaṃ*), that I abandon.

"'Thus, he attains equanimity' (evaṃ upekkhaṃ paṭilabhatī)": that *bhikkhu* thus attains insight-equanimity (*vipassanūpekkhaṃ*). That is the meaning.

"Would that *bhikkhu* attain complete extinction, or would he not attain complete extinction (parinibbāyeyya nu kho so, bhante, bhikkhu na vā parinibbāyeyyā)?" He asks, "What am I asking?" The *arahat* who has established the third *jhāna* as a basis, decline, practice, and rebirth have been spoken of, likewise for those who have established the fourth *jhāna*, etc., as a basis; nothing has been spoken of for the one who has established the base of neither perception nor non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*) as a basis. He asks, "What am I asking?"

"'Falling away' (apetthā)": also here.

"'He rejoices in that equanimity' (so taṃ upekkhaṃ abhinandatī)": he rejoices in that insight-equanimity with craving, views, and delight (*taṇhādiṭṭhiabhinandanāhi*).

The same method applies in the case of the other two terms.

"'Consciousness is dependent on that' (tannissitaṃ hoti viññāṇa)": consciousness is dependent on insight (*vipassanānissitaṃ*).

"'That is appropriation' (tadupādāna)": that consciousness of delight (*nikantiviññāṇaṃ*) is called its appropriation (*upādānaṃ nāma*), is called grasping (*gahaṇaṃ nāma*).

"'Having appropriation' (saupādāno)": having grasping (*sagahaṇo*).

"'He does not attain complete extinction' (na parinibbāyatī)": the *bhikkhu* who has attachment to insight (*vipassanāya sālayo bhikkhu*) does not attain complete extinction in my dispensation (*mama sāsane*).

But he shows that there is nothing to be said about the one who has attachment to monasteries, enclosures, attendants, etc. (*vihārapariveṇaupaṭṭhākādīsu sālayo*).

"'Where then?' (kahaṃ panā)": where then? "'Clinging' (upādiyamāno)":

"'He clings' (upādiyatī)": he grasps, taking rebirth (*paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhamāno gaṇhāti*).

"'That *bhikkhu* appropriates the best appropriation, venerable sir' (upādānaseṭṭhaṃ kira so, bhante)": Venerable sir, that *bhikkhu* appropriates the best, highest becoming (*bhavam upādiyati*), the place to be grasped (*gahetabbaṭṭhānaṃ seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ*), he grasps rebirth in the best becoming (*seṭṭhabhave paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhātīti attho*).

By this, the rebirth of that *bhikkhu* has been spoken of.

Now, to speak of his *arahat*ship, he says, "Here, Ānanda (idhānandā)," etc.

mula_pali: 72. ‘‘Idhānanda, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – ‘no cassa, no ca me siyā; na bhavissati, na me bhavissati; yadatthi, yaṃ bhūtaṃ – taṃ pajahāmī’ti. Evaṃ upekkhaṃ paṭilabhati. So taṃ upekkhaṃ nābhinandati, nābhivadati, na ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ upekkhaṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato na tannissitaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ na tadupādānaṃ. Anupādāno, ānanda, bhikkhu parinibbāyatī’’ti.
mula_english:
Here:

72. Here, Ānanda, a *bhikṣu* (Buddhist monk) is practicing thus: 'If it were not, it would not be mine; it will not be and it will not be mine. What exists, what has come to be, that I am abandoning.'
Thus he obtains *upekṣā* (equanimity).
He does not delight in that *upekṣā* (equanimity), welcome it, or remain holding to it.
Since he does not delight in that equanimity, welcome it, or remain holding to it, his *vijñāna* (consciousness) does not become dependent on it and does not cling to it.
A *bhikṣu* (Buddhist monk), Ānanda, who is without clinging attains *parinirvāṇa* (final *nirvāṇa*).”

mula_pali:
73. ‘‘Acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Nissāya nissāya kira no, bhante, bhagavatā oghassa nittharaṇā akkhātā. Katamo pana, bhante, ariyo vimokkho’’ti? ‘‘Idhānanda, bhikkhu ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmā, ye ca samparāyikā kāmā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā kāmasaññā, yā ca samparāyikā kāmasaññā; ye ca diṭṭhadhammikā rūpā, ye ca samparāyikā rūpā; yā ca diṭṭhadhammikā rūpasaññā, yā ca samparāyikā rūpasaññā; yā ca āneñjasaññā, yā ca ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā , yā ca nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññā – esa sakkāyo yāvatā sakkāyo. Etaṃ amataṃ yadidaṃ anupādā cittassa vimokkho. Iti, kho, ānanda, desitā mayā āneñjasappāyā paṭipadā, desitā ākiñcaññāyatanasappāyā paṭipadā, desitā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasappāyā paṭipadā, desitā nissāya nissāya oghassa nittharaṇā, desito ariyo vimokkho. Yaṃ kho, ānanda, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā. Etāni, ānanda, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyathānanda, mā pamādattha, mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī’’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā ānando bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Āneñjasappāyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.
mula_english:
73. “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir, how the crossing of the flood in dependence upon one support or another has been explained by the Blessed One.

What, venerable sir, is noble liberation?”

“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, a noble disciple, considers thus: ‘Sensual pleasures here and now and sensual pleasures in lives to come; sensual perceptions here and now and sensual perceptions in lives to come; material forms here and now and material forms in lives to come; perceptions of forms here and now and perceptions of forms in lives to come; perceptions of the imperturbable, perceptions of the base of nothingness, and perceptions of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception - this is personality (satkāya), as far as personality extends.

This is the Deathless (amata), namely, the liberation (vimokkha) of the mind (citta) through not clinging (anupādā).’

Thus, Ānanda, I have taught the way directed to the imperturbable (āneñjasappāya), I have taught the way directed to the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), I have taught the way directed to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), I have taught the crossing of the flood (oghassa nittharaṇā) in dependence upon one support or another, I have taught noble liberation (ariyo vimokkho).

What should be done for his disciples out of compassion by a teacher who seeks their welfare and has compassion for them, that I have done for you, Ānanda.

There are these roots of trees (rukkhamūlāni), these empty huts (suññāgārāni).

Meditate, Ānanda (jhāyathānanda), do not be negligent (mā pamādattha), lest you regret it later (mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha).

This is our instruction to you.”

This the Blessed One (bhagavā) said.

The venerable Ānanda (āyasmā ānanda), being pleased, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words (bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti).

The Āneñjasappāyasutta, the sixth, is finished.
commentary_pali:
73.Nissāya nissāyāti taṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ nissāya. Oghassa nittharaṇā akkhātāti oghataraṇaṃ kathitaṃ, tatiyajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitabhikkhuno oghanittharaṇā kathitā…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitabhikkhuno oghanittharaṇā kathitāti vadati.

Katamo pana, bhante, ariyo vimokkhoti idha kiṃ pucchati? Samāpattiṃ tāva padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhanto bhikkhu nāvaṃ vā uḷumpādīni vā nissāya mahoghaṃ taritvā pāraṃ gacchanto viya na kilamati. Sukkhavipassako pana pakiṇṇakasaṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ gaṇhanto bāhubalena sotaṃ chinditvā pāraṃ gacchanto viya kilamati. Iti imassa sukkhavipassakassa arahattaṃ pucchāmīti pucchati. Ariyasāvakoti sukkhavipassako ariyasāvako. Ayañhi heṭṭhā aṭṭhahi bhikkhūhi paññavantataro tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ attano cāti navannampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ekato katvā sammasati. Esa sakkāyo yāvatā sakkāyoti yattako tebhūmakavaṭṭasaṅkhāto sakkāyo nāma atthi, sabbopi so esa sakkāyo, na ito paraṃ sakkāyo atthīti paṭisañcikkhati.

Katamo pana, bhante, ariyo vimokkho Ariyasāvako Esa sakkāyo yāvatā sakkāyo

Etaṃamataṃ yadidaṃ anupādā cittassa vimokkhoti yo panesa cittassa anupādāvimokkho nāma, etaṃ amataṃ etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītanti paṭisañcikkhati. Aññattha ca ‘‘anupādā cittassa vimokkho’’ti nibbānaṃ vuccati. Imasmiṃ pana sutte sukkhavipassakassa arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

Etaṃ amataṃ yadidaṃ anupādā cittassa vimokkho

Kevalaṃ pana imasmiṃ sutte sattasu ṭhānesu osakkanā kathitā, aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu paṭisandhi, navasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ tāva pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa bhikkhuno osakkanā kathitā, paṭisandhi kathitā, arahattaṃ kathitaṃ, tathā catutthajjhānaṃ, tathā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ pana padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā ṭhitānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ osakkanā kathitā, paṭisandhi kathitā, arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Tathā ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa bhikkhuno. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ṭhitassa pana osakkanā natthi, paṭisandhi pana arahattañca kathitaṃ. Sukkhavipassakassa arahattameva kathitanti. Evaṃ sattasu ṭhānesu osakkanā kathitā, aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu paṭisandhi, navasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ. Imañca pana sattasu ṭhānesu osakkanaṃ aṭṭhasu paṭisandhiṃ navasu arahattaṃ samodhānetvā kathentena imaṃ āneñjasappāyasuttaṃ sukathitaṃ nāma hotīti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Āneñjasappāyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
73. "Relying on, relying on" means relying on that particular attainment.

"The crossing over the flood has been declared" means the crossing over the flood has been spoken of. The crossing over the flood has been spoken of for the monk who, having established the third jhāna as a foundation, remains...pe... It says that the crossing over the flood has been spoken of for the monk who, having established the realm of neither perception nor non-perception as a foundation, remains.

"But what, venerable sir, is the noble liberation?" Here, what is he asking? The monk who, having made attainment the basis and developed insight, attains arahantship, does not become weary, like one crossing the great flood relying on a boat or a raft and going to the other shore.

But the dry-insightful one, having comprehended the scattered formations and attained arahantship, becomes weary, like one cutting off the stream by the strength of his arm and going to the other shore. Thus, he asks, "I am asking about the arahantship of this dry-insightful one."

"A noble disciple" means a dry-insightful one is a noble disciple. For he is more wise than the eight monks below, and he comprehends the nine meditation subjects, namely, his own and those of the monks, having made them one.

"This is the existing body, as far as there is an existing body" means as much as there is an existing body, known as the round of existence in the three realms, all of that is this existing body. He reflects, "There is no existing body beyond this."

"But what, venerable sir, is the noble liberation?" "A noble disciple" "This is the existing body, as far as there is an existing body"

"This is the Deathless, that is, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging" means he reflects, "That which is the liberation of the mind through non-clinging, this is the Deathless, this is peace, this is excellent."

And elsewhere, "The liberation of the mind through non-clinging" is called Nibbāna.

In this sutta, the arahantship of the dry-insightful one is spoken of. The rest is clear throughout.

"This is the Deathless, that is, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging"

However, it should be understood that in this sutta, falling away is spoken of in seven places, rebirth in eight places, and arahantship in nine places.

How? Falling away is spoken of for the monk who, having established the third jhāna as a foundation, remains. Rebirth is spoken of, arahantship is spoken of, and likewise for the fourth jhāna, and likewise for the realm of infinite space.

But for the three monks who, having established the realm of infinite consciousness as a basis, remain, falling away is spoken of, rebirth is spoken of, arahantship is spoken of.

Likewise, for the monk who, having established the realm of nothingness as a foundation, remains.

However, for the one who, having established the realm of neither perception nor non-perception as a foundation, remains, there is no falling away, but rebirth and arahantship are spoken of.

Only the arahantship of the dry-insightful one is spoken of.

Thus, it should be understood that falling away is spoken of in seven places, rebirth in eight places, and arahantship in nine places.

By relating this falling away in seven places, rebirth in eight places, and arahantship in nine places, this Āneñjasappāyasutta is said to be well-spoken.

The Commentary on the Āneñjasappāyasutta is Finished.

mula_pali:
74. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde. Atha kho gaṇakamoggallāno gaṇakamoggalāno (ka.) brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho gaṇakamoggallāno brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, imassa migāramātupāsādassa dissati anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā yadidaṃ – yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarāः imesampi hi, bho gotama, brāhmaṇānaṃ dissati anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā yadidaṃ – ajjheneः imesampi hi, bho gotama, issāsānaṃ dissati anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā yadidaṃ – issatthe issatte (ka.). Amhākampi hi, bho gotama, gaṇakānaṃ gaṇanājīvānaṃ dissati anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā yadidaṃ – saṅkhāne. Mayañhi, bho gotama, antevāsiṃ labhitvā paṭhamaṃ evaṃ gaṇāpema – ‘ekaṃ ekakaṃ, dve dukā, tīṇi tikā, cattāri catukkā, pañca pañcakā, cha chakkā, satta sattakā, aṭṭha aṭṭhakā, nava navakā, dasa dasakā’ti; satampi mayaṃ, bho gotama, gaṇāpema, bhiyyopi gaṇāpema. Sakkā nu kho, bho gotama, imasmimpi dhammavinaye evameva anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā paññapetu’’nti?

issatte (ka.)
mula_english:
Thus I have heard: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Śrāvastī, in the Eastern Park, at the palace of Migāra's mother.

Then Gaṇakamoggallāna, the Brahmin, went to where the Blessed One was; having gone there, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.

Having exchanged courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, Gaṇakamoggallāna, the Brahmin, said this to the Blessed One:

“Just as, Master Gotama, a gradual training, a gradual doing, a gradual practice is evident in this palace of Migāra's mother, that is, up to the final staircase, so too, Master Gotama, a gradual training, a gradual doing, a gradual practice is evident among the Brahmins, that is, study; so too, Master Gotama, a gradual training, a gradual doing, a gradual practice is evident among archers, that is, archery.

So too, Master Gotama, a gradual training, a gradual doing, a gradual practice is evident among us accountants who live by calculation, that is, reckoning.

For, Master Gotama, having obtained a student, we first have them count like this: ‘One one, two twos, three threes, four fours, five fives, six sixes, seven sevens, eight eights, nine nines, ten tens.’ We have them count up to a hundred, Master Gotama, and even more.”

“Is it possible, Master Gotama, in this Dharma and Discipline too, to establish a gradual training, a gradual doing, a gradual practice?”
commentary_pali: 74.Evaṃme sutanti gaṇakamoggallānasuttaṃ. Tattha yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarāti yāva paṭhamasopānaphalakā ekadivaseneva sattabhūmiko pāsādo na sakkā kātuṃ, vatthuṃ sodhetvā thambhussāpanato paṭṭhāya pana yāva cittakammakaraṇā anupubbakiriyā cettha paññāyatīti dasseti. Yadidaṃ ajjheneti tayopi vedā na sakkā ekadivaseneva adhīyituṃ, etesaṃ ajjhenepi pana anupubbakiriyāva paññāyatīti dasseti. Issattheti āvudhavijjāyapi ekadivaseneva vālavedhi nāma na sakkā kātuṃ, ṭhānasampādanamuṭṭhikaraṇādīhi pana etthāpi anupubbakiriyā paññāyatīti dasseti. Saṅkhāneti gaṇanāya. Tattha anupubbakiriyaṃ attanāva dassento evaṃ gaṇāpemātiādimāha.
commentary_english:
74.
Thus, "me sutaṃ" means the Gaṇakamoggallānasuttaṃ.
There, "yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarā" means just as a seven-storied palace cannot be built in a single day starting from the first step-platform, but rather from purifying the site, erecting pillars, and up to doing decorative work, a gradual process (anupubbakiriyā) is evident here; this is what it shows.
"yadidaṃ ajjhene" means just as the three Vedas cannot be studied in a single day, but rather in their study also a gradual process is evident; this is what it shows.
"issatthe" means just as the feat of piercing a hair with an arrow (vālavedhi) cannot be done in a single day even in the science of weapons, but rather a gradual process is evident here involving achieving a stance, fist-making, and so forth; this is what it shows.
"saṅkhāne" means by calculation (gaṇanāya).
There, while showing the gradual process by himself, he says "evaṃ gaṇāpemā" and so forth.

mula_pali:
75. ‘‘Sakkā , brāhmaṇa, imasmimpi dhammavinaye anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā paññapetuṃ. Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, dakkho assadammako bhaddaṃ assājānīyaṃ labhitvā paṭhameneva mukhādhāne kāraṇaṃ kāreti, atha uttariṃ kāraṇaṃ kāreti; evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, tathāgato purisadammaṃ labhitvā paṭhamaṃ evaṃ vineti – ‘ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, sīlavā hohi, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharāhi ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, samādāya sikkhassu sikkhāpadesū’’’ti.

‘‘Yato kho, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu, tamenaṃ tathāgato uttariṃ vineti – ‘ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, indriyesu guttadvāro hohi, cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā mā nimittaggāhī hohi mānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjāhi; rakkhāhi cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjāhi. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya mā nimittaggāhī hohi mānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjāhi; rakkhāhi manindriyaṃ, manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjāhī’’’ti.

‘‘Yato kho, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hoti, tamenaṃ tathāgato uttariṃ vineti – ‘ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, bhojane mattaññū hohi. Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāreyyāsi – neva davāya na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya, yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāya vihiṃsūparatiyā brahmacariyānuggahāya – iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi, navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi, yātrā ca me bhavissati anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cā’’’ti.

‘‘Yato kho, brāhmaṇa , bhikkhu bhojane mattaññū hoti, tamenaṃ tathāgato uttariṃ vineti – ‘ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, jāgariyaṃ anuyutto viharāhi, divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhehi, rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhehi, rattiyā majjhimaṃ yāmaṃ dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappeyyāsi pāde pādaṃ accādhāya sato sampajāno uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasikaritvā, rattiyā pacchimaṃ yāmaṃ paccuṭṭhāya caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhehī’’’ti.

‘‘Yato kho, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti, tamenaṃ tathāgato uttariṃ vineti – ‘ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, satisampajaññena samannāgato hohi, abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī , ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī , uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī’’’ti.

‘‘Yato kho, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu satisampajaññena samannāgato hoti, tamenaṃ tathāgato uttariṃ vineti – ‘ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajāhi araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanapatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñja’nti. So vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanappatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñjaṃ. So pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā, ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya, parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So abhijjhaṃ loke pahāya vigatābhijjhena cetasā viharati, abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti; byāpādapadosaṃ pahāya abyāpannacitto viharati sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī, byāpādapadosā cittaṃ parisodheti; thinamiddhaṃ thīnamiddhaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) pahāya vigatathinamiddho viharati ālokasaññī sato sampajāno, thinamiddhā cittaṃ parisodheti; uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahāya anuddhato viharati ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto, uddhaccakukkuccā cittaṃ parisodheti; vicikicchaṃ pahāya tiṇṇavicikiccho viharati akathaṃkathī kusalesu dhammesu, vicikicchāya cittaṃ parisodheti.

thīnamiddhaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)
mula_english:
75. “It is possible, brahmin, to describe gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress in this *Dhamma* and Discipline. Just as, brahmin, when a clever horse-trainer obtains a fine thoroughbred colt, he first makes him get used to wearing the bit, and afterwards trains him further, so when the *Tathāgata* obtains a person to be tamed he first disciplines him thus: ‘Come, *bhikkhu*, be virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*, be perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, train by undertaking the training precepts.’”

“When, brahmin, the *bhikkhu* is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, trains by undertaking the training precepts, then the *Tathāgata* disciplines him further: ‘Come, *bhikkhu*, guard the doors of your sense faculties. On seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if you were to leave the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the eye faculty, undertake the restraint of the eye faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear…On smelling an odour with the nose…On tasting a flavour with the tongue…On touching a tangible with the body…On cognizing a mind-object with the mind, do not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if you were to leave the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the mind faculty, undertake the restraint of the mind faculty.’”

“When, brahmin, the *bhikkhu* guards the doors of his sense faculties, then the *Tathāgata* disciplines him further: ‘Come, *bhikkhu*, be moderate in eating. Reflecting wisely, you should take food neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, considering: “Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings and I shall be healthy and blameless and shall live in comfort.”’”

“When, brahmin, the *bhikkhu* is moderate in eating, then the *Tathāgata* disciplines him further: ‘Come, *bhikkhu*, be devoted to wakefulness. During the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive states. In the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive states. In the middle watch of the night you should lie down on the right side in fhe lion’s pose with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and fully aware, focusing on the idea of rising [at the proper time]. In the last watch of the night, on getting up, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive states.’”

“When, brahmin, the *bhikkhu* possesses mindfulness and full awareness, then the *Tathāgata* disciplines him further: ‘Come, *bhikkhu*, be one who acts with full awareness in going forward and returning; in looking ahead and looking around; in drawing in and stretching out [his limbs]; in wearing his outer robe, bowl, and robe; in eating, drinking, consuming, and tasting; in evacuating the bowels and urinating; in walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.’”

“When, brahmin, the *bhikkhu* possesses mindfulness and full awareness, then the *Tathāgata* disciplines him further: ‘Come, *bhikkhu*, resort to a secluded resting place: the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.’ He resorts to a secluded resting place: the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw. After his meal, on returning from his alms round, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect and establishing mindfulness before him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Abandoning ill will and hatred, he abides with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Abandoning sloth and torpor, he abides free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he abides unagitated, with a mind inwardly stilled; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he abides having overcome doubt, without perplexity about wholesome *dharmas*; he purifies his mind from doubt."
commentary_pali: 75.Seyyathāpi brāhmaṇāti idha bhagavā yasmā bāhirasamaye yathā yathā sippaṃ uggaṇhanti, tathā tathā kerāṭikā honti, tasmā attano sāsanaṃ bāhirasamayena anupametvā bhadraassājānīyena upamento seyyathāpītiādimāha. Bhadro hi assājānīyo yasmiṃ kāraṇe damito hoti, taṃ jīvitahetupi nātikkamati. Evameva sāsane sammāpaṭipanno kulaputto sīlavelaṃ nātikkamati. Mukhādhāneti mukhaṭṭhapane.
commentary_english:
"Just as, brāhmaṇas," here, the Blessed One, because in external doctrines, however much skill they learn, so much are they deceitful; therefore, without comparing his own teaching with external doctrines, but comparing it with a thoroughbred, he said, "Just as," etc.

Indeed, a thoroughbred, in whatever cause he is trained, does not transgress that, even for the sake of his life.

Just so, a clansman who has rightly entered the teaching does not transgress the boundary of morality (śīla).

"In placing the mouth (mukhādhāne)," is placing the mouth.

mula_pali:
76. ‘‘So ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati.

‘‘Ye kho te, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhū sekkhā sekhā (sabbattha) apattamānasā anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ patthayamānā viharanti tesu me ayaṃ evarūpī anusāsanī hoti. Ye pana te bhikkhū arahanto khīṇāsavā vusitavanto katakaraṇīyā ohitabhārā anuppattasadatthā parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanā sammadaññā vimuttā tesaṃ ime dhammā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya ceva saṃvattanti, satisampajaññāya cā’’ti.

sekhā (sabbattha)

Evaṃ vutte, gaṇakamoggallāno brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘kiṃ nu kho bhoto gotamassa sāvakā bhotā gotamena evaṃ ovadīyamānā evaṃ anusāsīyamānā sabbe accantaṃ niṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ ārādhenti udāhu ekacce nārādhentī’’ti? ‘‘Appekacce kho, brāhmaṇa, mama sāvakā mayā evaṃ ovadīyamānā evaṃ anusāsīyamānā accantaṃ niṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ ārādhenti, ekacce nārādhentī’’ti.

‘‘Ko nu kho, bho gotama, hetu ko paccayo yaṃ tiṭṭhateva nibbānaṃ, tiṭṭhati nibbānagāmī maggo, tiṭṭhati bhavaṃ gotamo samādapetā; atha ca pana bhoto gotamassa sāvakā bhotā gotamena evaṃ ovadīyamānā evaṃ anusāsīyamānā appekacce accantaṃ niṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ ārādhenti, ekacce nārādhentī’’ti?
mula_english:
76. “Having thus abandoned these five hindrances ( *pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya*), imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and abides in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ*), with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion (*vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ*).

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*), he enters upon and abides in the second *jhāna*, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind…

With the fading away as well of rapture (*pītiyā ca virāgā*), he enters upon and abides in the third *jhāna*.

With the abandoning of pleasure and pain (*sukhassa ca pahānā*), he enters upon and abides in the fourth *jhāna*.

“Those monks, O Brahmin, who are trainees (*sekkhā*) still striving in their minds, wishing for the unsurpassed security from bondage (*anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ patthayamānā viharanti*), for them, this is the kind of instruction I give. Those monks, however, who are *arahants*, with taints destroyed (*khīṇāsavā*), who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and are completely liberated through final knowledge (*sammad-aññā vimuttā*), these things conduce both to a pleasant abiding here and now (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya ceva saṃvattanti*) and to mindfulness and full awareness (*satisampajaññāya ca*).”

When this was said, the Brahmin Gaṇakamoggallāna said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, when your disciples are thus advised and instructed by you, do they all attain the ultimate goal, *Nirvāṇa* (*nibbānaṃ ārādhenti*), or do some not attain it?” “When, O Brahmin, my disciples are thus advised and instructed by me, some of them attain the ultimate goal, *Nirvāṇa*, and some do not attain it.”

“Master Gotama, what is the cause and reason why, even though *Nirvāṇa* exists, the path leading to *Nirvāṇa* exists, and Master Gotama exists as the guide, some of your disciples who are thus advised and instructed by you attain the ultimate goal, *Nirvāṇa*, while others do not?”
commentary_pali:
76.Satisampajaññāya cāti satisampajaññāhi samaṅgibhāvatthāya . Dve hi khīṇāsavā satatavihārī ca nosatatavihārī ca. Tattha satatavihārī yaṃkiñci kammaṃ katvāpi phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjituṃ sakkoti, no satatavihārī pana appamattakepi kicce kiccappasuto hutvā phalasamāpattiṃ appetuṃ na sakkoti.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira khīṇāsavatthero khīṇāsavasāmaṇeraṃ gahetvā araññavāsaṃ gato, tattha mahātherassa senāsanaṃ pattaṃ, sāmaṇerassa na pāpuṇāti, taṃ vitakkento thero ekadivasampi phalasamāpattiṃ appetuṃ nāsakkhi. Sāmaṇero pana temāsaṃ phalasamāpattiratiyā vītināmetvā ‘‘sappāyo , bhante, araññavāso jāto’’ti theraṃ pucchi. Thero ‘‘na jāto, āvuso’’ti āha. Iti yo evarūpo khīṇāsavo, so ime dhamme ādito paṭṭhāya āvajjitvāva samāpajjituṃ sakkhissatīti dassento ‘‘satisampajaññāya cā’’ti āha.
commentary_english:
76. *Satisampajaññāya ca* means for the sake of being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.

There are two types of those with taints destroyed: those who constantly abide and those who do not constantly abide.

There, the one who constantly abides, even having done some action, is able to attain the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*), but the one who does not constantly abide, even with a small task, having become intent on the task, is not able to attain the fruition-attainment.

This is the story there: It is said that once, an elder whose taints were destroyed, having taken a novice whose taints were destroyed, went to live in the forest. There, the seat was obtained by the great elder, but the novice did not obtain it. The elder, considering this, was not able to attain the fruition-attainment even for a single day.
