‘Sāriputta, forms cognizable by the eye are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’ So it was said by the Blessed One with reference to this.

<pb ed="p" n="3.0056"/> <pb ed="m" n="3.0103"/> “Sāriputta, sounds cognizable by the ear... Venerable sir... Such sounds cognizable by the ear should not be cultivated... Such sounds cognizable by the ear should be cultivated... Such odours cognizable by the nose should not be cultivated... Such <pb ed="p" n="3.0057"/> odours cognizable by the nose should be cultivated... Such flavours cognizable by the tongue should not be cultivated... Such <pb ed="t" n="3.0160"/> flavours cognizable by the tongue should be cultivated... Sāriputta, tangibles cognizable by the body <pb ed="v" n="3.0104"/>... Such tangibles cognizable by the body should not be cultivated... Such tangibles cognizable by the body should be cultivated."

<pb ed="p" n="3.0057"/> <pb ed="t" n="3.0160"/> <pb ed="v" n="3.0104"/> "Sāriputta, mind-objects cognizable by the mind are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.' So it was said by the Blessed One.

What was said with reference to what? Venerable sir, such mind-objects cognizable by the mind, if, in one who cultivates them, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish, such <pb ed="p" n="3.0058"/> mind-objects cognizable by the mind should not be cultivated; but such mind-objects cognizable by the mind, if, in one who cultivates them, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase, such mind-objects cognizable by the mind should be cultivated.

'Sāriputta, mind-objects cognizable by the mind are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.' So it was said by the Blessed One with reference to this.

Venerable sir, I understand the detailed meaning of the Blessed One’s utterance, which he has spoken in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, to be thus.”
commentary_pali:
119.Cakkhuviññeyyantiādīsu yasmā ekaccassa tasmiṃyeva rūpe rāgādayo uppajjanti, abhinandati assādeti, abhinandanto assādento anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇāti, ekaccassa nuppajjanti, nibbindati virajjati, nibbindanto virajjanto nibbutiṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā ‘‘tañca aññamañña’’nti na vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyyunti ettha ke bhagavato imassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti, ke na ājānantīti? Ye tāva imassa suttassa pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca uggaṇhitvā takkarā na honti, yathāvuttaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃ na paṭipajjanti, te na ājānanti nāma. Ye pana takkarā honti, yathāvuttaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjanti, te ājānanti nāma. Evaṃ santepi sapaṭisandhikānaṃ tāva dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hotu, appaṭisandhikānaṃ kathaṃ hotīti. Appaṭisandhikā anupādānā viya jātavedā parinibbāyanti, kappasatasahassānampi accayena tesaṃ puna dukkhaṃ nāma natthi. Iti ekaṃsena tesaṃyeva dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyyu

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Sevitabbāsevitabbasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
119. Because, in the case of things knowable by the eye ( *cakkhuviññeyya* ) and so on, liking and other passions arise in one person for that very form, he welcomes it and savors it; while welcoming it and savoring it, he encounters misfortune and ruin; but in the case of another person, they do not arise, he is disenchanted with it and becomes detached from it; and being disenchanted and detached, he attains *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it was not said "both are mutually..."

This method applies to all the other cases.

Those who understand in detail the meaning in this way—who are they who understand the meaning of what the Blessed One said, and who are they who do not understand it? Those who, having learned the text (*pāḷi*) and commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) of this *sūtra*, are not speculative thinkers, and do not practice the *anulomapaṭipadā* as it has been described, they do not understand it.

But those who are speculative thinkers, and practice the *anulomapaṭipadā* as it has been described, they understand it.

Even so, may it be for the long-term benefit and happiness of those who are bound to rebirth; but how can it be for those who are not bound to rebirth?

Those not bound to rebirth are like fire, without fuel, they are fully extinguished; after the lapse of hundreds of thousands of *kalpas*, suffering no longer exists for them.

Thus, with certainty, it is for the long-term benefit and happiness of those very beings.

The rest is clear throughout.

Thus, understanding the meaning in detail.

The commentary to the *Majjhimanikāya* entitled *Papañcasūdanī*.

The exposition of the *Sevitabbāsevitabbasutta* is finished.

mula_pali:
120. ‘‘Sādhu sādhu, sāriputta! Sādhu kho tvaṃ, sāriputta, imassa mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa, vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa, evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāsi. ‘Cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ mayā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Yathārūpaṃ, sāriputta, cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti evarūpaṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ na sevitabbaṃ; yathārūpañca kho, sāriputta, cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti evarūpaṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ sevitabbaṃ. ‘Cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ mayā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

‘‘Sotaviññeyyaṃ saddaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta…pe… evarūpo sotaviññeyyo saddo na sevitabbo… evarūpo sotaviññeyyo saddo sevitabbo… evarūpo ghānaviññeyyo gandho na sevitabbo… evarūpo ghānaviññeyyo gandho sevitabbo… evarūpo jivhāviññeyyo raso na sevitabbo… evarūpo jivhāviññeyyo raso sevitabbo… evarūpo kāyaviññeyyo phoṭṭhabbo na sevitabbo… evarūpo kāyaviññeyyo phoṭṭhabbo sevitabbo.

‘‘Manoviññeyyaṃ dhammaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta…pe… evarūpo manoviññeyyo dhammo na sevitabbo… evarūpo manoviññeyyo dhammo sevitabbo. ‘Manoviññeyyaṃ dhammaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ mayā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Imassa kho, sāriputta, mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo.
mula_english:
It is good, Sāriputta! It is good that you, Sāriputta, understand thus in detail the meaning of my utterance, which I spoke in brief, without expounding the detailed meaning.

'Sāriputta, forms cognizable by the eye (cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ) are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated (sevitabbaṃ) and not to be cultivated (asevitabbaṃ).' So it was said by me.

And what was said with reference to this? Sāriputta, such forms cognizable by the eye (cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ) as cause unwholesome states (akusalā dhammā) to increase (abhivaḍḍhanti) and wholesome states (kusalā dhammā) to diminish (parihāyanti) in one who cultivates them should not be cultivated (na sevitabbaṃ); but such forms cognizable by the eye (cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ) as cause unwholesome states (akusalā dhammā) to diminish (parihāyanti) and wholesome states (kusalā dhammā) to increase (abhivaḍḍhanti) in one who cultivates them should be cultivated (sevitabbaṃ).

‘Sāriputta, forms cognizable by the eye (cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ) are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated (sevitabbaṃ) and not to be cultivated (asevitabbaṃ).' So it was with reference to this that what was said by me was spoken.

‘Sāriputta, sounds cognizable by the ear (sotaviññeyyaṃ saddaṃ)...pe... such sounds cognizable by the ear (sotaviññeyyo saddo) should not be cultivated (na sevitabbo)... such sounds cognizable by the ear (sotaviññeyyo saddo) should be cultivated (sevitabbo)... such odours cognizable by the nose (ghānaviññeyyo gandho) should not be cultivated (na sevitabbo)... such odours cognizable by the nose (ghānaviññeyyo gandho) should be cultivated (sevitabbo)... such flavours cognizable by the tongue (jivhāviññeyyo raso) should not be cultivated (na sevitabbo)... such flavours cognizable by the tongue (jivhāviññeyyo raso) should be cultivated (sevitabbo)... such tangibles cognizable by the body (kāyaviññeyyo phoṭṭhabbo) should not be cultivated (na sevitabbo)... such tangibles cognizable by the body (kāyaviññeyyo phoṭṭhabbo) should be cultivated (sevitabbo).’

‘Sāriputta, mind-objects cognizable by the mind (manoviññeyyaṃ dhammaṃ)...pe... such mind-objects cognizable by the mind (manoviññeyyo dhammo) should not be cultivated (na sevitabbo)... such mind-objects cognizable by the mind (manoviññeyyo dhammo) should be cultivated (sevitabbo).’

'Sāriputta, mind-objects cognizable by the mind (manoviññeyyaṃ dhammaṃ) are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated (sevitabbaṃ) and not to be cultivated (asevitabbaṃ).' So it was with reference to this that what was said by me was spoken.

Sariputta, the detailed meaning of my utterance, which I spoke in brief, should be regarded thus.

mula_pali:
121. ‘‘Cīvaraṃpāhaṃ , sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampi…pe… piṇḍapātaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta… senāsanaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta… gāmaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta… nigamaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta… nagaraṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta… janapadaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta… puggalaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’’ti.

Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā sāriputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘imassa kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa, vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa, evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmi. ‘Cīvaraṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Yathārūpaṃ, bhante, cīvaraṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti evarūpaṃ cīvaraṃ na sevitabbaṃ; yathārūpañca kho, bhante, cīvaraṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti evarūpaṃ cīvaraṃ sevitabbaṃ. ‘Cīvaraṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

‘‘Piṇḍapātaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta…pe… evarūpo piṇḍapāto na sevitabbo… evarūpo piṇḍapāto sevitabbo… senāsanaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta…pe… evarūpaṃ senāsanaṃ na sevitabbaṃ… evarūpaṃ senāsanaṃ sevitabbaṃ… gāmaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta …pe… evarūpo gāmo na sevitabbo… evarūpo gāmo sevitabbo… evarūpo nigamo na sevitabbo… evarūpo nigamo sevitabbo… evarūpaṃ nagaraṃ na sevitabbaṃ… evarūpaṃ nagaraṃ sevitabbaṃ… evarūpo janapado na sevitabbo… evarūpo janapado sevitabbo.

‘‘‘Puggalaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Yathārūpaṃ, bhante, puggalaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti evarūpo puggalo na sevitabbo; yathārūpañca kho, bhante, puggalaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti evarūpo puggalo sevitabbo. ‘Puggalaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttanti. Imassa kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa, vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmī’’ti.
mula_english:
121. “Sāriputta, robes (*cīvara*) are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated... Alms food (*piṇḍapāta*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta... Resting place (*senāsana*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta... A village (*gāma*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta... A town (*nigama*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta... A city (*nagara*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta... A district (*janapada*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta... A person (*puggala*) is of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated."

When this was said, the venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I understand the detailed meaning of the Blessed One’s utterance, which he has spoken in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, to be thus: ‘Sāriputta, robes are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’ So it was said by the Blessed One.

What was said with reference to this? Venerable sir, such robes as cause unwholesome states (*akusala dharma*) to increase and wholesome states (*kusala dharma*) to diminish in one who cultivates them should not be cultivated; but such robes as cause unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase in one who cultivates them should be cultivated.

“So it was with reference to this that it was said by the Blessed One: ‘Sāriputta, robes are of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’

“Alms food (*piṇḍapāta*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta… Alms food of this kind should not be cultivated… Alms food (*piṇḍapāta*) of this kind should be cultivated… Resting place (*senāsana*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta… Resting place (*senāsana*) of this kind should not be cultivated… Resting place (*senāsana*) of this kind should be cultivated… A village (*gāma*) is of two kinds, I say, Sāriputta… A village (*gāma*) of this kind should not be cultivated… A village (*gāma*) of this kind should be cultivated… A town (*nigama*) is of two kinds, I say… A town (*nigama*) of this kind should not be cultivated… A town (*nigama*) of this kind should be cultivated… A city (*nagara*) is of two kinds, I say… A city (*nagara*) of this kind should not be cultivated… A city (*nagara*) of this kind should be cultivated… A district (*janapada*) is of two kinds, I say… A district (*janapada*) of this kind should not be cultivated… A district (*janapada*) of this kind should be cultivated.

“'Sāriputta, a person (*puggala*) is of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.' So it was said by the Blessed One.

What was said with reference to this? Venerable sir, association with such persons as causes unwholesome states (*akusala dharma*) to increase and wholesome states (*kusala dharma*) to diminish should not be cultivated; but association with such persons as causes unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase should be cultivated.

“So it was with reference to this that it was said by the Blessed One: ‘Sāriputta, a person (*puggala*) is of two kinds, I say: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’

“Venerable sir, I understand the detailed meaning of the Blessed One’s utterance, which he has spoken in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, to be thus.”

mula_pali:
122. ‘‘Sādhu sādhu, sāriputta! Sādhu kho tvaṃ, sāriputta, imassa mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa, vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāsi. ‘Cīvaraṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi , asevitabbampī’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ mayā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Yathārūpaṃ, sāriputta, cīvaraṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti evarūpaṃ cīvaraṃ na sevitabbaṃ; yathārūpañca kho, sāriputta, cīvaraṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti evarūpaṃ cīvaraṃ sevitabbaṃ. ‘Cīvaraṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ mayā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. (Yathā paṭhamaṃ tathā vitthāretabbaṃ) evarūpo piṇḍapāto… evarūpaṃ senāsanaṃ… evarūpo gāmo… evarūpo nigamo… evarūpaṃ nagaraṃ… evarūpo janapado.

‘‘‘Puggalaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ mayā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Yathārūpaṃ, sāriputta, puggalaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti evarūpo puggalo na sevitabbo; yathārūpañca kho, sāriputta, puggalaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti evarūpo puggalo sevitabbo. ‘Puggalaṃpāhaṃ, sāriputta, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ mayā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Imassa kho, sāriputta, mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo.
mula_english:
122.
’’Excellent! Excellent, Sāriputta! It is good that you, Sāriputta, understand the detailed meaning of my utterance, which I spoke in brief, without expounding the detailed meaning, to be thus.

‘I say, Sāriputta, that robes are of two kinds: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’ So it was with reference to this that it was said by me.

What was said with reference to this? Sāriputta, such robes as cause unwholesome states (*akuśalā dharma*) to increase and wholesome states (*kuśalā dharma*) to diminish in one who cultivates them should not be cultivated. But such robes as cause unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase in one who cultivates them should be cultivated.

‘I say, Sāriputta, that robes are of two kinds: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’ So it was with reference to this that it was said by me.

(As before, so it should be expounded in detail.) Such almsfood… such a resting place… such a village… such a town… such a city… such a district.

‘‘‘I say, Sāriputta, that persons (*pudgala*) are of two kinds: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’ So it was with reference to this that it was said by me.

What was said with reference to this? Sāriputta, association with such persons as causes unwholesome states (*akuśalā dharma*) to increase and wholesome states (*kuśalā dharma*) to diminish in one who cultivates it should not be cultivated. But association with such persons as causes unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase in one who cultivates it should be cultivated.

‘I say, Sāriputta, that persons (*pudgala*) are of two kinds: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’ So it was with reference to this that it was said by me.

Sāriputta, the detailed meaning of my utterance, which I spoke in brief, should be regarded thus.

mula_pali:
123. ‘‘Sabbepi ce, sāriputta, khattiyā imassa mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyyuṃ, sabbesānampissa khattiyānaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya. Sabbepi ce , sāriputta, brāhmaṇā…pe… sabbepi ce, sāriputta, vessā… sabbepi ce, sāriputta, suddā imassa mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyyuṃ, sabbesānampissa suddānaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya. Sadevakopi ce, sāriputta, loko samārako sabrahmako sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā sadevamanussā imassa mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyya, sadevakassapissa lokassa samārakassa sabrahmakassa sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā sāriputto bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Sevitabbāsevitabbasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.
mula_english:
“Sāriputta, if all nobles understood thus the detailed meaning of my utterance, which I spoke in brief, it would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.

Sāriputta, if all *brāhmaṇas*… all *vaiśyas*…all *śūdras* understood thus the meaning of my utterance, which I spoke in brief, it would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.

If the world with its gods ( *sadevaka*), its Māras ( *samāraka*), and its Brahmās ( *sabrahmaka*), this generation with its ascetics (*śramaṇa*) and *brāhmaṇas*, its princes and its people, understood thus the detailed meaning of my utterance, which I spoke in brief, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of the world for a long time.”

This is what the Blessed One said.

The venerable Sāriputta was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

The fourth discourse, the Sevitabbāsevitabbasuttaṃ, is finished.

mula_pali:
124. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘bhikkhavo’’ti. ‘‘Bhadante’’ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

‘‘Yāni kānici, bhikkhave, bhayāni uppajjanti sabbāni tāni bālato uppajjanti, no paṇḍitato; ye keci upaddavā uppajjanti sabbe te bālato uppajjanti, no paṇḍitato; ye keci upasaggā uppajjanti sabbe te bālato uppajjanti, no paṇḍitato. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave , naḷāgārā vā tiṇāgārā vā aggi mutto aggimukko (sī. pī.) kūṭāgārānipi dahati ullittāvalittāni nivātāni phusitaggaḷāni pihitavātapānāni; evameva kho, bhikkhave, yāni kānici bhayāni uppajjanti sabbāni tāni bālato uppajjanti, no paṇḍitato; ye keci upaddavā uppajjanti sabbe te bālato uppajjanti, no paṇḍitato; ye keci upasaggā uppajjanti sabbe te bālato uppajjanti, no paṇḍitato. Iti kho, bhikkhave, sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito; saupaddavo bālo, anupaddavo paṇḍito; saupasaggo bālo, anupasaggo paṇḍito. Natthi, bhikkhave, paṇḍitato bhayaṃ, natthi paṇḍitato upaddavo, natthi paṇḍitato upasaggo. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘paṇḍitā bhavissāma vīmaṃsakā’ti – evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabba’’nti.

aggimukko (sī. pī.)

Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, paṇḍito bhikkhu ‘vīmaṃsako’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu dhātukusalo ca hoti, āyatanakusalo ca hoti, paṭiccasamuppādakusalo ca hoti, ṭhānāṭhānakusalo ca hoti – ettāvatā kho, ānanda, paṇḍito bhikkhu ‘vīmaṃsako’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.
mula_english:
[124.] Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One (Bhagavā) was dwelling at Anāthapindika’s monastery, in the Jeta Grove, near Sāvatthi.

There the Fortunate One addressed the monks (bhikkhus), saying: "Monks (bhikkhavo)!"

"Venerable sir (bhadante)," those monks replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, whatever fears (bhayāni) arise, all arise because of the fool (bāla), not because of the wise man (paṇḍita); whatever troubles (upaddavā) arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man; whatever calamities (upasaggā) arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man.

Just as a fire that starts in a shed made of rushes (naḷāgārā) or grass (tiṇāgārā) burns down even a house (kūṭāgārāni) with a peaked roof, with walls plastered (ullittāvalittāni) inside and outside, shut off (nivātāni), secured by bars (phusitaggaḷāni), with shuttered windows (pihitavātapānāni); so too, bhikkhus, whatever fears (bhayāni) arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man; whatever troubles (upaddavā) arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man; whatever calamities (upasaggā) arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man.

Thus, bhikkhus, the fool (bālo) brings fear (sappaṭibhayo), the wise man (paṇḍito) brings no fear (appaṭibhayo); the fool brings trouble (saupaddavo), the wise man brings no trouble (anupaddavo); the fool brings calamity (saupasaggo), the wise man brings no calamity (anupasaggo).

No fear (bhayaṃ) comes from the wise man (paṇḍitato), no trouble (upaddavo) comes from the wise man, no calamity (upasaggo) comes from the wise man.

Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train thus: ‘We shall be wise men (paṇḍitā), we shall be inquirers (vīmaṃsakā).’”

Having said this, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "To what extent, venerable sir (bhante), is a wise bhikkhu (paṇḍito bhikkhu) 'an inquirer' (vīmaṃsako) fit to be called?"

"Ānanda, to the extent that a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements (dhātukusalo), skilled in the sense bases (āyatanakusalo), skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādakusalo), skilled in what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhānakusalo) – to this extent, Ānanda, a wise bhikkhu is ‘an inquirer’ fit to be called."
commentary_pali:
124.Evaṃme sutanti bahudhātukasuttaṃ. Tattha bhayānītiādīsu bhayanti cittutrāso. Upaddavoti anekaggatākāro. Upasaggoti upasaṭṭhākāro tattha tattha lagganākāro. Tesaṃ evaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ – pabbatādivisamanissitā corā janapadavāsīnaṃ pesenti ‘‘mayaṃ asukadivase nāma tumhākaṃ gāmaṃ paharissāmā’’ti. Taṃ pavattiṃ sutakālato paṭṭhāya bhayaṃ santāsaṃ āpajjanti. Ayaṃ cittutrāso nāma. ‘‘Idha no corā kupitā anatthampi āvaheyyu’’nti hatthasāraṃ gahetvā dvipadacatuppadehi saddhiṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha tattha bhūmiyaṃ nipajjanti, ḍaṃsamakasādīhi khajjamānā gumbantarāni pavisanti, khāṇukaṇṭake maddanti. Tesaṃ evaṃ vicarantānaṃ vikkhittabhāvo anekaggatākāro nāma. Tato coresu yathāvutte divase anāgacchantesu ‘‘tucchakasāsanaṃ taṃ bhavissati, gāmaṃ pavisissāmā’’ti saparikkhārā gāmaṃ pavisanti, atha tesaṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā gāmaṃ parivāretvā dvāre aggiṃ datvā manusse ghātetvā corā sabbaṃ vibhavaṃ vilumpetvā gacchanti. Tesu ghātitāvasesā aggiṃ nibbāpetvā koṭṭhacchāyabhitticchāyādīsu tattha tattha laggitvā nisīdanti naṭṭhaṃ anusocamānā. Ayaṃ upasaṭṭhākāro lagganākāro nāma.

Naḷāgārāti naḷehi paricchannā agārā, sesasambhārā panettha rukkhamayā honti. Tiṇāgārepi eseva nayo. Bālato uppajjantīti bālameva nissāya uppajjanti. Bālo hi apaṇḍitapuriso rajjaṃ vā uparajjaṃ vā aññaṃ vā pana mahantaṃ ṭhānaṃ patthento katipaye attanā sadise vidhavāputte mahādhutte gahetvā ‘‘etha ahaṃ tumhe issare karissāmī’’ti pabbatagahanādīni nissāya antante gāme paharanto dāmarikabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā anupubbena nigamepi janapadepi paharati, manussā gehāni chaḍḍetvā khemantaṭṭhānaṃ patthayamānā pakkamanti, te nissāya vasantā bhikkhūpi bhikkhuniyopi attano attano vasanaṭṭhānāni pahāya pakkamanti. Gatagataṭṭhāne bhikkhāpi senāsanampi dullabhaṃ hoti. Evaṃ catunnaṃ parisānaṃ bhayaṃ āgatameva hoti. Pabbajitesupi dve bālā bhikkhū aññamaññaṃ vivādaṃ paṭṭhapetvā codanaṃ ārabhanti . Iti kosambivāsikānaṃ viya mahākalaho uppajjati, catunnaṃ parisānaṃ bhayaṃ āgatameva hotīti evaṃ yāni kānici bhayāni uppajjanti, sabbāni tāni bālato uppajjantīti veditabbāni.

Naḷāgārā Bālato uppajjantī

Etadavocāti bhagavatā dhammadesanā matthakaṃ apāpetvāva niṭṭhāpitā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ dasabalaṃ pucchitvā sabbaññutaññāṇenevassa desanāya pāripūriṃ kareyyanti cintetvā etaṃ ‘‘kittāvatā nu kho, bhante’’tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

Etadavocā
commentary_english:
124. Thus I have heard: the *bahudhātukasutta*.

There, *bhayānī* and so forth, *bhaya* means mental trembling (*cittutrāsa*).

*Upaddavo* means a state of non-singleness of mind (*anekaggatākāro*).

*Upasaggo* means a state of being attached (*upasaṭṭhākāro*), a state of clinging there and there (*tattha tattha lagganākāro*).

Thus, their diversity should be understood: robbers relying on uneven places such as mountains, send [messengers] to the inhabitants of the country, "We, on such and such a day, will strike your village."

From that time of the communication, they encounter fear and dread, starting from when they heard it (*sutakālato*).

This is called mental trembling (*cittutrāso nāma*).

"Here, the angry robbers may bring misfortune," taking the essence of their possessions, entering the forest together with two-footed and four-footed [beings], they lie down there and there on the ground, being eaten by horseflies, mosquitoes, and so on, they enter the interiors of thickets, they trample on stumps and thorns.

Thus, for those wandering in this way, the scattered state is called a state of non-singleness of mind (*anekaggatākāro nāma*).

Then, when the robbers do not come on the day specified, "That teaching of the empty ones will come to pass, we will enter the village," with all their equipment, they enter the village, then, knowing that they have entered, surrounding the village, setting fire to the door, killing the people, the robbers go away plundering all the wealth.

Those remaining after the killing, extinguishing the fire, clinging to the shadows of storehouses, the shadows of walls, etc., sit there and there lamenting what is lost.

This is called a state of being attached (*upasaṭṭhākāro lagganākāro nāma*).

*Naḷāgārā* means houses covered with reeds (*naḷehi paricchannā agārā*), the remaining equipment here is made of trees (*rukkhamayā honti*).

The same rule applies to a grass house (*tiṇāgārepi eseva nayo*).

*Bālato uppajjantī* means arising relying only on the fool (*bālameva nissāya uppajjanti*).

For a fool (*bālo hi*), an unlearned person (*apaṇḍitapuriso*), desiring a kingdom (*rajjaṃ vā*) or a sub-kingdom (*uparajjaṃ vā*) or anything else (*aññaṃ vā*) that is great (*mahantaṃ ṭhānaṃ*), taking a few widow's sons (*vidhavāputte*) like himself (*attanā sadise*), great rogues (*mahādhutte*), "Come, I will make you lords," relying on mountains, dense forests, etc., striking villages at the very borders, making known the state of banditry (*dāmarikabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā*) gradually strikes at market towns and also at districts, people abandoning their homes, desiring a safe place, depart, monks and nuns dwelling in reliance on them, abandoning their own dwelling places, depart.

In places gone and gone, almsfood and lodging are difficult to obtain (*dullabhaṃ hoti*).

Thus, fear has indeed come to the four assemblies (*evaṃ catunnaṃ parisānaṃ bhayaṃ āgatameva hoti*).

Even among those gone forth, two foolish monks having started a dispute with each other, begin accusation.

Thus, like the inhabitants of Kosambī, a great quarrel arises, fear has indeed come to the four assemblies, thus whatever fears arise, all those should be known as arising from the fool (*sabbāni tāni bālato uppajjantīti veditabbāni*).

*Naḷāgārā*, *bālato uppajjantī*.

*Etadavocā* means the teaching of the Dharma (*dhammadesanā*) was completed by the Blessed One (*bhagavatā*) without reaching the summit (*matthakaṃ apāpetvāva niṭṭhāpitā*).

"Indeed, I should ask about the ten powers and by means of the knowledge of omniscience, I should make the teaching complete (*pāripūriṃ kareyyanti*)," thinking this, he spoke this statement beginning with "How far, O Blessed One (*kittāvatā nu kho, bhante*)."

*Etadavocā*.

mula_pali:
125. ‘‘Kittāvatā pana, bhante, ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Aṭṭhārasa kho imā, ānanda, dhātuyo – cakkhudhātu, rūpadhātu, cakkhuviññāṇadhātu; sotadhātu, saddadhātu, sotaviññāṇadhātu; ghānadhātu, gandhadhātu, ghānaviññāṇadhātu; jivhādhātu, rasadhātu, jivhāviññāṇadhātu; kāyadhātu, phoṭṭhabbadhātu, kāyaviññāṇadhātu; manodhātu, dhammadhātu, manoviññāṇadhātu. Imā kho, ānanda, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo yato jānāti passati – ettāvatāpi kho, ānanda, ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.

‘‘Siyā pana, bhante, aññopi pariyāyo, yathā ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Siyā, ānanda. Chayimā, ānanda, dhātuyo – pathavīdhātu, āpodhātu, tejodhātu, vāyodhātu, ākāsadhātu, viññāṇadhātu. Imā kho, ānanda, cha dhātuyo yato jānāti passati – ettāvatāpi kho, ānanda, ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.

‘‘Siyā pana, bhante, aññopi pariyāyo, yathā ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Siyā, ānanda. Chayimā, ānanda, dhātuyo – sukhadhātu , dukkhadhātu, somanassadhātu, domanassadhātu, upekkhādhātu, avijjādhātu. Imā kho, ānanda, cha dhātuyo yato jānāti passati – ettāvatāpi kho, ānanda, ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.

‘‘Siyā pana, bhante, aññopi pariyāyo, yathā ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Siyā, ānanda. Chayimā, ānanda, dhātuyo – kāmadhātu, nekkhammadhātu, byāpādadhātu, abyāpādadhātu, vihiṃsādhātu , avihiṃsādhātu. Imā kho, ānanda, cha dhātuyo yato jānāti passati – ettāvatāpi kho, ānanda, ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.

‘‘Siyā pana, bhante, aññopi pariyāyo, yathā ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Siyā, ānanda. Tisso imā, ānanda, dhātuyo – kāmadhātu, rūpadhātu, arūpadhātu. Imā kho, ānanda, tisso dhātuyo yato jānāti passati – ettāvatāpi kho, ānanda, ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.

‘‘Siyā pana, bhante, aññopi pariyāyo, yathā ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Siyā, ānanda. Dve imā, ānanda, dhātuyo – saṅkhatādhātu, asaṅkhatādhātu. Imā kho, ānanda, dve dhātuyo yato jānāti passati – ettāvatāpi kho, ānanda, ‘dhātukusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.
mula_english:
“But to what extent, venerable sir, is one justified in saying ‘a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements’?”

“There are these eighteen elements (aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo), Ānanda: the eye element (cakkhudhātu), the form element (rūpadhātu), the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu); the ear element (sotadhātu), the sound element (saddadhātu), the ear-consciousness element (sotaviññāṇadhātu); the nose element (ghānadhātu), the odour element (gandhadhātu), the nose-consciousness element (ghānaviññāṇadhātu); the tongue element (jivhādhātu), the flavour element (rasadhātu), the tongue-consciousness element (jivhāviññāṇadhātu); the body element (kāyadhātu), the tangible element (phoṭṭhabbadhātu), the body-consciousness element (kāyaviññāṇadhātu); the mind element (manodhātu), the mind-object element (dhammadhātu), the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). When he knows and sees these eighteen elements, Ānanda, a bhikkhu can be called skilled in the elements.”

“But, venerable sir, could there be any other way in which one could be justified in saying ‘a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements’?”

“There could, Ānanda. There are these six elements (cha dhātuyo): the earth element (pathavīdhātu), the water element (āpodhātu), the fire element (tejodhātu), the air element (vāyodhātu), the space element (ākāsadhātu), and the consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu). When he knows and sees these six elements, Ānanda, a bhikkhu can be called skilled in the elements.”

“But, venerable sir, could there be any other way in which one could be justified in saying ‘a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements’?”

“There could, Ānanda. There are these six elements (cha dhātuyo): the pleasure element (sukhadhātu), the pain element (dukkhadhātu), the joy element (somanassadhātu), the grief element (domanassadhātu), the equanimity element (upekkhādhātu), and the ignorance element (avijjādhātu). When he knows and sees these six elements, Ānanda, a bhikkhu can be called skilled in the elements.”

“But, venerable sir, could there be any other way in which one could be justified in saying ‘a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements’?”

“There could, Ānanda. There are these six elements (cha dhātuyo): the desire element (kāmadhātu), the renunciation element (nekkhammadhātu), the ill-will element (byāpādadhātu), the non-ill-will element (abyāpādadhātu), the harmfulness element (vihiṃsādhātu), [and] the harmlessness element (avihiṃsādhātu). When he knows and sees these six elements, Ānanda, a bhikkhu can be called skilled in the elements.”

“But, venerable sir, could there be any other way in which one could be justified in saying ‘a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements’?”

“There could, Ānanda. There are these three elements (tisso dhātuyo): the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the form realm (rūpadhātu), and the formless realm (arūpadhātu). When he knows and sees these three elements, Ānanda, a bhikkhu can be called skilled in the elements.”

“But, venerable sir, could there be any other way in which one could be justified in saying ‘a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements’?”

“There could, Ānanda. There are these two elements (dve dhātuyo): the conditioned element (saṅkhatādhātu) and the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatādhātu). When he knows and sees these two elements, Ānanda, a bhikkhu can be called skilled in the elements.”
commentary_pali:
125. Aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggaho, aḍḍhaṭṭhamakadhātuyo arūpapariggahoti rūpārūpapariggahova kathito. Sabbāpi khandhavasena pañcakkhandhā honti. Pañcapi khandhā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesaṃ samuṭṭhāpikā taṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccaṃ. Iti catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panetā dhātuyo visuddhimagge kathitāva. Jānāti passatīti saha vipassanāya maggo vutto.

Pathavīdhātuādayo saviññāṇakakāyaṃ suññato nissattato dassetuṃ vuttā. Tāpi purimāhi aṭṭhārasahi dhātūhi pūretabbā. Pūrentena viññāṇadhātuto nīharitvā pūretabbā. Viññāṇadhātu hesā cakkhuviññāṇādivasena chabbidhā hoti. Tattha cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā pariggahitāya tassā vatthu cakkhudhātu, ārammaṇaṃ rūpadhātūti dve dhātuyo pariggahitāva honti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Manoviññāṇadhātuyā pana pariggahitāya tassā purimapacchimavasena manodhātu, ārammaṇavasena dhammadhātūti dve dhātuyo pariggahitāva honti. Iti imāsu aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggahoti purimanayeneva idampi ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti.

Sukhadhātūtiādīsu sukhañca taṃ nissattasuññataṭṭhena dhātu cāti sukhadhātu. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ettha ca purimā catasso dhātuyo sappaṭipakkhavasena gahitā, pacchimā dve sarikkhakavasena. Avibhūtabhāvena hi upekkhādhātu avijjādhātuyā sarikkhā. Ettha ca sukhadukkhadhātūsu pariggahitāsu kāyaviññāṇadhātu pariggahitāva hoti, sesāsu pariggahitāsu manoviññāṇadhātu pariggahitāva hoti. Imāpi cha dhātuyo heṭṭhā aṭṭhārasahiyeva pūretabbā. Pūrentena upekkhādhātuto nīharitvā pūretabbā. Iti imāsu aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggahoti purimanayeneva idampi ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti.

Sukhadhātū

Kāmadhātuādīnaṃ dvedhāvitakke (ma. ni. 1.206) kāmavitakkādīsu vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Abhidhammepi ‘‘tattha katamā kāmadhātu, kāmapaṭisaṃyutto takko vitakko’’tiādinā (vibha. 182) nayeneva etāsaṃ vitthāro āgatoyeva. Imāpi cha dhātuyo heṭṭhā aṭṭhārasahiyeva pūretabbā. Pūrentena kāmadhātuto nīharitvā pūretabbā. Iti imāsu aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggahoti purimanayeneva idampi ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti.

Kāmadhātuādīsu pañca kāmāvacarakkhandhā kāmadhātu nāma, pañca rūpāvacarakkhandhā rūpadhātu nāma, cattāro arūpāvacarakkhandhā arūpadhātu nāma. Abhidhamme pana ‘‘tattha katamā kāmadhātu, heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā’’tiādinā (vibha. 182) nayena etāsaṃ vitthāro āgatoyeva. Imāpi tisso dhātuyo heṭṭhā aṭṭhārasahiyeva pūretabbā. Pūrentena kāmadhātuto nīharitvā pūretabbā. Iti imāsu aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggahoti purimanayeneva idampi ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti.

Saṅkhatāti paccayehi samāgantvā katā, pañcannaṃ khandhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Na saṅkhatā asaṅkhatā. Nibbānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Imāpi dve dhātuyo heṭṭhā aṭṭhārasahiyeva pūretabbā. Pūrentena saṅkhatadhātuto nīharitvā pūretabbā. Iti imāsu aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu aḍḍhekādasadhātuyo rūpapariggahoti purimanayeneva idampi ekassa bhikkhuno niggamanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathitaṃ hoti.

Saṅkhatā asaṅkhatā
commentary_english:
125. Among the eighteen *dhātus*, eleven and a half *dhātus* are included in form (*rūpa*), and six and a half *dhātus* are included in the formless (*arūpa*); thus, the inclusion in form and the formless has been spoken of. All are the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*) in terms of aggregates. The five aggregates are the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasaccaṃ*), the craving that causes them is the truth of origin (*samudayasaccaṃ*), the non-arising of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasaccaṃ*), the practice of knowing cessation is the truth of the path (*maggasaccaṃ*). Thus, the four truths of the foundations of mindfulness are spoken of, bringing the departure of one monk to a conclusion. This is the summary here, but these *dhātus* have already been spoken of in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "He knows and sees" (*jānāti passatī*) means the path together with insight (*vipassanā*) has been spoken of. The earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) and so on have been spoken of to show the conscious body (*saviññāṇakakāyaṃ*) as empty (*suññato*) and without essence (*nissattato*). Those should also be filled with the previous eighteen *dhātus*. When filling, they should be filled by taking them out of the consciousness element (*viññāṇadhātu*). That consciousness element (*viññāṇadhātu*) is sixfold, such as eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) and so on. There, when the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*) is included, its base, the eye element (*cakkhudhātu*), and its object, the form element (*rūpadhātu*) – these two *dhātus* are already included. This method applies to all cases ( *esa nayo sabbattha*). However, when the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) is included, the mind element (*manodhātu*) in terms of previous and subsequent, and the *dharma* element (*dhammadhātu*) in terms of object – these two *dhātus* are already included. Thus, among these eighteen *dhātus*, eleven and a half *dhātus* are included in form (*rūpapariggaho*); in the same way as before, this departure of one monk has been spoken of, bringing it to a conclusion. In *sukhadhātū* etc., *sukha* is *sukha*, and it is a *dhātu* by way of being without essence and empty; therefore, *sukhadhātu*. This method applies to all cases (*esa nayo sabbattha*). Here, the previous four *dhātus* are taken as having an opponent, and the latter two are taken as being similar. Indeed, the equanimity element (*upekkhādhātu*) is similar to the ignorance element (*avijjādhātu*) due to its unmanifest nature. Here, when the pleasure and pain elements (*sukhadukkhadhātūsu*) are included, the body-consciousness element (*kāyaviññāṇadhātu*) is already included; when the remaining ones are included, the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) is already included. These six *dhātus* should also be filled in the same way as the eighteen below. When filling, they should be filled by taking them out of the equanimity element (*upekkhādhātu*). Thus, among these eighteen *dhātus*, eleven and a half *dhātus* are included in form (*rūpapariggaho*); in the same way as before, this departure of one monk has been spoken of, bringing it to a conclusion. The meaning of desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) etc. should be understood in the same way as spoken of in the two kinds of thinking (Dvedhāvitakka) (Ma. Ni. 1.206) and in the desire-thinking etc. Even in the *Abhidhamma*, the expansion of these has already come in the same way as "What is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there? Thinking (*takko*) is connected with desire (*kāmapaṭisaṃyutto*)" etc. (Vibha. 182). These six *dhātus* should also be filled in the same way as the eighteen below. When filling, they should be filled by taking them out of the desire element (*kāmadhātu*). Thus, among these eighteen *dhātus*, eleven and a half *dhātus* are included in form (*rūpapariggaho*); in the same way as before, this departure of one monk has been spoken of, bringing it to a conclusion. Among the desire realm etc., the five aggregates belonging to the desire realm (*pañca kāmāvacarakkhandhā*) are called the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the five aggregates belonging to the form realm (*pañca rūpāvacarakkhandhā*) are called the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the four aggregates belonging to the formless realm (*cattāro arūpāvacarakkhandhā*) are called the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*). Moreover, in the Abhidhamma, it is said, "Which is the *kāmadhātu*? Making the *avīciniraya* the lower limit," etc. (Vibha. 182). The expansion of these comes in this way. These three *dhātus* should also be filled in below in the same way as the eighteen. Having removed the *kāmadhātu* with the one who fills, it should be filled. Thus, in these eighteen *dhātus*, eleven and a half *dhātus* are the inclusion of form. Just as in the previous method, this also is said to bring the departure of a certain *bhikkhu* to its culmination.

*Saṅkhatā* means made by coming together with conditions; this is a designation for the five *khandhas*. Not *saṅkhatā*, *asaṅkhatā*. This is a designation for *nirvāṇa*. These two *dhātus* should also be filled in below in the same way as the eighteen. Having removed the *saṅkhatadhātu* with the one who fills, it should be filled. Thus, in these eighteen *dhātus*, eleven and a half *dhātus* are the inclusion of form. Just as in the previous method, this also is said to bring the departure of a certain *bhikkhu* to its culmination.

*Saṅkhatā* *asaṅkhatā*

mula_pali:
126. ‘‘Kittāvatā pana, bhante, ‘āyatanakusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Cha kho panimāni, ānanda, ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni – cakkhuceva rūpā ca sotañca saddā ca ghānañca gandhā ca jivhā ca rasā ca kāyo ca phoṭṭhabbā ca mano ca dhammā ca. Imāni kho, ānanda, cha ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni yato jānāti passati – ettāvatā kho, ānanda, ‘āyatanakusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.

‘‘Kittāvatā pana, bhante, ‘paṭiccasamuppādakusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Idhānanda, bhikkhu evaṃ pajānāti – ‘imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati, imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhati, yadidaṃ – avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ, saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo , bhavapaccayā jāti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassūpāyāsā sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho, saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho, viññāṇanirodhā nāmarūpanirodho, nāmarūpanirodhā saḷāyatananirodho, saḷāyatananirodhā phassanirodho, phassanirodhā vedanānirodho, vedanānirodhā taṇhānirodho, taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho, upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho, bhavanirodhā jātinirodho, jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassūpāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti’. Ettāvatā kho, ānanda, ‘paṭiccasamuppādakusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti.
mula_english:
126. “In what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu skilled in the sense bases?”

“Ānanda, there are these six internal and external sense bases: the eye and forms (rūpa), the ear and sounds (śabda), the nose and odours (gandha), the tongue and flavours (rasa), the body and tangibles (sparśa), the mind and mind-objects (dharma). Ānanda, when a bhikkhu knows and sees these six internal and external sense bases, in that way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu can be called skilled in the sense bases.”

“In what way, venerable sir, is a *bhikkhu* skilled in dependent origination ( *pratītyasamutpāda*)?”

“Here, Ānanda, a *bhikkhu* understands thus: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.’ That is, with ignorance ( *avidyā*) as condition, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness (*vijñāna*); with consciousness as condition, name and form (*nāmarūpa*); with name and form as condition, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); with the six sense bases as condition, contact (*sparśa*); with contact as condition, feeling (*vedanā*); with feeling as condition, craving (*tṛṣṇā*); with craving as condition, clinging (*upādāna*); with clinging as condition, becoming (*bhava*); with becoming as condition, birth (*jāti*); with birth as condition, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), pain (*duḥkha*), grief (*daurmanasya*), and despair (*upāyāsa*) come to be. Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering (*duḥkhakkhandha*).

But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance (*avidyā*) comes the cessation of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna*); with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name and form (*nāmarūpa*); with the cessation of name and form, the cessation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact (*sparśa*); with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling (*vedanā*); with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); with the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging (*upādāna*); with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming (*bhava*); with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth (*jāti*); with the cessation of birth, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), pain (*duḥkha*), grief (*daurmanasya*), and despair (*upāyāsa*) cease. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering (*duḥkhakkhandha*)’. In this way, Ānanda, a *bhikkhu* can be called skilled in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)."
commentary_pali:
126.Ajjhattikabāhirānīti ajjhattikāni ca bāhirāni ca. Ettha hi cakkhuādīni ajjhattikāni cha, rūpādīni bāhirāni cha. Idhāpi jānāti passatīti saha vipassanāya maggo kathito.

Imasmiṃsati idantiādi mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaye vitthāritameva.

Imasmiṃ sati ida
commentary_english:
126. *ajjhattikabāhirānī* means *ajjhattikāni ca bāhirāni ca*.

Here, *cakkhuādīni* are the six internal ones, and *rūpādīni* are the six external ones.

Here also, *jānāti passatī* means the path together with insight has been described.

In this, sati ida, etc., has been extensively explained in the destruction of great craving.

In this, sati ida.

mula_pali: 127. ‘‘Kittāvatā pana, bhante, ‘ṭhānāṭhānakusalo bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā’’ti? ‘‘Idhānanda, bhikkhu ‘aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci kiñci (syā. kaṃ. ka.) saṅkhāraṃ niccato upagaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ puthujjano kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato upagaccheyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ puthujjano kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagaccheyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti. ‘Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci dhammaṃ attato upagaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti, ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ puthujjano kañci dhammaṃ attato upagaccheyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti.
mula_english:
127. "But in what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu skilled in what is possible and impossible?"

"Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands: 'It is impossible, it cannot happen that a person possessing right view (*dṛṣṭisampanna*) could treat any formation (*saṅkhāra*) as permanent (*nityato*) - there is no such possibility.' And he understands: 'It is possible that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) might treat some formation as permanent - there is such a possibility.' He understands: 'It is impossible, it cannot happen that a person possessing right view could treat any formation as pleasurable (*sukhato*) - there is no such possibility.' And he understands: 'It is possible that an ordinary person might treat some formation as pleasurable - there is such a possibility.' He understands: 'It is impossible, it cannot happen that a person possessing right view could treat anything as self (*ātman*) - there is no such possibility.' And he understands: 'It is possible that an ordinary person might treat something as self - there is such a possibility.'"
commentary_pali:
127.Aṭṭhānanti hetupaṭikkhepo. Anavakāsoti paccayapaṭikkhepo. Ubhayenāpi kāraṇameva paṭikkhipati. Kāraṇañhi tadāyattavuttitāya attano phalassa ṭhānanti ca avakāsoti ca vuccati. Yanti yena kāraṇena. Diṭṭhisampannoti maggadiṭṭhiyā sampanno sotāpanno ariyasāvako. Kañci saṅkhāranti catubhūmakesu saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu kañci ekasaṅkhārampi. Niccato upagaccheyyāti niccoti gaṇheyya. Netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthi na upalabbhati. Yaṃ puthujjanoti yena kāraṇena puthujjano. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjatīti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthi. Sassatadiṭṭhiyā hi so tebhūmakesu saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato gaṇheyyāti attho. Catutthabhūmakasaṅkhārā pana tejussadattā divasaṃ santatto ayoguḷo viya makkhikānaṃ diṭṭhiyā vā aññesaṃ vā akusalānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na honti. Iminā nayena kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhatotiādīsupi attho veditabbo.

Sukhato upagaccheyyāti ‘‘ekantasukhī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā’’ti (ma. ni. 3.21, 22) evaṃ attadiṭṭhivasena sukhato gāhaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhivippayuttacittena pana ariyasāvako pariḷāhābhibhūto pariḷāhavūpasamatthaṃ mattahatthiṃ parittāsito viya, cokkhabrāhmaṇo viya ca gūthaṃ kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagacchati. Attavāre kasiṇādipaṇṇattisaṅgahatthaṃ saṅkhāranti avatvā kañci dhammanti vuttaṃ. Idhāpi ariyasāvakassa catubhūmakavasena veditabbo, puthujjanassa tebhūmakavasena. Sabbavāresu ariyasāvakassāpi tebhūmakavaseneva paricchedo vaṭṭati. Yaṃ yañhi puthujjano gaṇhāti, tato tato ariyasāvako gāhaṃ viniveṭheti. Puthujjano hi yaṃ yaṃ niccaṃ sukhaṃ attāti gaṇhāti, taṃ taṃ ariyasāvako aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti gaṇhanto taṃ gāhaṃ viniveṭheti.

Sukhato upagaccheyyā
commentary_english:
127.
"***Aṭṭhāna***nti" means rejection of cause (hetupratikkhepo).
"***Anavakāso***ti" means rejection of condition (pratyayapaṭikkhepo).
By both, one rejects the cause (kāraṇa) itself.
Because the cause (kāraṇaṃ) is dependent on that, its nature (vuttitāya) is the place of its own fruit (phalassa ṭhānaṃ), thus it is called opportunity (avakāso).

"Ya"nti means by which cause (yena kāraṇena).
"***Diṭṭhisampanno***ti" means the noble disciple (ariyasāvako) who is a stream-enterer (sotāpanno), endowed with the path of view (maggadiṭṭhiyā sampanno).
"***Kañci saṅkhāra***nti" means any one conditioned thing (ekasaṅkhārampi) among the conditioned things (saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu) in the four realms (catubhūmakesu).
"***Niccato upagaccheyyā***ti" means one should grasp (gaṇheyya) as permanent (niccoti).
"***Netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī***ti" means this is not the cause (etaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthi), it is not found (na upalabbhati).
"***Yaṃ puthujjano***ti" means by which cause (yena kāraṇena) the ordinary person (puthujjano).
"***Ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī***ti" means this is the cause (etaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthi).
Because of the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhiyā), he grasps any conditioned thing (kañci saṅkhāraṃ) as permanent (niccato gaṇheyyāti) among the conditioned things (saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu) in the three realms (tebhūmakesu); this is the meaning (attho).
The formations (saṅkhārā) of the fourth realm (catutthabhūmaka) are like a heated iron ball (santatto ayoguḷo viya) made of pure fire (tejussadattā), they are not the object (ārammaṇaṃ na honti) of the sight (diṭṭhiyā) of flies (makkhikānaṃ) or of other (aññesaṃ vā) unwholesome things (akusalānaṃ).
In this way (iminā nayena), the meaning (attho) should be understood (veditabbo) also in the case of "***kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato***tiādīsupi".

"***Sukhato upagaccheyyā***ti" means "The self is utterly happy (ekantasukhī attā hoti), free from disease (arogo) after death (paraṃ maraṇā)," (Ma.
Ni.
3.21, 22) thus, with the view of self (attadiṭṭhivasena), this is said (vuttaṃ) having in mind the grasping of happiness (sukhato gāhaṃ sandhāya).
But with a mind detached from views (diṭṭhivippayuttacittena pana), the noble disciple (ariyasāvako), overcome by burning (pariḷāhābhibhūto), approaches happiness (sukhato upagacchati) in any formation (kañci saṅkhāraṃ) like an elephant made drunk (mattahatthiṃ) fearful of burning (pariḷāhavūpasamatthaṃ parittāsito viya), like a clean Brahman (cokkhabrāhmaṇo viya) to excrement (gūthaṃ).
In the case of self (attavāre), without saying formation (saṅkhāranti), the meaning (saṅgahatthaṃ) is that a teaching (dhammanti) is spoken about, beginning with the *kasiṇa* (kasiṇādipaṇṇatti).
Here too (idhāpi), it should be understood (veditabbo) according to the four realms (catubhūmakavasena) for the noble disciple (ariyasāvakassa), and according to the three realms (tebhūmakavasena) for the ordinary person (puthujjanassa).
In all cases (sabbavāresu), the limitation (paricchedo) is fitting (vaṭṭati) only by way of the three realms (tebhūmakavaseneva) even for the noble disciple (ariyasāvakassāpi).
Whatever (yaṃ yañhi) the ordinary person (puthujjano) grasps (gaṇhāti), from that (tato tato) the noble disciple (ariyasāvako) disentangles (viniveṭheti) the grasping (gāhaṃ).
Whatever (yaṃ yaṃ) the ordinary person (puthujjano hi) grasps (gaṇhāti) as permanent (niccaṃ), happiness (sukhaṃ), self (attāti), that (taṃ taṃ) the noble disciple (ariyasāvako), grasping (gaṇhanto) as impermanent (aniccaṃ), suffering (dukkhaṃ), not-self (anattāti), disentangles (viniveṭheti) that grasping (taṃ gāhaṃ).

***Sukhato upagaccheyyā***

mula_pali: 128. ‘‘‘Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ puthujjano mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti. ‘Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo pitaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya…pe… arahantaṃ jīvitā voropeyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo duṭṭhacitto tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādeyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ puthujjano duṭṭhacitto tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādeyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti. ‘Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo saṅghaṃ bhindeyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ puthujjano saṅghaṃ bhindeyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti. ‘Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ puthujjano aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti.
mula_english:
“He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen that a person possessing right view (*dṛṣṭi-sampanna*) could deprive his mother (*mātaraṃ*) of life - there is no such possibility.’ And he understands: ‘It is possible that an ordinary person (*pṛthujjana*) might deprive his mother of life - there is such a possibility.’

He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen that a person possessing right view could deprive his father (*pitaraṃ*) of life…could deprive an *arhat* of life - there is no such possibility.’ And he understands: ‘It is possible that an ordinary person might deprive his father of life…might deprive an *arhat* of life - there is such a possibility.’ He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen that a person possessing right view could, with a mind of hate, shed a *Tathāgata’s* blood - there is no such possibility.’ And he understands: ‘It is possible that an ordinary person might, with a mind of hate, shed a *Tathāgata’s* blood - there is such a possibility.’

He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen that a person possessing right view could cause a schism in the *Saṃgha* - there is no such possibility.’ And he understands: ‘It is possible that an ordinary person might cause a schism in the *Saṃgha* - there is such a possibility.’

He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen that a person possessing right view could acknowledge another teacher - there is no such possibility.’ And he understands: ‘It is possible that an ordinary person might acknowledge another teacher - there is such a possibility.’
commentary_pali:
128.Mātarantiādīsu janikāva mātā, janako pitā, manussabhūtova khīṇāsavo arahāti adhippeto. Kiṃ pana ariyasāvako aññaṃ jīvitā voropeyyāti? Etampi aṭṭhānaṃ. Sacepi hi bhavantaragataṃ ariyasāvakaṃ attano ariyabhāvaṃ ajānantampi koci evaṃ vadeyya ‘‘imaṃ kunthakipillikaṃ jīvitā voropetvā sakalacakkavāḷagabbhe cakkavattirajjaṃ paṭipajjāhī’’ti , neva so taṃ jīvitā voropeyya. Athāpi naṃ evaṃ vadeyya ‘‘sace imaṃ na ghātessasi, sīsaṃ te chindissāmā’’ti. Sīsamevassa chindeyya, na ca so taṃ ghāteyya. Puthujjanabhāvassa pana mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthaṃ ariyasāvakassa ca baladīpanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – sāvajjo puthujjanabhāvo, yatra hi nāma puthujjano mātughātādīnipi ānantariyāni karissati. Mahābalo ca ariyasāvako, yo etāni kammāni na karotīti.

Duṭṭhacittoti vadhakacittena paduṭṭhacitto. Lohitaṃ uppādeyyāti jīvamānakasarīre khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitaṃ uppādeyya. Saṅghaṃ bhindeyyāti samānasaṃvāsakaṃ samānasīmāya ṭhitaṃ pañcahi kāraṇehi saṅghaṃ bhindeyya. Vuttañhetaṃ ‘‘pañcahupāli ākārehi saṅgho bhijjati. Kammena uddesena voharanto anussāvanena salākaggāhenā’’ti (pari. 458).

Duṭṭhacitto Lohitaṃ uppādeyyā Saṅghaṃ bhindeyyā

Tattha kammenāti apalokanādīsu catūsu kammesu aññatarena kammena. Uddesenāti pañcasu pātimokkhuddesesu aññatarena uddesena. Voharantoti kathayanto, tāhi tāhi uppattīhi adhammaṃ dhammotiādīni aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni dīpento. Anussāvanenāti nanu tumhe jānātha mayhaṃ uccākulā pabbajitabhāvaṃ bahussutabhāvañca, mādiso nāma uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ gāheyyāti cittampi uppādetuṃ tumhākaṃ yuttaṃ, kiṃ mayhaṃ avīci nīluppalavanaṃ viya sītalo, kiṃ ahaṃ apāyato na bhāyāmītiādinā nayena kaṇṇamūle vacībhedaṃ katvā anussāvanena. Salākaggāhenāti evaṃ anussāvetvā tesaṃ cittaṃ upatthambhetvā anivattidhamme katvā ‘‘gaṇhatha imaṃ salāka’’nti salākaggāhena.

kammenā Uddesenā Voharanto Anussāvanenā Salākaggāhenā

Ettha ca kammameva uddeso vā pamāṇaṃ, vohārānussāvanasalākaggāhā pana pubbabhāgā. Aṭṭhārasavatthudīpanavasena hi voharantena tattha rucijananatthaṃ anussāvetvā salākāya gāhitāyapi abhinnova hoti saṅgho. Yadā pana evaṃ cattāro vā atirekā vā salākaṃ gāhetvā āveṇikaṃ kammaṃ vā uddesaṃ vā karonti, tadā saṅgho bhinno nāma hoti. Evaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo saṅghaṃ bhindeyyāti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ettāvatā mātughātādīni pañca ānantariyakammāni dassitāni honti, yāni puthujjano karoti, na ariyasāvako, tesaṃ āvibhāvatthaṃ –

Kammato dvārato ceva, kappaṭṭhitiyato tathā;

Pākasādhāraṇādīhi, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Tattha kammato tāva – ettha hi manussabhūtasseva manussabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā api parivattaliṅgaṃ jīvitā voropentassa kammaṃ ānantariyaṃ hoti, tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhissāmīti sakalacakkavāḷaṃ mahācetiyappamāṇehi kañcanathūpehi pūretvāpi sakalacakkavāḷaṃ pūretvā nisinnabhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvāpi buddhassa bhagavato saṅghāṭikaṇṇaṃ amuñcanto vicaritvāpi kāyassa bhedā nirayameva upapajjati. Yo pana sayaṃ manussabhūto tiracchānabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā, sayaṃ vā tiracchānabhūto manussabhūtaṃ, tiracchānoyeva vā tiracchānabhūtaṃ jīvitā voropeti, tassa kammaṃ ānantariyaṃ na hoti, bhāriyaṃ pana hoti, ānantariyaṃ āhacceva tiṭṭhati. Manussajātikānaṃ pana vasena ayaṃ pañho kathito.

kammato

Tattha eḷakacatukkaṃ saṅgāmacatukkaṃ coracatukkañca kathetabbaṃ. Eḷakaṃ māremīti abhisandhināpi hi eḷakaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ manusso manussabhūtaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā mārento ānantariyaṃ phusati. Eḷakābhisandhinā pana mātāpitāabhisandhinā vā eḷakaṃ mārento ānantariyaṃ na phusati. Mātāpitāabhisandhinā mātāpitaro mārento phusateva. Eseva nayo itarasmimpi catukkadvaye. Yathā ca mātāpitūsu, evaṃ arahantepi etāni catukkāni veditabbāni.

Manussaarahantameva māretvā ānantariyaṃ phusati, na yakkhabhūtaṃ. Kammaṃ pana bhāriyaṃ, ānantariyasadisameva. Manussaarahantassa ca puthujjanakāleyeva satthappahāre vā vise vā dinnepi yadi so arahattaṃ patvā teneva marati, arahantaghāto hotiyeva. Yaṃ pana puthujjanakāle dinnaṃ dānaṃ arahattaṃ patvā paribhuñjati, puthujjanasseva dinnaṃ hoti. Sesaariyapuggale mārentassa ānantariyaṃ natthi. Kammaṃ pana bhāriyaṃ, ānantariyasadisameva.

Lohituppāde tathāgatassa abhejjakāyatāya parūpakkamena cammacchedaṃ katvā lohitapaggharaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Sarīrassa pana antoyeva ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne lohitaṃ samosarati. Devadattena paviddhasilato bhijjitvā gatā sakalikāpi tathāgatassa pādantaṃ pahari, pharasunā pahaṭo viya pādo antolohitoyeva ahosi. Tathā karontassa ānantariyaṃ hoti. Jīvako pana tathāgatassa ruciyā satthakena cammaṃ chinditvā tamhā ṭhānā duṭṭhalohitaṃ nīharitvā phāsumakāsi, tathā karontassa puññakammameva hoti.

Lohituppāde

Atha ye ca parinibbute tathāgate cetiyaṃ bhindanti, bodhiṃ chindanti dhātumhi upakkamanti, tesaṃ kiṃ hotīti? Bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ hoti ānantariyasadisaṃ. Sadhātukaṃ pana thūpaṃ vā paṭimaṃ vā bādhamānaṃ bodhisākhaṃ chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Sacepi tattha nilīnā sakuṇā cetiye vaccaṃ pātenti, chindituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Paribhogacetiyato hi sarīracetiyaṃ mahantataraṃ. Cetiyavatthuṃ bhinditvā gacchantaṃ bodhimūlampi chinditvā harituṃ vaṭṭati. Yā pana bodhisākhā bodhigharaṃ bādhati, taṃ geharakkhaṇatthaṃ chindituṃ na labhati, bodhiatthañhi gehaṃ, na gehatthāya bodhi. Āsanagharepi eseva nayo. Yasmiṃ pana āsanaghare dhātu nihitā hoti, tassa rakkhaṇatthāya bodhisākhaṃ chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Bodhijagganatthaṃ ojoharaṇasākhaṃ vā pūtiṭṭhānaṃ vā chindituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva, bhagavato sarīrapaṭijaggane viya puññampi hoti.

Saṅghabhede sīmaṭṭhakasaṅghe asannipatite visuṃ parisaṃ gahetvā katavohārānussāvana-salākaggāhassa kammaṃ vā karontassa, uddesaṃ vā uddisantassa bhedo ca hoti ānantariyakammañca. Samaggasaññāya pana vaṭṭatīti kammaṃ karontassa bhedova hoti, na ānantariyakammaṃ, tathā navato ūnaparisāyaṃ. Sabbantimena paricchedena navannaṃ janānaṃ yo saṅghaṃ bhindati , tassa ānantariyakammaṃ hoti. Anuvattakānaṃ adhammavādīnaṃ mahāsāvajjakammaṃ. Dhammavādino pana anavajjā.

Tattha navannameva saṅghabhede idaṃ suttaṃ – ‘‘ekato upāli cattāro honti, ekato cattāro, navamo anussāveti, salākaṃ gāheti ‘ayaṃ dhammo ayaṃ vinayo idaṃ satthusāsanaṃ, idaṃ gaṇhatha, imaṃ rocethā’ti, evaṃ kho, upāli, saṅgharāji ceva hoti saṅghabhedo ca. Navannaṃ vā, upāli, atirekanavannaṃ vā saṅgharāji ceva hoti saṅghabhedo cā’’ti (cūḷava. 351). Etesu pana pañcasu saṅghabhedo vacīkammaṃ, sesāni kāyakammānīti. Evaṃ kammato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Dvāratoti sabbāneva cetāni kāyadvāratopi vacīdvāratopi samuṭṭhahanti. Purimāni panettha cattāri āṇattikavijjāmayapayogavasena vacīdvārato samuṭṭhahitvāpi kāyadvārameva pūrenti, saṅghabhedo hatthamuddāya bhedaṃ karontassa kāyadvārato samuṭṭhahitvāpi vacīdvārameva pūretīti. Evamettha dvāratopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Dvārato

Kappaṭṭhitiyatoti saṅghabhedoyeva cettha kappaṭṭhitiyo. Saṇṭhahante hi kappe kappavemajjhe vā saṅghabhedaṃ katvā kappavināseyeva muccati. Sacepi hi sveva kappo vinassissatīti ajja saṅghabhedaṃ karoti, sveva muccati, ekadivasameva niraye paccati. Evaṃ karaṇaṃ pana natthi. Sesāni cattāri kammāni ānantariyāneva honti, na kappaṭṭhitiyānīti evamettha kappaṭṭhitiyatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Kappaṭṭhitiyato

Pākatoti yena ca pañcape’tāni kammāni katāni honti, tassa saṅghabhedoyeva paṭisandhivasena vipaccati, sesāni ‘‘ahosikammaṃ, nāhosi kammavipāko’’ti evamādīsu saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Saṅghassa bhedābhāve lohituppādo, tadabhāve arahantaghāto, tadabhāve ca sace pitā sīlavā hoti, mātā dussīlā, no vā tathā sīlavatī, pitughāto paṭisandhivasena vipaccati. Sace mātāpitughāto, dvīsupi sīlena vā dussīlena vā samānesu mātughātova paṭisandhivasena vipaccati . Mātā hi dukkarakārinī bahūpakārā ca puttānanti evamettha pākatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Pākato

Sādhāraṇādīhīti purimāni cattāri sabbesampi gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ sādhāraṇāni. Saṅghabhedo pana ‘‘na kho, upāli bhikkhunī, saṅghaṃ bhindati, na sikkhamānā, na sāmaṇero, na sāmaṇerī, na upāsako, na upāsikā saṅghaṃ bhindati, bhikkhu kho, upāli, pakatatto samānasaṃvāsako samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhito saṅghaṃ bhindatī’’ti (cūḷava. 351) vacanato vuttappakārassa bhikkhunova hoti, na aññassa, tasmā asādhāraṇo. Ādisaddena sabbepi te dukkhavedanāsahagatā dosamohasampayuttā cāti evamettha sādhāraṇādīhipi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Sādhāraṇādīhī

Aññaṃ satthāranti ‘‘ayaṃ me satthā satthukiccaṃ kātuṃ asamattho’’ti bhavantarepi aññaṃ titthakaraṃ ‘‘ayaṃ me satthā’’ti evaṃ gaṇheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti attho.

Aññaṃ satthāra
commentary_english:
128. In "mother" etc., *mātā* is like a birth-giver, *pitā* is like a begetter; it is with this intention that the khīṇāsava (one who has destroyed the āsavas) is considered an *araha*.

Furthermore, would an *ariyasāvaka* deprive another of life? This is also impossible.

Even if, when an *ariyasāvaka* has reached another existence, someone not knowing his noble state would say: "Having deprived this small ant of life, take possession of the universal sovereignty within the entire universe," he would never deprive it of life.

However, if someone should say to him, "If you do not kill this [ant], we will cut off your head," he would have his head cut off, but he would not kill it.

This was said in order to show the great blameworthiness of the state of a *puthujjana* (worldling), and to reveal the power of an *ariyasāvaka*.

The intention here is this: the state of a *puthujjana* is blameworthy, for it is there that a *puthujjana* will commit even the *ānantariya* deeds (deeds with immediate result), such as matricide etc.

And the *ariyasāvaka* is of great strength, for he does not do these deeds.

*Duṭṭhacitto* means "with an afflicted mind," with a mind corrupted by murderous thoughts.

*Lohitaṃ uppādeyyā* means even the drawing of blood by a small fly from a living body is the production of blood.

*Saṅghaṃ bhindeyyā* means "he might cause a schism in the Saṅgha," one dwelling in communion, established within a common boundary, might cause a schism in the Saṅgha in five ways.

It was said, "In five ways, Upāli, is the Saṅgha divided: through a legal procedure (*kammena*), through recitation (*uddesena*), through speaking (*voharanto*), through a proclamation (*anussāvanena*), and through voting (*salākaggāhenā*)" (Pari. 458).

*Duṭṭhacitto, lohitaṃ uppādeyyā, saṅghaṃ bhindeyyā*

There, *kammenā* means by one or another of the four legal procedures, beginning with *apalokana*.

*Uddesenā* means by one or another of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha.

*Voharanto* means speaking, revealing the eighteen grounds for schism, such as "what is not the Dharma is the Dharma," and so on, by means of various utterances.

*Anussāvanenā* means, "Surely you know that I am of high birth, that I have gone forth, and that I have much learning; is it fitting for you to produce even the thought that one like me would accept what is not the Dharma, what is contrary to the Discipline, and the Teacher’s Dispensation? Is Avīci hell as cool for me as a grove of blue lotuses? Am I not afraid of the lower realms?", and by making a division in the words in this way, near the ear, by means of a proclamation.

*Salākaggāhenā* means, having proclaimed thus, having encouraged their minds, and having made [them] of unwavering Dharma, "Take this voting ticket," by means of taking a voting ticket.

*Kammenā, uddesenā, voharanto, anussāvanenā, salākaggāhenā*

Here, *kamma* alone, or *uddesa*, is the measure, but the speaking, the proclamation, and the taking of voting tickets are preliminary.

For by speaking, in dependence upon revealing the eighteen grounds, and by proclaiming, with the aim of arousing inclination there, the Saṅgha is not divided even by the taking of a voting ticket.

When, however, in this way four or more take a voting ticket and perform a distinct *kamma* or *uddesa*, then the Saṅgha is said to be divided.

Thus, it is impossible that a person endowed with right view could cause a schism in the Saṅgha.

To this extent, the five *ānantariya-kamma*s, beginning with matricide, have been shown, which the *puthujjana* does, but not the *ariyasāvaka*, for the sake of their manifestation –

By means of action, by means of the door, and likewise by means of the duration of a *kappa* (aeon);

By means of *pāka*, by means of the commonality etc., the determination is to be understood.

There, first of all by means of action (*kammato*) – here, indeed, for a human being to intentionally deprive a human being, either his mother or his father, or even one of changed gender, of life, is an *ānantariya-kamma*; even if, thinking "I will ward off its ripening," having filled the entire universe with golden stūpas equal in measure to the great caitya, and having filled the entire universe and given a great gift to the Saṅgha of seated monks, and though not releasing hold of the edge of the *saṃghāṭī* (robe) of the Blessed Buddha, he lives wandering about, at the breaking up of the body he is reborn in hell itself.

But whoever, himself being a human being, deprives an animal mother or father, or whoever, himself being an animal, [deprives] a human being, or even just an animal [deprives] an animal, of life, his *kamma* is not an *ānantariya-kamma*, but it is weighty; the *ānantariya-kamma* remains having been committed.

But this question is spoken of in terms of the class of human beings.

By means of action

There, the *eḷakacatukka*, the *saṅgāmacatukka*, and the *coracatukka* are to be told.

Even with the intention of killing a goat, a person, standing in the place of a goat, if he kills a human mother or father, touches the *ānantariya*.
However, if one kills a lamb with the intention of killing the lamb, or with the intention of killing one's parents, it does not result in immediate retribution.
If one kills one's parents with the intention of killing one's parents, it certainly results in immediate retribution.
The same principle applies to the other pair of fourfold classifications.
And just as with one's parents, these fourfold classifications should also be understood in the case of an *arhat*.

Only by killing a human *arhat* does one incur immediate retribution, not by killing a *yaksha* or a ghost.
But the *karma* is weighty, just like that of immediate retribution.
And if a person gives a blow with a weapon or poison to a human *arhat*, even when that person was still a common person, and if that *arhat* attains *arhatship* and dies from that very cause, then it certainly constitutes the killing of an *arhat*.
However, whatever gift was given during the time when one was a common person, and one enjoys it having attained *arhatship*, it is considered to have been given to a common person.
There is no immediate retribution for killing a remaining noble individual.
But the *karma* is weighty, just like that of immediate retribution.

<hi rend="bold">In the production of blood,</hi> there is no such thing as the Tathāgata's body being indivisible such that cutting the skin with external effort would result in the flow of blood.
But the blood from the body gathers within in a single place.
When Devadatta threw a stone, a fragment broke off and struck the Tathāgata's foot, and like a foot struck by an ax, the foot became internally bloody.
Doing so results in immediate retribution.
But Jīvaka, with the Tathāgata's consent, cut the skin with a scalpel and removed the corrupted blood from that place, making it comfortable, and doing so resulted only in meritorious action.

<hi rend="bold">In the production of blood</hi>

Then, what happens to those who, when the Tathāgata is completely liberated, break a *cetiya*, cut down a *bodhi* tree, or make an attempt on a relic? The *karma* is weighty, resembling that of immediate retribution.
But it is permissible to cut down a branch of the *bodhi* tree that is obstructing a *thūpa* or an image containing relics.
Even if birds nested there were to excrete waste on the *cetiya*, it would still be permissible to cut it down.
For the *sarīracetiya* is greater than the *paribhogacetīya*.
It is permissible to destroy a *cetiyavatthu* that is in the way, and even to cut down and carry away the root of the *bodhi* tree.
But if a branch of the *bodhi* tree obstructs the *bodhi-ghara*, it is not permissible to cut it down for the sake of protecting the house, for the house is for the sake of the *bodhi* tree, not the *bodhi* tree for the sake of the house.
The same principle applies to the *āsanaghara*.
However, in an *āsanaghara* where a relic is deposited, it is permissible to cut down a branch of the *bodhi* tree for the sake of protecting it.
For the sake of caring for the *bodhi* tree, it is certainly permissible to cut down a branch that draws away its vitality or a branch that is rotting; just like caring for the body of the *bhagavat*, it is also meritorious.

In the case of schism in the *saṅgha*, if the community at the boundary marker is not assembled and one takes a separate assembly, one who performs an act of reciting the *vohāra* or taking the lot, or one who recites the *uddesa*, there is both schism and immediate retribution.
However, if one performs an act thinking that it is permissible with the consent of the whole, there is only schism, not immediate retribution, and likewise in an assembly of fewer than nine.
By the last determination, one who splits the *saṅgha* of nine people has immediate retribution.
For those who follow, it is a greatly blameworthy action for those who speak against the Dharma.
But those who speak in accordance with the Dharma are blameless.

There, in the schism of the *saṅgha* of nine, this *sūtra* [applies]: "On one side, *Upāli*, there are four, on one side four, the ninth announces, takes the lot, [saying] 'This is the Dharma, this is the Discipline, this is the Teacher's instruction, take this, approve of this', thus, *Upāli*, there is both agreement and schism in the *saṅgha*."
And if there are nine or more monks, then this is both a fracture in the *saṅgha* and also a schism in the *saṅgha* (cūḷava. 351). Among these five, schism in the *saṅgha* is verbal action, the remaining ones are actions of the body. Thus, the exposition should be understood by *karma*.

By way of the doors (*dvāra*): All these volitions originate from the door of the body and from the door of speech. Among these, the first four, due to the force of injunction, knowledge, and application, although arising from the door of speech, only fill the door of the body. Schism in the *saṅgha*, for one who is making a split by means of hand gestures, although arising from the door of the body, only fills the door of speech. Thus, the exposition should be understood here by way of the doors (*dvāra*).

By way of the doors (*dvāra*) and duration of a *kappa*: Schism in the *saṅgha* is indeed the duration of a *kappa* here. Existing in a *kappa*, either in the middle of a *kappa*, having created a schism in the *saṅgha*, one is liberated only in the destruction of the *kappa*. Even if the *kappa* itself will be destroyed tomorrow, having created a schism in the *saṅgha* today, he is liberated tomorrow, he is cooked in hell for only one day. Thus, there is no such doing. The remaining four actions are indeed of immediate result, not of the duration of a *kappa*. Thus, the exposition should be understood here by way of the duration of a *kappa*.

By way of the duration of a *kappa* and manifestation (*pākato*): And by whichever of these five actions have been done, for him, schism in the *saṅgha* ripens by way of rebirth, the remaining ones go to the count in such expressions as "the action was fruitless, the result of the action was fruitless." In the absence of schism in the *saṅgha*, there is the production of blood, in the absence of that, there is the killing of an *arhat*, and in the absence of that, if the father is virtuous ( *śīlavā*), the mother is immoral (*dussīlā*), or if she is not virtuous in that way, patricide ripens by way of rebirth. If there is matricide and patricide, in both when they are the same in virtue or immorality, matricide alone ripens by way of rebirth. For the mother is one who does difficult things and is of great help to her sons. Thus, the exposition should be understood here by way of manifestation (*pākato*).

By way of manifestation (*pākato*) and commonality etc.: The first four are common to all, householders and renunciants alike. But schism in the *saṅgha*, "It is not, Upāli, a *bhikṣuṇī* who causes a schism in the *saṅgha*, not a female trainee (*sikkhamānā*), not a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*), not a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*), not a male lay follower (*upāsaka*), not a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) who causes a schism in the *saṅgha*. It is, Upāli, a monk (*bhikkhu*) who is competent, living in communion, abiding within the same boundary, who causes a schism in the *saṅgha* " (cūḷava. 351). By the word, according to the manner spoken, it is only for a monk, not for another; therefore it is uncommon. By the word "etc.," all those accompanied by painful feeling, connected with hatred and delusion. Thus, the exposition should be understood here by way of commonality and so on.

By way of commonality and so on: "Another teacher (*satthāra*)": "'This is my teacher, he is incapable of doing the work of a teacher.' Even in another existence, he might take another heretical teacher (*tirthakara*) saying, 'This is my teacher.' " This is not a tenable position, is the meaning.

mula_pali: 129. ‘‘‘Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyuṃ, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā eko arahaṃ sammāsambuddho uppajjeyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti. ‘Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve rājāno cakkavattino apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyuṃ, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti; ‘ṭhānañca kho etaṃ vijjati yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā eko rājā cakkavattī uppajjeyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’ti pajānāti.
mula_english:
