That wheel-treasure travels above and above the treetops, not too high, in the region of the sky, so that those who desire the fruits, flowers, and leaves of the trees are able to easily grasp them. Those standing on the ground are able to recognize, "This is the king, this is the viceroy, this is the general."
In the postures beginning with standing, one goes by whatever [posture] one desires.
Those skilled in painting and other crafts go doing their own respective tasks.
Just as on the earth, so their all their tasks succeed in the sky.
Having taken the *cakravartin*'s retinue in this way, that wheel-treasure, leaving Mount Sumeru on its left side, travels over the sea to *Pūrvavideha*, a distance of eight thousand *yojanas*.

There, that earth region, being charming, level, clean, and provided with shade and water, is capable of accommodating a settlement with a circumference of twelve *yojanas* and a perimeter of thirty-six *yojanas*, and is easily equipped with food and other necessities. Above that, that wheel-treasure stands in the sky as if fixed to an axle.
Then, by that sign, that great crowd descends and establishes a dwelling, doing all the tasks beginning with bathing and eating as they please. Therefore it was said, "In whatever region that wheel-treasure stands, there the *cakravartin* king takes up residence together with his four-constituent army."

0221"/>
Thus, when the *cakravartin* has taken up residence, whatever kings are there, even having heard, "A foreign army has come," do not assemble an armed force and become ready for battle.
Immediately upon the arising of the wheel-treasure, there is no being such that, with a hostile intention towards the king, would dare to lift a weapon.
This is the power of the wheel-treasure.

Due to the power of the wheel,
all the remaining enemies go to self-control;
the wheel of the king is called the subduer of enemies
because it subdues the enemy.

Therefore,
all those kings, taking tribute corresponding to their own royal glory and prosperity, approach that king, and, with bowed heads, performing the foot-worship with the anointing of the light from the jewels in their own diadems, they submit to his command with words such as, "Come, great king!"
Therefore it was said, "Those who in the east..., the great king instructs..."

Those who in the east... the great king instructs..." There, "welcome" means "good coming."
For upon one's arrival they grieve, and upon departure they rejoice.
Upon one's arrival they rejoice, and upon departure they grieve.
You are such that they rejoice at your arrival and grieve at your departure; therefore, your arrival is said to be a good arrival.
Thus, when it has been said, the *cakravartin* neither says, "You should provide me with so much tribute every year," nor does he take the property of one and give it to another.
But, examining things such as the killing of living beings with wisdom corresponding to his state as a righteous king, with a lovely, sweet voice he teaches the Dharma in a way such as, "See, fathers, killing living beings, if practiced, cultivated, and made abundant, is conducive to hell," and he gives the instruction beginning with, "Living beings should not be killed."
Therefore it was said, "The *cakravartin* king says this: Living beings should not be killed... one should eat moderately."

The *cakravartin* king says this: Living beings should not be killed... one should eat moderately." Do all the kings accept this instruction of the king?
Even all the Buddhas are not accepted; how much less will they accept [the instruction] of a king?
Therefore, those who are wise and discerning accept it.
But all become followers.
Therefore, he said "Those who, monks..."

Then that wheel-treasure, when the instruction to those residing in *Pūrvavideha* has been given, after the morning meal, rising up into the sky by the power of the *cakravartin*'s army, plunges into the eastern ocean.
And as it plunges into it, just as a *nāga*-king with retracted hood, having smelled the scent of medicine, contracts the spreading of his waves, it stands in the inner ocean, having gone down a *yojana*-measure into the water of the great ocean, like a wall of *vaiḍūrya*.
And at that very moment, as if desiring to see the royal fortune of that king, various jewels scattered on the floor of the great ocean, coming from here and there, fill that region.
Then that royal retinue, seeing that floor of the great ocean filled with various jewels, takes [them] as they please with their laps and other [means]; they rejoice as they please in the taken jewels.
But, the wheel-jewel turns back to the assembly.

And as it turns back, the assembly is in the lead, the king in the middle, and the wheel-jewel at the end.

That ocean water, as if being allured by the splendor of the *cakraratna*, and as if not tolerating separation from it, constantly approaches, striking against the edge of the *nemi-maṇḍala*.

mula_pali:
257. ‘‘Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā ajjhogahetvā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) paccuttaritvā dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pavattati…pe… dakkhiṇaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā pacchimaṃ disaṃ pavattati… pacchimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā uttaraṃ disaṃ pavattati anvadeva rājā cakkavattī saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Yasmiṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, padese cakkaratanaṃ patiṭṭhāti tattha rājā cakkavattī vāsaṃ upeti saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya.

‘‘Ye kho pana, bhikkhave, uttarāya disāya paṭirājāno te rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘ehi kho, mahārāja! Svāgataṃ te, mahārāja! Sakaṃ te, mahārāja! Anusāsa, mahārājā’ti. Rājā cakkavattī evamāha – ‘pāṇo na hantabbo, adinnaṃ nādātabbaṃ, kāmesumicchā na caritabbā, musā na bhāsitabbā, majjaṃ na pātabbaṃ; yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā’ti. Ye kho pana, bhikkhave, uttarāya disāya paṭirājāno te rañño cakkavattissa anuyantā bhavanti.

‘‘Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, cakkaratanaṃ samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ abhivijinitvā tameva rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā rañño cakkavattissa antepuradvāre akkhāhataṃ maññe tiṭṭhati rañño cakkavattissa antepuradvāraṃ upasobhayamānaṃ. Rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavati.
mula_english:
257. “Then, monks, that wheel-treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean, and emerging again, turns forward in the southern direction… Then, having plunged into the southern ocean, and emerging again, it turns forward in the western direction… Having plunged into the western ocean, and emerging again, it turns forward in the northern direction. And the *cakravartin* king follows right along with his four-constituent army. Now in whatever region the wheel-treasure pauses, there the *cakravartin* king takes up his abode with his four-constituent army.

“And those opposing kings in the northern direction approach the *cakravartin* king and say to him: ‘Come, great king! Welcome to you, great king! We are yours, great king! Rule us, great king!’ The *cakravartin* king speaks thus: ‘Life should not be taken; what is not given should not be taken; one should not misconduct oneself in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu-micchā*); one should not speak falsehood; intoxicants should not be drunk; and you should eat what you are accustomed to eat.’ And those opposing kings in the northern direction become followers of the *cakravartin* king.

“Then, monks, that wheel-treasure, having conquered the earth to the ocean's edge, returns to that very capital city and remains, as if fixed on its axle, at the gate of the *cakravartin* king's inner palace, adorning the gate of the *cakravartin* king's inner palace. Such a wheel-treasure appears to the *cakravartin* king.
commentary_pali:
257. Evaṃ rājā cakkavattī puratthimasamuddapariyantaṃ pubbavidehaṃ abhivijinitvā dakkhiṇasamuddapariyantaṃ jambudīpaṃ vijetukāmo cakkaratanadesitena maggena dakkhiṇasamuddābhimukho gacchati. Tena vuttaṃ atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pavattatīti. Evaṃ pavattamānassa pana tassa pavattanavidhānaṃ senāsanniveso paṭirājagamanaṃ tesaṃ anusāsanippadānaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhanaṃ samuddasalilassa ogacchanaṃ ratanādānanti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Vijinitvā pana taṃ dasasahassayojanappamāṇaṃ jambudīpaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddatopi paccuttaritvā sattayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ aparagoyānaṃ vijetuṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva gantvā tampi samuddapariyantaṃ tatheva abhivijinitvā pacchimasamuddatopi paccuttaritvā aṭṭhayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ uttarakuruṃ vijetuṃ tatheva gantvā tampi samuddapariyantaṃ tatheva abhivijiya uttarasamuddatopi paccuttarati.

Ettāvatā raññā cakkavattinā cāturantāya pathaviyā ādhipaccaṃ adhigataṃ hoti. So evaṃ vijitavijayo attano rajjasirisampattidassanatthaṃ sapariso uddhaṃ gaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghitvā suvikasitapadumuppalapuṇḍarīkavanavicitte cattāro jātassare viya pañcasatapañcasataparittadīpaparivāre cattāro mahādīpe oloketvā cakkaratanadesiteneva maggena yathānukkamaṃ attano rājadhānimeva paccāgacchati. Atha taṃ cakkaratanaṃ antepuradvāraṃ sobhayamānaṃ viya hutvā tiṭṭhati.

Evaṃ patiṭṭhite pana tasmiṃ cakkaratane rājantepure ukkāhi vā dīpikāhi vā kiñci karaṇīyaṃ na hoti, cakkaratanobhāsoyeva rattiṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamati. Ye ca pana rattiṃ andhakāratthikā honti, tesaṃ andhakārameva hoti. Tena vuttaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā…pe… evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

dakkhiṇasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā…pe… evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavatī

Hatthiratanavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
257. Thus, the wheel-turning monarch, having conquered Pubbavideha as far as the eastern sea, desiring to conquer Jambudīpa as far as the southern sea, proceeds towards the southern sea by the path indicated by the wheel-jewel (cakkaratana).
As it was said, "Then, monks, that wheel-jewel, having plunged into the eastern sea, rises up and proceeds towards the southern direction."

However, the manner of its proceeding, the encampment of the army, the arrival of opposing kings, the instruction given to them, the plunging into the southern sea, the receding of the sea water, and the acceptance of tribute, all this should be understood in the same way as before.

Having conquered that Jambudīpa, which is ten thousand yojanas in extent, he rises up from the southern sea and, going in the manner described before to conquer Aparagoyāna, which is seven thousand yojanas in extent, having conquered that too, as far as its sea coast, he rises up from the western sea and, going in the same way to conquer Uttarakuru, which is eight thousand yojanas in extent, having conquered that too, as far as its sea coast, he rises up from the northern sea.

Thus, the wheel-turning monarch gains sovereignty over the four-quartered earth (cāturantāya pathaviyā).
So, having achieved such a victory, along with his retinue, he leaps up into the sky to show the glory and prosperity of his kingdom. He surveys the four great islands, which are adorned with well-blossomed lotus, উৎপল, and white lotus forests, and which are surrounded by five hundred and five hundred minor islands, like molten gold. Following the path indicated by the wheel-jewel, he returns to his own capital in due course.

Then that wheel-jewel stands as if adorning the inner gate of the palace.

When that wheel-jewel is thus established in the royal palace, there is no need for torches or lamps; the light of the wheel-jewel itself dispels the darkness at night. And those who desire darkness at night have darkness.
As it was said, "Having plunged into the southern sea... such a wheel-jewel appears."

Having plunged into the southern sea... such a wheel-jewel appears.
Description of the elephant-jewel (hatthiratana).

mula_pali:
258. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño cakkavattissa hatthiratanaṃ pātubhavati – sabbaseto sattappatiṭṭho iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo uposatho nāma nāgarājā. Taṃ disvāna rañño cakkavattissa cittaṃ pasīdati – ‘bhaddakaṃ vata, bho, hatthiyānaṃ, sace damathaṃ upeyyā’ti. Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, hatthiratanaṃ seyyathāpi nāma bhaddo hatthājānīyo dīgharattaṃ suparidanto evameva damathaṃ upeti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī tameva hatthiratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno pubbaṇhasamayaṃ abhiruhitvā samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anusaṃyāyitvā tameva rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā pātarāsamakāsi. Rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa evarūpaṃ hatthiratanaṃ pātubhavati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño cakkavattissa assaratanaṃ pātubhavati – sabbaseto kāḷasīso muñjakeso iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo valāhako nāma assarājā. Taṃ disvāna rañño cakkavattissa cittaṃ pasīdati – ‘bhaddakaṃ vata, bho, assayānaṃ, sace damathaṃ upeyyā’ti. Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, assaratanaṃ seyyathāpi nāma bhaddo assājānīyo dīgharattaṃ suparidanto evameva damathaṃ upeti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī tameva assaratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno pubbaṇhasamayaṃ abhiruhitvā samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anusaṃyāyitvā tameva rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā pātarāsamakāsi. Rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa evarūpaṃ assaratanaṃ pātubhavati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño cakkavattissa maṇiratanaṃ pātubhavati. So hoti maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato . Tassa kho pana, bhikkhave, maṇiratanassa ābhā samantā yojanaṃ phuṭā hoti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī tameva maṇiratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā maṇiṃ dhajaggaṃ āropetvā rattandhakāratimisāya pāyāsi. Ye kho pana, bhikkhave, samantā gāmā ahesuṃ te tenobhāsena kammante payojesuṃ ‘divā’ti maññamānā. Rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa evarūpaṃ maṇiratanaṃ pātubhavati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño cakkavattissa itthiratanaṃ pātubhavati. Sā abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā nātidīghā nātirassā nātikisā nātithūlā nātikāḷikā nātikāḷī (sī. pī.) nāccodātā, atikkantā mānusaṃ vaṇṇaṃ, appattā dibbaṃ vaṇṇaṃ. Tassa kho pana, bhikkhave, itthiratanassa evarūpo kāyasamphasso hoti seyyathāpi nāma tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vā. Tassa kho pana, bhikkhave, itthiratanassa sīte uṇhāni gattāni honti, uṇhe sītāni gattāni honti. Tassa kho pana, bhikkhave, itthiratanassa kāyato candanagandho vāyati, mukhato uppalagandho vāyati. Taṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, itthiratanaṃ rañño cakkavattissa pubbuṭṭhāyinī hoti pacchānipātinī kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī manāpacārinī piyavādinī. Taṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, itthiratanaṃ rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ manasāpi no aticarati, kuto pana kāyena? Rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa evarūpaṃ itthiratanaṃ pātubhavati.

nātikāḷī (sī. pī.)

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño cakkavattissa gahapatiratanaṃ pātubhavati. Tassa kammavipākajaṃ dibbacakkhu pātubhavati, yena nidhiṃ passati sassāmikampi assāmikampi. So rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – ‘appossukko tvaṃ, deva, hohi. Ahaṃ te dhanena dhanakaraṇīyaṃ dhanena karaṇīyaṃ (ka.) karissāmī’ti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī tameva gahapatiratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno nāvaṃ abhiruhitvā majjhe gaṅgāya nadiyā sotaṃ ogāhitvā ogahetvā (sī. pī.) gahapatiratanaṃ etadavoca – ‘attho me, gahapati, hiraññasuvaṇṇenā’ti. ‘Tena hi, mahārāja, ekaṃ tīraṃ nāvā upetū’ti. ‘Idheva me, gahapati, attho hiraññasuvaṇṇenā’ti. Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, gahapatiratanaṃ ubhohi hatthehi udake omasitvā pūraṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇassa kumbhiṃ uddharitvā rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ etadavoca – ‘alamettāvatā, mahārāja! Katamettāvatā, mahārāja! Pūjitamettāvatā, mahārājā’ti. Rājā cakkavattī evamāha – ‘alamettāvatā, gahapati! Katamettāvatā, gahapati! Pūjitamettāvatā, gahapatī’ti . Rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa evarūpaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pātubhavati.

dhanena karaṇīyaṃ (ka.) ogahetvā (sī. pī.)

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño cakkavattissa pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavati – paṇḍito byatto medhāvī paṭibalo rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ upayāpetabbaṃ upayāpetuṃ upaṭṭhapetabbaṃ upaṭṭhapetuṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) apayāpetabbaṃ apayāpetuṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetuṃ. So rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – ‘appossukko tvaṃ , deva, hohi. Ahamanusāsissāmī’ti. Rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa evarūpaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavati. Rājā, bhikkhave, cakkavattī imehi sattahi ratanehi samannāgato hoti.

upaṭṭhapetabbaṃ upaṭṭhapetuṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)
mula_english:
"Furthermore, monks, the elephant-treasure appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch: a royal nāga named Uposatha, all white, with firm footing, endowed with supernormal powers, and able to travel through the sky. On seeing him, the Wheel-turning Monarch's mind is pleased: 'It would be wonderful to ride the elephant, if he would undergo taming!' Then, monks, that elephant-treasure undergoes taming just like a fine thoroughbred elephant well tamed for a long time. It so happened that the Wheel-turning Monarch, when testing that elephant-treasure, mounted him in the morning and, after traversing the whole earth to the edge of the ocean, returned to the royal capital to take his morning meal. Such is the elephant-treasure that appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch. "Furthermore, monks, the horse-treasure appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch: a king of horses named Valāhaka ‘Thundercloud’, all white, with raven-black head, with mane like muñja grass, endowed with supernormal power, and able to travel through the sky. On seeing him, the Wheel-turning Monarch's mind is pleased: 'It would be wonderful to ride the horse if he would undergo taming!' Then, monks, that horse-treasure undergoes taming just like a fine thoroughbred horse well tamed for a long time. It so happened that the Wheel-turning Monarch, when testing that horse-treasure, mounted him in the morning and, after traversing the whole earth to the edge of the ocean, returned to the royal capital to take his morning meal. Such is the horse-treasure that appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch. "Furthermore, monks, the jewel-treasure appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch. This jewel is a beryl, beautiful, of good birth, eight-faceted, well-worked. Now the radiance of the jewel-treasure spreads around for a whole league ( *yojana* ). It so happened that when the Wheel-turning Monarch was testing that jewel-treasure, he drew up his four-constituent army in array, and mounting the jewel on top of his banner, he set forth in the darkness and gloom of the night. Then all the inhabitants of the villages nearby began their work by its light, thinking that it was day. Such is the jewel-treasure that appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch. "Furthermore, monks, the woman-treasure appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch. She is beautiful, comely and graceful, possessing the supreme beauty of complexion, neither too tall nor too short, neither too slim nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair, surpassing human beauty without reaching divine beauty. The touch of the woman-treasure is such that it is like a tuft of cotton-wool or a tuft of *kappāsa* cotton-wool. When it is cool, her limbs are warm; when it is warm, her limbs are cool. From the body of the woman-treasure the scent of sandalwood wafts, and from her mouth the scent of lotuses wafts. That woman-treasure rises before the Wheel-turning Monarch and retires after him. She is eager to serve, agreeable in conduct, and sweet in speech. That woman-treasure does not transgress the Wheel-turning Monarch even in thought, let alone in deed. Such is the woman-treasure that appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch. 0214"/>

Again, monks, the householder-treasure appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch. The divine eye born of past action appears to him, whereby he sees hidden treasures, both with owners and ownerless. He approaches the Wheel-turning Monarch and says thus: ‘Sire, remain at ease. I shall take care of your monetary affairs.’ Once upon a time, monks, the king, a Wheel-turning Monarch, testing that very householder-treasure, boarded a boat, and going into the current in the middle of the river Ganges, he said this to the householder-treasure: ‘I need gold and bullion, steward.’ ‘Then, Your Majesty, let the boat be steered to one bank.’ ‘Steward, it is here that I need gold and bullion.’ Then, monks, that householder-treasure plunged both hands into the water and, drawing up a pot full of gold and bullion, said this to the Wheel-turning Monarch: ‘Is this enough, Your Majesty? Is this sufficient, Your Majesty? Is this satisfactory, Your Majesty?’ The Wheel-turning Monarch said thus: ‘It is enough, steward! It is sufficient, steward! It is satisfactory, steward!’ Such a householder-treasure appears to the Wheel-turning Monarch.

dhaneṇa karaṇīyaṃ (ka. ) ogāhetvā (sī. pī. )

Again, monks, the counselor-treasure appears to the Wheel-turning Monarch—[one who is] learned, intelligent, wise, and capable of approaching the Wheel-turning Monarch, [capable] of causing [others] to approach [him], [capable] of turning [others] away, [capable] of establishing [them]. He approaches the Wheel-turning Monarch and says thus: ‘Sire, remain at ease. I shall counsel you.’ Such a counselor-treasure appears to the Wheel-turning Monarch. Monks, the Wheel-turning Monarch possesses these seven treasures.

upaṭṭhāpetabbaṃ upaṭṭhāpetuṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. )
commentary_pali:
258. Evaṃ pātubhūtacakkaratanassa panassa cakkavattino amaccā pakatimaṅgalahatthiṭṭhānaṃ sucibhūmibhāgaṃ kāretvā haricandanādīhi surabhigandhehi upalimpāpetvā heṭṭhā vicittavaṇṇasurabhikusumasamākiṇṇaṃ upari suvaṇṇatārakānaṃ antarantarā samosaritamanuñña-kusumadāmappaṭimaṇḍitavitānaṃ devavimānaṃ viya abhisaṅkharitvā ‘‘evarūpassa nāma deva hatthiratanassa āgamanaṃ cintethā’’ti vadanti. So pubbe vuttanayeneva mahādānaṃ datvā sīlāni samādāya taṃ puññasampattiṃ āvajjanto nisīdati, athassa puññānubhāvacodito chaddantakulā vā uposathakulā vā taṃ sakkāravisesaṃ anubhavitukāmo taruṇaravimaṇḍalābhirattacaraṇa-gīvamukhappaṭimaṇḍitavisuddhasetasarīro sattappatiṭṭho susaṇṭhitaṅgapaccaṅgasanniveso vikasitaratta-padumacārupokkharo iddhimā yogī viya vehāsaṃ gamanasamattho manosilācuṇṇarañjitapariyanto viya rajatapabbato hatthiseṭṭho tasmiṃ padese patiṭṭhāti. So chaddantakulā āgacchanto sabbakaniṭṭho āgacchati, uposathakulā sabbajeṭṭho. Pāḷiyaṃ pana ‘‘uposatho nāgarājā’’ icceva āgacchati. Svāyaṃ pūritacakkavattivattānaṃ cakkavattīnaṃ sutte vuttanayeneva cintayantānaṃ āgacchati, na itaresaṃ. Sayameva pakatimaṅgalahatthiṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā maṅgalahatthiṃ apanetvā tattha tiṭṭhati. Tena vuttaṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… nāgarājāti.

Evaṃ pātubhūtaṃ pana taṃ hatthiratanaṃ disvā hatthigopakādayo haṭṭhatuṭṭhā vegena gantvā rañño ārocenti. Rājā turitaturitaṃ āgantvā taṃ disvā pasannacitto ‘‘bhaddakaṃ vata bho hatthiyānaṃ, sace damathaṃ upeyyā’’ti cintayanto hatthaṃ pasāreti. Atha so gharadhenuvacchako viya kaṇṇe olambetvā sūratabhāvaṃ dassento rājānaṃ upasaṅkamati, rājā taṃ abhiruhitukāmo hoti. Athassa parijanā adhippāyaṃ ñatvā taṃ hatthiratanaṃ sovaṇṇaddhajaṃ sovaṇṇālaṅkāraṃ hemajālapaṭicchannaṃ katvā upanenti. Rājā taṃ anisīdāpetvāva sattaratanamayāya nisseṇiyā abhiruyha ākāsaṃ gamananinnacitto hoti. Tassa saha cittuppādeneva so hatthirājā rājahaṃso viya indanīlamaṇippabhājālanīlagaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghati, tato cakkacārikāya vuttanayeneva sakalarājaparisā. Iti sapariso rājā antopātarāseyeva sakalapathaviṃ anusaṃyāyitvā rājadhāniṃ paccāgacchati, evaṃ mahiddhikaṃ cakkavattino hatthiratanaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ disvāna rañño cakkavattissa…pe… evarūpaṃ hatthiratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

hatthiratanaṃ disvāna rañño cakkavattissa…pe… evarūpaṃ hatthiratanaṃ pātubhavatī

Assaratanavaṇṇanā

Evaṃ pātubhūtahatthiratanassa pana cakkavattino parisā pakatimaṅgalaassaṭṭhānaṃ sucisamatalaṃ kāretvā alaṅkaritvā ca purimanayeneva rañño tassa āgamanacintanatthaṃ ussāhaṃ janenti. So purimanayeneva katadānasakkāro samādinnasīlova pāsādatale nisinno puññasampattiṃ samanussarati, athassa puññānubhāvacodito sindhavakulato vijjullatāvinaddhasaradakālasetavalāhakarāsisassiriko rattapādo rattatuṇḍo candappabhāpuñjasadisasuddhasiniddhaghanasaṅghātasarīro kākagīvā viya indanīlamaṇi viya ca kāḷavaṇṇena sīsena samannāgatattā kāḷasīso suṭṭhu kappetvā ṭhapitehi viya muñjasadisehi saṇhavaṭṭaujugatigatehi kesehi samannāgatattā muñjakeso vehāsaṅgamo valāhako nāma assarājā āgantvā tasmiṃ ṭhāne patiṭṭhāti. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ hatthiratane vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evarūpaṃ assaratanaṃ sandhāya bhagavā puna caparantiādimāha.

kāḷasīso muñjakeso vehāsaṅgamo assaratanaṃ puna capara

Maṇiratanavaṇṇanā

Evaṃ pātubhūtaassaratanassa pana rañño cakkavattissa catuhatthāyāmaṃ sakaṭanābhisamappamāṇaṃ ubhosu antesu kaṇṇikapariyantato viniggatasuparisuddhamuttākalāpehi dvīhi kañcanapadumehi alaṅkataṃ caturāsītimaṇisahassaparivāraṃ tārāgaṇaparivutassa puṇṇacandassa siriṃ paṭippharamānaṃ viya vepullapabbatato maṇiratanaṃ āgacchati. Tassevaṃ āgatassa muttājālake ṭhapetvā veḷuparamparāya saṭṭhihatthappamāṇaṃ ākāsaṃ āropitassa rattibhāge samantā yojanappamāṇaṃ okāsaṃ ābhā pharati, yāya sabbo so okāso aruṇuggamanavelā viya sañjātāloko hoti. Tato kassakā kasikammaṃ, vāṇijā āpaṇugghāṭanaṃ , te te ca sippino taṃ taṃ kammantaṃ payojenti divāti maññamānā. Tena vuttaṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… maṇiratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

maṇiratanaṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… maṇiratanaṃ pātubhavatī

Itthiratanavaṇṇanā

Evaṃ pātubhūtamaṇiratanassa pana cakkavattissa visayasukhavisesakāraṇaṃ itthiratanaṃ pātubhavati. Maddarājakulato vā hissa aggamahesiṃ ānenti, uttarakuruto vā puññānubhāvena sayaṃ āgacchati. Avasesā panassā sampatti ‘‘puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño cakkavattissa itthiratanaṃ pātubhavati abhirūpā dassanīyā’’tiādinā nayena pāḷiyaṃyeva āgatā.

itthiratanaṃ

Tattha saṇṭhānapāripūriyā adhikaṃ rūpaṃ assāti abhirūpā. Dissamānā ca cakkhūni pīṇayati, tasmā aññaṃ kiccavikkhepaṃ hitvāpi daṭṭhabbāti dassanīyā. Dissamānā ca somanassavasena cittaṃ pasādetīti pāsādikā. Paramāyāti evaṃ pasādāvahattā uttamāya. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti vaṇṇasundaratāya. Samannāgatāti upetā. Abhirūpā vā yasmā nātidīghā nātirassā dassanīyā yasmā nātikisā nātithūlā, pāsādikā yasmā nātikāḷikā naccodātā. Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā yasmā atikkantā mānusaṃ vaṇṇaṃ appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ. Manussānañhi vaṇṇābhā bahi na niccharati, devānaṃ atidūraṃ niccharati, tassā pana dvādasahatthappamāṇaṃ padesaṃ sarīrābhā obhāseti.

abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā. Paramāyā Vaṇṇapokkharatāyā Samannāgatā Abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā

Nātidīghādīsu cassā paṭhamayugaḷena ārohasampatti, dutiyayugaḷena pariṇāhasampatti, tatiyayugaḷena vaṇṇasampatti vuttā. Chahi vāpi etehi kāyavipattiyā abhāvo, atikkantā mānusaṃ vaṇṇanti iminā kāyasampatti vuttā.

Tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vāti sappimaṇḍe pakkhipitvā ṭhapitassa satavihatassa tūlapicuno vā satavihatassa kappāsapicuno vā kāyasamphasso hoti. Sīteti rañño sītakāle. Uṇheti rañño uṇhakāle. Candanagandhoti niccakālameva supisitassa abhinavassa catujjātisamāyojitassa haricandanassa gandho kāyato vāyati. Uppalagandhoti hasitakathitakālesu mukhato nikkhanto taṅkhaṇaṃ vikasitasseva nīluppalassa atisurabhigandho vāyati.

Tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vā Sīte Uṇhe Candanagandho Uppalagandho

Evaṃ rūpasamphassagandhasampattiyuttāya panassā sarīrasampattiyā anurūpaṃ ācāraṃ dassetuṃ taṃ kho panātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rājānaṃ disvā nisinnāsanato aggidaḍḍhā viya paṭhamameva uṭṭhātīti pubbuṭṭhāyinī. Tasmiṃ nisinne tassa rañño tālavaṇṭena bījanādikiccaṃ katvā pacchā nipatati nisīdatīti pacchānipātinī. Kiṃ karomi devāti tassa kiṃkāraṃ paṭissāvetīti kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī. Rañño manāpameva carati karotīti manāpacārinī. Yaṃ rañño piyaṃ, tadeva vadatīti piyavādinī.

taṃ kho panā pubbuṭṭhāyinī pacchānipātinī kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī manāpacārinī piyavādinī

Idāni svāssā ācāro bhāvasuddhiyā eva, na sāṭheyyenāti dassetuṃ taṃ kho panātiādimāha. Tattha no aticaratīti na atikkamitvā carati, aññaṃ purisaṃ cittenapi na patthetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha ye tassā ādimhi ‘‘abhirūpā’’tiādayo ante ‘‘pubbuṭṭhāyinī’’tiādayo guṇā vuttā, te pakatiguṇā eva ‘‘atikkantā mānusaṃ vaṇṇa’’ntiādayo pana cakkavattino puññaṃ upanissāya cakkaratanapātubhāvato paṭṭhāya purimakammānubhāvena nibbattantīti veditabbā. Abhirūpatādikāpi vā cakkaratanapātubhāvato paṭṭhāya sabbākārapāripūrā jātā. Tenāha evarūpaṃ itthiratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

taṃ kho panā no aticaratī evarūpaṃ itthiratanaṃ pātubhavatī

Gahapatiratanavaṇṇanā

Evaṃ pātubhūtaitthiratanassa pana rañño cakkavattissa dhanakaraṇīyānaṃ kiccānaṃ yathāsukhappavattanatthaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pātubhavati. So pakatiyāva mahābhogo mahābhogakule jāto rañño dhanarāsivaḍḍhako seṭṭhi gahapati hoti, cakkaratanānubhāvasahitaṃ panassa kammavipākajaṃ dibbacakkhu pātubhavati, yena antopathaviyaṃ yojanabbhantare nidhiṃ passati. So taṃ sampattiṃ disvā tuṭṭhahadayo gantvā rājānaṃ dhanena pavāretvā sabbāni dhanakaraṇīyāni sampādeti. Tena vuttaṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… evarūpaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pātubhavatīti.

gahapatiratanaṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… evarūpaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pātubhavatī

Pariṇāyakaratanavaṇṇanā

Evaṃ pātubhūtagahapatiratanassa pana rañño cakkavattissa sabbakiccasaṃvidhānasamatthaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavati. So rañño jeṭṭhaputtova hoti . Pakatiyā eva paṇḍito byatto medhāvī, rañño puññānubhāvaṃ nissāya panassa attano kammānubhāvena paracittañāṇaṃ uppajjati. Yena dvādasayojanāya rājaparisāya cittācāraṃ ñatvā rañño ahite hite ca vavatthapetuṃ samattho hoti. Sopi taṃ attano ānubhāvaṃ disvā tuṭṭhahadayo rājānaṃ sabbakiccānusāsanena pavāreti. Tena vuttaṃ puna caparaṃ…pe… pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavatīti. Tattha ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetunti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhānantare ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetuṃ.

pariṇāyakaratanaṃ puna caparaṃ…pe… pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavatī ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetu
commentary_english:
258. Thus, when the wheel jewel had appeared, the advisors of the universal monarch had a suitable auspicious elephant-station prepared, cleaning a section of ground, and after having it smeared with fragrant scents such as *haricandana*, they covered the bottom with various colored fragrant flowers, and the top with a canopy adorned with closely-set pleasing garlands of gold stars, having elaborately prepared it like a divine mansion, they say, “O Lord, contemplate the arrival of an elephant jewel of this form!”

He, having given a great gift according to the method stated earlier, undertaking sīla, reflecting on that merit-sampatti, sits down. Then, impelled by the power of merit, either from the Chaddanta lineage or the Uposatha lineage, desiring to experience that special honor, the best of elephants, his body the color of pure white, adorned with a young sunlike disc, with red feet and neck and face, well-established, with well-arranged major and minor limbs, with lovely blossoming red lotuslike lotus leaves, capable of going into space like a powerful yogi, with its surroundings painted with *manosilā* powder, like a silver mountain, stands in that place.

That one, coming from the Chaddanta lineage, comes as the youngest of all, and the one from the Uposatha lineage is the eldest of all.

In the Pāḷi, however, it only comes as “Uposatha, the Nāga king.”

That one, contemplating in accordance with the method stated in the sutras of the universal monarchs who have fulfilled the duties of a universal monarch, comes; it does not come to others.

That one himself, having come to the appropriate auspicious elephant-station, having removed the auspicious elephant, stands there.

Therefore it was said, “Again, further, *bhikkhus*…pe… the Nāga king.”

Having seen that elephant jewel which had thus appeared, the elephant-keepers and others, delighted and joyful, quickly go and announce it to the king.

The king, having come very quickly, seeing that, his mind pleased, thinking, “Indeed, a fine elephant vehicle; if it would submit to taming!” extends his hand.

Then that one, showing a gentle disposition, having hung down his ear like a calf of a domestic cow, approaches the king; the king wants to mount him.

Then his attendants, knowing his intention, prepare that elephant jewel, making it with a golden banner, with golden ornaments, covered with a golden net, and bring it near.

The king, without having him sit down, ascends by means of a staircase made of the seven jewels, his mind intent on going into the sky.

As soon as his mind arises, that elephant king, like a royal goose, crosses over the blue sky surface shimmering with the light of sapphire jewels. Then, in accordance with the method stated for the wheel-journey, the entire royal retinue…

Thus, the king, together with his retinue, having traveled around the entire earth in but the time it takes to drink a sip, returns to the capital. Thus is the elephant jewel of a universal monarch greatly powerful.

Therefore it was said, “Having seen the elephant jewel of the king, the universal monarch…pe… an elephant jewel of this form appears.”

*Elephant Jewel.
Having seen the elephant jewel of the king, the universal monarch…pe… an elephant jewel of this form appears.* Description of the Horse Jewel

Thus, when the elephant jewel had appeared, the retinue of the universal monarch, having had a suitable auspicious horse-station prepared, cleaned, and leveled, and having decorated it, just as before, generate enthusiasm for the king’s thought of arriving.

He, just as before, having performed the giving of gifts and honor, sits down on the palace terrace, undertaking sīla, recollecting the merit-sampatti. Then, impelled by the power of merit, from the Sindhava lineage, with the splendor of a heap of autumn clouds white like the season of clear lightning flashes, with red feet, with a red beak, his body the color of a dense mass of pure, smooth moonbeams, his head possessing a dark color like a crow’s neck and like a sapphire jewel, therefore, with a “black head”, with hairs like *muñja* grass, with smooth, round, upright, straight tresses, therefore, with “*muñja* hair, a space-goer,” a horse king named Valāhaka, having come, stands in that place.

Everything else should be understood according to the method stated for the elephant jewel.

Referring to a horse jewel of such a form, the Blessed One said, “Again, further,” etc.

*Black Head, Muñja Hair, Space-goer.
Horse Jewel.
Again, further.* Description of the Jewel Jewel

Thus, when the horse jewel had appeared, there comes to the king, the universal monarch, from Mount Vepulla, a jewel jewel four cubits long, its circumference equal to the nave of a cartwheel, adorned at both ends with two golden lotuses with clusters of very pure pearls coming forth from the *kaṇṇikā* perimeter, surrounded by eighty-four thousand jewels, repelling the glory of the full moon surrounded by a host of stars.

For that one who has thus come, having placed it in a pearl net, having raised it into the sky a height of sixty cubits by means of a series of bamboos, in the night portion, the light shines all around for a distance of one *yojana*, by which that entire space has a light that is like the time of the rising of the dawn.

Then the farmers perform farming work, the merchants perform the opening of the shops, and those craftsmen apply themselves to that particular work, thinking that it is daytime.

Therefore it was said, “Again, further, *bhikkhus*…pe… a jewel jewel appears.”

*Jewel Jewel.
Again, further, *bhikkhus*…pe… a jewel jewel appears.* Description of the Woman Jewel

Thus, when the jewel jewel has appeared, a woman jewel, the special cause of sensual pleasure, appears to the universal monarch.

Either they bring his chief queen from the Madda royal lineage, or, by the power of merit, she comes herself from Uttarakuru.
Moreover, the remaining qualities of this woman-treasure of the wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), such as "again, furthermore, monks, a jewel of a woman appears to the wheel-turning monarch, beautiful, lovely," etc., are found in the Pali canon itself.

Woman-treasure:

There, *abhirūpā* [beautiful] means she has an abundance of beauty because of the completeness of her form.

*Dassanīyā* [lovely] means that when seen, she pleases the eyes; therefore, she should be looked at even after abandoning other distracting tasks.

*Pāsādikā* [delightful] means that when seen, she gladdens the mind by way of joy.

*Paramāya* [supreme] means superior because she is the bringer of delight; excellent.

*Vaṇṇapokkharatāyā* [endowed with the beauty of a lotus] means beautiful in color.

*Samannāgatā* [possessed of] means endowed.

*Abhirūpā* [beautiful] because she is neither too tall nor too short; *dassanīyā* [lovely] because she is neither too thin nor too stout; *pāsādikā* [delightful] because she is neither too swarthy nor exceedingly fair.

*Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā* [possessed of the supreme beauty of a lotus] because she has surpassed human complexion and has not attained divine complexion.

Indeed, the radiance of humans' complexions does not go out far, but that of the gods goes out extremely far; however, the radiance of her body illuminates an area measuring twelve handbreadths.

*Abhirūpā* [beautiful], *dassanīyā* [lovely], *pāsādikā* [delightful].

*Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā* [possessed of the supreme beauty of a lotus]. In the series beginning with "neither too tall," her rising excellence is stated by the first pair, her roundness of limb excellence by the second pair, and her color excellence by the third pair.

Also, by these six, the absence of bodily misfortune [is stated], and by this [statement], "she has surpassed human complexion," bodily success is stated.

"Like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of wool": the touch of her body is like that of cotton that has been placed in curdled ghee and then struck a hundred times, or like that of wool that has been struck a hundred times.

*Sīte* [in the cold] means in the king's cold season.

*Uṇhe* [in the heat] means in the king's hot season.

*Candanagandho* [sandalwood fragrance] means that at all times a sandalwood fragrance blows from her body, [a fragrance] of fresh red sandalwood that has been well-ground and combined from four kinds [of sandalwood].

*Uppalagandho* [blue-lotus fragrance] means that at the times of smiling and speaking, a very fragrant fragrance, like that of a just-blossomed blue lotus, blows from her mouth.

Like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of wool.

In this way, to show conduct that is appropriate to her bodily success that is endowed with excellence of form, touch, and smell, "Then, indeed," etc., was said.

There, *pubbuṭṭhāyinī* [one who rises early] means that upon seeing the king, she rises immediately from her seat as if burned by fire.

*Pacchānipātinī* [one who retires late] means that after he sits, she attends him with fanning and other such services, and only then retires to her seat.

*Kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī* [one who replies "What should I do?"] means that when [the king] says, "What should I do, O god?" she replies to his question.

*Manāpacārinī* [one who acts agreeably] means that she behaves and acts only in ways that are pleasing to the king.

*Piyavādinī* [one who speaks affectionately] means that she speaks only what is dear to the king.

Now, to show that her conduct is out of purity of heart alone and not out of deceit, "[Then, indeed,]" etc., was said.

There, *no aticaratī* [she does not transgress] means that she does not behave transgressively; it is said that she does not desire another man even in thought.

There, the qualities that were stated at the beginning of her, such as "beautiful," etc., and at the end, such as "one who rises early," etc., are merely natural qualities, but the ones beginning with "she has surpassed human complexion," etc., should be understood to come into being by the power of former karma, relying on the merit of the wheel-turning monarch, from the moment the wheel-treasure appears.

Or, her being beautiful, etc., also became completely perfect in every way from the moment the wheel-treasure appeared.

Therefore, he said, "A woman-treasure of this sort appears."

*Gahapatiratana-vaṇṇanā* [Description of the treasurer-treasure]

Furthermore, for the sake of the easy execution of tasks involving wealth for the wheel-turning monarch who possesses such a woman-treasure, a treasurer-treasure (*gahapati-ratana*) appears.

He is naturally very wealthy and born into a very wealthy family, and he is a treasurer and householder who increases the king's store of riches; moreover, a divine eye (*divyacakṣu*) arises in him as a result of karma-ripening, endowed with the power of the wheel-treasure, by which he sees treasures within a *yojana* beneath the earth.

Having seen that wealth,
Having a delighted heart, he goes to the king, satisfies him with wealth, and accomplishes all wealth-related tasks.

Therefore, it was said, "Again, monks...pe...such a householder-jewel appears."

*Gahapatiratanaṃ*

Again, monks...pe...such a householder-jewel appears.

*Pariṇāyakaratanavaṇṇanā* (Explanation of the advisor-jewel)

Thus, for the king, the wheel-turner, who has the householder-jewel that has appeared, an *advisor-jewel* (*pariṇāyaka-ratanaṃ*) appears, who is capable of managing all affairs. He is like the eldest son of the king. By nature, he is wise, clever, and intelligent, and relying on the king's meritorious power, knowledge of others' minds arises in him due to his own karmic power. By this, knowing the conduct of the minds of the royal assembly within twelve yojanas, he is capable of determining what is harmful and beneficial to the king. He, too, seeing that power of his, with a delighted heart, satisfies the king by instructing him in all matters.

Therefore, it was said, "Again...pe...the advisor-jewel appears."

There, *ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetu* means to place what should be placed in each respective place.

*Pariṇāyakaratanaṃ*

Again...pe...the advisor-jewel appears.

*ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetu*

mula_pali:
259. ‘‘Katamāhi catūhi iddhīhi? Idha, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī abhirūpo hoti dassanīyo pāsādiko paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato ativiya aññehi manussehi. Rājā, bhikkhave, cakkavattī imāya paṭhamāya iddhiyā samannāgato hoti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī dīghāyuko hoti ciraṭṭhitiko ativiya aññehi manussehi. Rājā, bhikkhave, cakkavattī imāya dutiyāya iddhiyā samannāgato hoti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī appābādho hoti appātaṅko samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya ativiya aññehi manussehi. Rājā, bhikkhave, cakkavattī imāya tatiyāya iddhiyā samannāgato hoti.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pitā puttānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo, evameva kho, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo. Raññopi, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa brāhmaṇagahapatikā piyā honti manāpā. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pitu puttā piyā honti manāpā, evameva kho, bhikkhave, raññopi cakkavattissa brāhmaṇagahapatikā piyā honti manāpā.

‘‘Bhūtapubbaṃ , bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī caturaṅginiyā senāya uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyāsi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, brāhmaṇagahapatikā rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘ataramāno, deva, yāhi yathā taṃ mayaṃ cirataraṃ passeyyāmā’ti. Rājāpi, bhikkhave, cakkavattī sārathiṃ āmantesi – ‘ataramāno , sārathi, pesehi yathā maṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikā cirataraṃ passeyyu’nti. Rājā, bhikkhave, cakkavattī imāya catutthāya iddhiyā samannāgato hoti. Rājā, bhikkhave, cakkavattī imāhi catūhi iddhīhi samannāgato hoti.

‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu kho rājā cakkavattī imehi sattahi ratanehi samannāgato imāhi catūhi ca iddhīhi tatonidānaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvediyethā’’ti? ‘‘Ekamekenapi, bhante, ratanena tena ratanena (sī.) samannāgato rājā cakkavattī tatonidānaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvediyetha, ko pana vādo sattahi ratanehi catūhi ca iddhīhī’’ti?

tena ratanena (sī.)
mula_english:
259. "Which are the four kinds of success? Here, monks, a Wheel-turning Monarch is handsome (abhirūpa), comely (dassanīya), and graceful (pāsādika), possessing the supreme beauty of complexion (paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya), and he surpasses other human beings (manussehi) in that respect. This is the first kind of success (paṭhamāya iddhiyā) that a Wheel-turning Monarch possesses.

“Again (puna caparaṃ), monks, a Wheel-turning Monarch is long-lived (dīghāyuko) and enduring (ciraṭṭhitiko), and he surpasses other human beings in that respect. This is the second kind of success (dutiyāya iddhiyā) that a Wheel-turning Monarch possesses.

“Again (puna caparaṃ), monks, a Wheel-turning Monarch is free from illness (appābādho) and affliction (appātaṅko), possessing a good digestion (samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā) that is neither too cool (nātisītāya) nor too warm (nāccuṇhāya), and he surpasses other human beings in that respect. This is the third kind of success (tatiyāya iddhiyā) that a Wheel-turning Monarch possesses.

“Again (puna caparaṃ), monks, a Wheel-turning Monarch is dear (piyo) and agreeable (manāpo) to *brāhmaṇas* and householders (*gahapatis*). Just as (seyyathāpi), monks, a father is dear (piyo) and agreeable (manāpo) to his children (*puttā*), so too (evameva kho), monks, a Wheel-turning Monarch is dear (piyo) and agreeable (manāpo) to *brāhmaṇas* and householders (*gahapatis*). *Brāhmaṇas* and householders (*gahapatis*) too, are dear (piyā) and agreeable (manāpā) to a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavattissa). Just as (seyyathāpi), monks, children (*puttā*) are dear (piyā) and agreeable (manāpā) to a father (*pitu*), so too (evameva kho), monks, *brāhmaṇas* and householders (*gahapatis*) are dear (piyā) and agreeable (manāpā) to a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavattissa).

“Once (bhūtapubbaṃ), monks, a Wheel-turning Monarch was driving in a pleasure park (uyyānabhūmiṃ) with his four-constituent army (caturaṅginiyā senāya). Then (atha kho), monks, *brāhmaṇas* and householders (*gahapatis*) went to the Wheel-turning Monarch (rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ), and spoke thus (evamāhaṃsu): ‘Sire (deva), drive slowly (ataramāno), that we (mayaṃ) may see (passeyyāma) you (taṃ) longer (cirataraṃ).’ And so the Wheel-turning Monarch (rājāpi cakkavattī), monks, told his charioteer (sārathiṃ āmanteti): ‘Charioteer (sārathi), drive slowly (ataramāno), that the *brāhmaṇas* and householders (*gahapatis*) may see (passeyyuṃ) me (maṃ) longer (cirataraṃ).’ This is the fourth kind of success (catutthāya iddhiyā) that a Wheel-turning Monarch possesses. A Wheel-turning Monarch (rājā cakkavattī), monks, possesses these four kinds of success (imāhi catūhi iddhīhi).

“What do you think (taṃ kiṃ maññatha), monks? Would a Wheel-turning Monarch (rājā cakkavattī), because of possessing these seven treasures (imehi sattahi ratanehi) and these four kinds of success (imāhi catūhi ca iddhīhi), experience pleasure (sukhaṃ) and joy (somanassaṃ)?” “Venerable sir (bhante), a Wheel-turning Monarch (rājā cakkavattī) would experience pleasure (sukhaṃ) and joy (somanassaṃ) because of possessing even one treasure (ekamekenapi ratanena), let alone seven treasures (sattahi ratanehi) and four kinds of success (catūhi ca iddhīhi)!”
commentary_pali: 259.Samavepākiniyātiādi heṭṭhā vuttameva.
commentary_english: 259. The same can be said [about other examples] such as *samavepākinīyā*, etc., [which was] stated below.

mula_pali:
260. Atha kho bhagavā parittaṃ pāṇimattaṃ pāsāṇaṃ gahetvā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamo nu kho mahantataro – yo cāyaṃ mayā paritto pāṇimatto pāsāṇo gahito yo ca himavā pabbatarājā’’ti? ‘‘Appamattako ayaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā paritto pāṇimatto pāsāṇo gahito; himavantaṃ pabbatarājānaṃ upanidhāya saṅkhampi na upeti; kalabhāgampi na upeti; upanidhampi na upetī’’ti. ‘‘Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ rājā cakkavattī sattahi ratanehi samannāgato catūhi ca iddhīhi tatonidānaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti taṃ dibbassa sukhassa upanidhāya saṅkhampi na upeti; kalabhāgampi na upeti; upanidhampi na upeti’’.

‘‘Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito sace kadāci karahaci dīghassa addhuno accayena manussattaṃ āgacchati, yāni tāni uccākulāni – khattiyamahāsālakulaṃ vā brāhmaṇamahāsālakulaṃ vā gahapatimahāsālakulaṃ vā tathārūpe kule paccājāyati aḍḍhe mahaddhane mahābhoge pahūtajātarūparajate pahūtavittūpakaraṇe pahūtadhanadhaññe. So ca hoti abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato, lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa. So kāyena sucaritaṃ carati, vācāya sucaritaṃ carati, manasā sucaritaṃ carati. So kāyena sucaritaṃ caritvā, vācāya sucaritaṃ caritvā, manasā sucaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, akkhadhutto paṭhameneva kaṭaggahena mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ adhigaccheyya; appamattako so, bhikkhave, kaṭaggaho yaṃ so akkhadhutto paṭhameneva kaṭaggahena mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ adhigaccheyya. Atha kho ayameva tato mahantataro kaṭaggaho yaṃ so paṇḍito kāyena sucaritaṃ caritvā, vācāya sucaritaṃ caritvā, manasā sucaritaṃ caritvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, kevalā paripūrā paṇḍitabhūmī’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Bālapaṇḍitasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.
mula_english:
260. Then, taking a small stone the size of his hand, the Blessed One addressed the *bhikkhus* thus: “What do you think, *bhikkhus*? Which is the greater, this small stone that I have taken, the size of my hand, or Himavat, the king of mountains?”

“Venerable sir, the small stone that the Blessed One has taken, the size of his hand, does not count beside Himavat, the king of mountains; it is not even a fraction, there is no comparison.”

“So too, *bhikkhus*, the pleasure and joy that a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakravartin*) would experience because of possessing the seven treasures (*saptaratna*) and the four kinds of success does not count beside the happiness of heaven; it is not even a fraction, there is no comparison.

“If, some time or other, at the end of a long period, the wise man (*paṇḍita*) comes back to the human state, it is into a high family that he is reborn - into a family of well-to-do nobles (*khattiyamahāsālakula*), or well-to-do *brāhmaṇas* (*brāhmaṇamahāsālakula*), or well-to-do householders (*gahapatimahāsālakula*) - one that is rich,-of great wealth, of great possessions, with abundant gold (*jātarūpa*) and silver (*rajata*), with abundant assets and means, and with abundant money and grain.

He is handsome, comely and graceful, possessing the supreme beauty of complexion. He obtains food and drink, clothes, vehicles, garlands, scents and unguents, bed, lodging, and light.

He conducts himself well in body (*kāyena*), speech (*vācāya*), and mind (*manasā*).

Having conducted himself well in body, speech, and mind, on the dissolution of the body (*kāyassa bhedā*), after death (*maraṇā*), he reappears in a happy destination (*sugati*), even in heaven (*svarga*), the world (*loka*).

“Bhikkhus, suppose a gambler at the very first lucky throw won a great fortune, yet a lucky throw such as that is negligible."

it is a far more lucky throw when a wise man (*paṇḍita*) who conducts himself well in body (*kāyena*), speech (*vācāya*), and mind (*manasā*), on the dissolution of the body (*kāyassa bhedā*), after death (*maraṇā*), reappears in a happy destination (*sugati*), even in heaven (*svarga*), the world (*loka*).

This is the complete perfection of the wise man’s grade.”

Thus spoke the Lord (*bhagavān*).

Elated, those *bhikkhus* delighted in the Blessed One’s statement.

The *Bālapaṇḍitasutta* is finished, the ninth.
commentary_pali:
260.Kaṭaggahenāti jayaggāhena. Mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhanti ekappahāreneva dve vā tīṇi vā satasahassāni. Kevalā paripūrā paṇḍitabhūmīti paṇḍito tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā sagge nibbattati, tato manussalokaṃ āgacchanto kularūpabhogasampattiyaṃ nibbattati, tattha ṭhito tīṇi ca sucaritāni pūretvā puna sagge nibbattatīti ayaṃ sakalā paripuṇṇā paṇḍitabhūmi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Bālapaṇḍitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
260. *kaṭaggahenā* means by seizing the branch.
*mahantaṃ bhogakkhandha* means by a single blow, either two or three hundred thousand.
*kevalā paripūrā paṇḍitabhūmī* means the wise man, having fulfilled three good practices, is reborn in heaven; then, coming to the world of humans, he is reborn with family, form, enjoyment and prosperity; abiding there, and again fulfilling three good practices, he is reborn in heaven again; this is the complete and perfect ground of the wise.
The rest is clear throughout.

The commentary to the Bālapaṇḍitasutta in the Papañcasūdanī, commentary to the Majjhimanikāya, is finished.

mula_pali:
261. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘bhikkhavo’’ti. ‘‘Bhadante’’ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dve agārā sadvārā sandhidvārā (ka.), tattha cakkhumā puriso majjhe ṭhito passeyya manusse gehaṃ pavisantepi nikkhamantepi anucaṅkamantepi anuvicarantepi; evameva kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe, sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāmi – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapannā. Ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā ; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā’’’ti.

sandhidvārā (ka.)
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One (bhagavā) was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park (Jetavane Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme). There the Blessed One (bhagavā) addressed the monks (bhikkhū), saying: "Monks (bhikkhavo)!" "Venerable sir (bhadante)," those monks (bhikkhū) replied to the Blessed One (bhagavato). The Blessed One (bhagavā) said this: "Suppose, monks (bhikkhave), there were two houses with doors sandhidvārā (ka.), and a man with good sight standing in the middle could see people entering and leaving, walking back and forth, and wandering about. In the same way, monks (bhikkhave), with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā) that is purified and surpasses the human, I see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. I understand beings passing on according to their actions: ‘These worthy beings (sattā) were endowed with good conduct of body (kāyasucaritena), good conduct of speech (vacīsucaritena), and good conduct of mind (manosucaritena); they were not revilers of the noble ones (ariyānaṃ anupavādakā), held right view (sammādiṭṭhikā), and undertook actions governed by right view (sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā). With the breakup of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), they have reappeared in a good destination (sugatiṃ), a heavenly world (saggaṃ lokaṃ).' "Or these worthy beings (sattā) were endowed with good conduct of body (kāyasucaritena), good conduct of speech (vacīsucaritena), and good conduct of mind (manosucaritena); they were not revilers of the noble ones (ariyānaṃ anupavādakā), held right view (sammādiṭṭhikā), and undertook actions governed by right view (sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā). With the breakup of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), they have reappeared among human beings (manussesu upapannā)." "But these worthy beings (sattā) were endowed with bad conduct of body (kāyaduccaritena), bad conduct of speech (vacīduccaritena), and bad conduct of mind (manoduccaritena); they were revilers of the noble ones (ariyānaṃ upavādakā), held wrong view (micchādiṭṭhikā), and undertook actions governed by wrong view (micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā); with the breakup of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), they have reappeared in the realm of ghosts (pettivisayaṃ upapannā)." "Or these worthy beings (sattā) were endowed with bad conduct of body (kāyaduccaritena), bad conduct of speech (vacīduccaritena), and bad conduct of mind (manoduccaritena); they were revilers of the noble ones (ariyānaṃ upavādakā), held wrong view (micchādiṭṭhikā), and undertook actions governed by wrong view (micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā); with the breakup of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), they have reappeared in the animal realm (tiracchānayoniṃ upapannā)." "Or these worthy beings (sattā) were endowed with bad conduct of body (kāyaduccaritena), bad conduct of speech (vacīduccaritena), and bad conduct of mind (manoduccaritena); they were revilers of the noble ones (ariyānaṃ upavādakā), held wrong view (micchādiṭṭhikā), and undertook actions governed by wrong view (micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā); with the breakup of the body (kāyassa bhedā), after death (paraṃ maraṇā), they have reappeared in a state of deprivation (apāyaṃ), a bad destination (duggatiṃ), a lower realm (vinipātaṃ), in hell (nirayaṃ upapannā)."

sandhidvārā (ka.)
commentary_pali: 261.Evaṃme sutanti devadūtasuttaṃ. Tattha dve agārātiādi assapurasutte vitthāritameva.
commentary_english:
Thus have I heard, the *devadūtasutta*.

There, the passage beginning with "two houses" (*dve agārā*) has already been explained in detail in the Assapura Sutta.

mula_pali:
262. ‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā nānābāhāsu gahetvā yamassa rañño dassenti – ‘ayaṃ, deva, puriso amatteyyo apetteyyo asāmañño abrāhmañño, na kule jeṭṭhāpacāyī. Imassa devo daṇḍaṃ paṇetū’ti. Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā paṭhamaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjati samanugāhati samanubhāsati – ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṃ addasa manussesu paṭhamaṃ devadūtaṃ pātubhūta’nti? So evamāha – ‘nāddasaṃ, bhante’ti.

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṃ addasa manussesu daharaṃ kumāraṃ mandaṃ uttānaseyyakaṃ sake muttakarīse palipannaṃ semāna’nti? So evamāha – ‘addasaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, tassa te viññussa sato mahallakassa na etadahosi – ahampi khomhi jātidhammo, jātiṃ anatīto. Handāhaṃ kalyāṇaṃ karomi kāyena vācāya manasā’ti? So evamāha – ‘nāsakkhissaṃ, bhante, pamādassaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

‘‘Tamenaṃ , bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, pamādavatāya na kalyāṇamakāsi kāyena vācāya manasā. Taggha tvaṃ, ambho purisa, tathā karissanti yathā taṃ pamattaṃ. Taṃ kho pana te etaṃ pāpakammaṃ pāpaṃ kammaṃ (sī. pī.) neva mātarā kataṃ na pitarā kataṃ na bhātarā kataṃ na bhaginiyā kataṃ na mittāmaccehi kataṃ na ñātisālohitehi kataṃ na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṃ na devatāhi kataṃ, tayāvetaṃ pāpakammaṃ pāpaṃ kammaṃ (sī. pī.) kataṃ, tvaññevetassa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedissasī’’’ti.

pāpaṃ kammaṃ (sī. pī.) pāpaṃ kammaṃ (sī. pī.)
mula_english:
262. “Then, monks, the wardens of hell, seizing him by various arms, present him to Yama, the king, saying: ‘Sire, this man has been disrespectful to his mother (*amāteyya*), disrespectful to his father (*apetteyya*), disrespectful to ascetics (*asāmañño*), disrespectful to brahmins (*abrāhmañño*), and he had no respect for the elders of his clan (*na kule jeṭṭhāpacāyī*).

Let the king order his punishment (*imassa devo daṇḍaṃ paṇetū’ti*).”

“Then, monks, Yama, the king, questions him about the first divine messenger, examines him, and addresses him: ‘Good man (*ambho purisa*), did you not see the first divine messenger appearing among humans (*na tvaṃ addasa manussesu paṭhamaṃ devadūtaṃ pātubhūta’nti*)?’ He replies, ‘I did not see, venerable sir (*nāddasaṃ, bhante’ti*).’”

“Then, monks, Yama, the king, says to him: ‘Good man (*ambho purisa*), did you not see among humans a tender (*daharaṃ*) child (*kumāraṃ*), weak (*mandaṃ*), lying on its back (*uttānaseyyakaṃ*), wallowing in its own urine and excrement (*sake muttakarīse palipannaṃ semāna’nti*)?’ He replies, ‘I did see, venerable sir (*addasaṃ, bhante’’’ti*).”

“Then, monks, Yama, the king, says to him: ‘Good man (*ambho purisa*), did it not occur to you—an intelligent (*viññussa*), mindful (*sato*), mature (*mahallakassa*) man—that I, too, am subject to birth (*jātidhammo*), not exempt from birth (*jātiṃ anatīto*)?

Why then did I not do good by body, speech, and mind (*handāhaṃ kalyāṇaṃ karomi kāyena vācāya manasā’ti*)?’ He replies, ‘I was not able, venerable sir (*nāsakkhissaṃ, bhante*), I was negligent, venerable sir (*pamādassaṃ, bhante’’’ti*).”

“Then, monks, Yama, the king, says to him: ‘Good man (*ambho purisa*), through negligence (*pamādavatāya*) you did not do good (*na kalyāṇamakāsi*) by body (*kāyena*), speech (*vācāya*), and mind (*manasā*).

Indeed (*taggha*), good man (*ambho purisa*), they will deal with you according to your negligence (*tathā karissanti yathā taṃ pamattaṃ*).

That evil action (*pāpakammaṃ*) of yours was not done by your mother (*mātarā kataṃ*), nor by your father (*pitarā kataṃ*), nor by your brother (*bhātarā kataṃ*), nor by your sister (*bhaginiyā kataṃ*), nor by your friends and companions (*mittāmaccehi kataṃ*), nor by your relatives (*ñātisālohitehi kataṃ*), nor by ascetics and brahmins (*samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṃ*), nor by the gods (*devatāhi kataṃ*); that evil action (*pāpakammaṃ*) was done by you alone (*tayāvetaṃ pāpakammaṃ kataṃ*), and you alone will experience its result (*tvaññevetassa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedissasī’’’ti*).”
commentary_pali:
262.Nirayaṃ upapannāti bhagavā katthaci nirayato paṭṭhāya desanaṃ devalokena osāpeti, katthaci devalokato paṭṭhāya nirayena osāpeti. Sace saggasampattiṃ vitthāretvā kathetukāmo hoti, nirayadukkhaṃ ekadesato katheti, tiracchānayonidukkhaṃ pettivisayadukkhaṃ manussalokasampattiṃ ekadesato katheti, saggasampattimeva vitthāreti. Sace nirayadukkhaṃ vitthāretvā kathetukāmo hoti, devalokamanussalokesu sampattiṃ tiracchānayonipettivisayesu ca dukkhaṃ ekadesato katheti, nirayadukkhameva vitthāreti. So imasmiṃ sutte nirayadukkhaṃ vitthāretukāmo, tasmā devalokato paṭṭhāya desanaṃ nirayena osāpeti. Devalokamanussalokasampattiyo tiracchānayonipettivisayadukkhāni ca ekadesato kathetvā nirayadukkhameva vitthārena kathetuṃ tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, nirayapālātiādimāha.

Tattha ekacce therā ‘‘nirayapālā nāma natthi, yantarūpaṃ viya kammameva kāraṇaṃ kāretī’’ti vadanti. Tesaṃ taṃ ‘‘atthi niraye nirayapālāti, āmantā, atthi ca kāraṇikā’’tiādinā nayena abhidhamme (kathā. 866) paṭisedhitameva. Yathā hi manussaloke kammakāraṇakārakā atthi, evameva niraye nirayapālā atthīti. Yamassa raññoti yamarājā nāma vemānikapetarājā, ekasmiṃ kāle dibbavimāne dibbakapparukkhadibbauyyānadibbanāṭakādisampattiṃ anubhavati, ekasmiṃ kāle kammavipākaṃ, dhammiko rājā. Na cesa ekova hoti, catūsu pana dvāresu cattāro janā honti. Nāddasanti attano santike pesitassa kassaci devadūtassa abhāvaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vadati. Atha naṃ yamo ‘‘nāyaṃ bhāsitassa atthaṃ sallakkhetī’’ti ñatvā sallakkhāpetukāmo ambhotiādimāha.

‘‘nirayapālā Yamassa rañño Nāddasa ambho

Jātidhammoti jātisabhāvo, aparimutto jātiyā, jāti nāma mayhaṃ abbhantareyeva atthīti. Parato jarādhammotiādīsupi eseva nayo.

Jātidhammo jarādhammo
commentary_english:
262. "Having been born in hell": In some instances, the Blessed One brings his teaching to a close with the heavenly realm, beginning with hell, and in other instances, he brings his teaching to a close with hell, beginning with the heavenly realm.

If he wishes to expound on the prosperity of the heavenly realm, he speaks in brief about the suffering of hell, the suffering of the animal realm, the suffering of the realm of the departed spirits, and the prosperity of the human realm, but he expounds at length only on the prosperity of the heavenly realm.

If he wishes to expound on the suffering of hell, he speaks in brief about prosperity in the heavenly and human realms, and the suffering in the animal realm and the realm of departed spirits, but he expounds at length only on the suffering of hell.

So, in this *sutta*, he wishes to expound on the suffering of hell, therefore, beginning with the heavenly realm, he brings his teaching to a close with hell.

After speaking in brief about prosperity in the heavenly and human realms, and the sufferings in the animal realm and the realm of departed spirits, he speaks at length about the suffering of hell, [saying,] "Then, *bhikkhus*, the hell-wardens," and so on.

There, some *theras* say, "There are no so-called 'hell-wardens'; karma itself, like a machine, is the agent that causes [suffering]."

Their [view] is refuted in the *Abhidhamma* (in the *Kathā-vatthu*, 866) with the line, "Are there hell-wardens in hell? Yes. And are there judicial agents?"

Just as in the human realm there are agents who do actions, so too in hell there are hell-wardens.

"*Yamassa rañño*": Yama, the king, is a king of departed spirits who is in a celestial mansion. At one time he experiences the prosperity of a divine palace, divine wish-fulfilling trees, divine parks, divine theatrical performances, and so on; at another time, he [experiences] the result of karma. He is a righteous king.

And he is not alone; but at the four gates there are four people.

"*Nāddasa*": He says this in reference to the absence of any divine messenger sent to his presence.

Then Yama, knowing that "This one does not understand the meaning of what has been said," wishing to make him understand, says, "*Ambho*," and so on.

"*Nirayapālā yamassa rañño nāddasa ambho*":

"*Jātidhammo*": "*Jāti-sabhāvo*, subject to birth, not freed from birth, 'birth' exists within me."

And so the same method [applies] in the following [phrases,] "*jarādhammo*," and so on.

*Jātidhammo jarādhammo*

mula_pali:
263. ‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā paṭhamaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjitvā samanugāhitvā samanubhāsitvā dutiyaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjati samanugāhati samanubhāsati – ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṃ addasa manussesu dutiyaṃ devadūtaṃ pātubhūta’nti? So evamāha – ‘nāddasaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṃ addasa manussesu itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā ( ) (āsītikaṃ vā nāvutikaṃ vā vassasatikaṃ vā jātiyā) (ka. sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) tikaṅguttarepi jiṇṇaṃ gopānasivaṅkaṃ bhoggaṃ daṇḍaparāyanaṃ pavedhamānaṃ gacchantaṃ āturaṃ gatayobbanaṃ khaṇḍadantaṃ palitakesaṃ vilūnaṃ khalitasiraṃ khalitaṃsiro (sī.), khalitaṃsiraṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī.) valinaṃ tilakāhatagatta’nti? So evamāha – ‘addasaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

(āsītikaṃ vā nāvutikaṃ vā vassasatikaṃ vā jātiyā) (ka. sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) tikaṅguttarepi khalitaṃsiro (sī.), khalitaṃsiraṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī.)

‘‘Tamenaṃ , bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, tassa te viññussa sato mahallakassa na etadahosi – ahampi khomhi jarādhammo, jaraṃ anatīto. Handāhaṃ kalyāṇaṃ karomi kāyena vācāya manasā’ti? So evamāha – ‘nāsakkhissaṃ, bhante, pamādassaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, pamādavatāya na kalyāṇamakāsi kāyena vācāya manasā. Taggha tvaṃ, ambho purisa, tathā karissanti yathā taṃ pamattaṃ. Taṃ kho pana te etaṃ pāpakammaṃ neva mātarā kataṃ na pitarā kataṃ na bhātarā kataṃ na bhaginiyā kataṃ na mittāmaccehi kataṃ na ñātisālohitehi kataṃ na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṃ na devatāhi kataṃ, tayāvetaṃ pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, tvaññevetassa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedissasī’’’ti.
mula_english:
263. “Then, monks, King Yama, having questioned, examined, and conversed with him about the first divine messenger, questions, examines, and converses with the second divine messenger, saying: ‘Good man, did you not see the second divine messenger appearing among humankind?’ He replies: ‘I did not see, venerable sir.’”

“Then, monks, King Yama said to him: ‘Good man, did you not see among humans a woman or a man (eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old by birth), decrepit, bent like a roof rafter, frail, leaning on a staff, trembling, going along, sick, youth gone, with broken teeth, gray hair, thinning, bald-headed, wrinkled, a body marred by moles?’ He replies: ‘I saw, venerable sir.’”

“Then, monks, King Yama said: ‘Good man, did it never occur to you—an intelligent and mature person—"I, too, am subject to old age, not exempt from old age. Let me do good by body, speech, and mind?"’ He replies: ‘I was not able, venerable sir, I was negligent, venerable sir.’”

“Then, monks, King Yama said: ‘Good man, through negligence, you did no good through body, speech, and mind. Indeed, good man, they will do to you as befits your negligence. That evil deed was not done by your mother, nor done by your father, nor done by your brother, nor done by your sister, nor done by friends and companions, nor done by relatives, nor done by ascetics and *brāhmaṇas*, nor done by deities; but that evil deed was done by you alone, and you alone will experience its result.’”
commentary_pali:
263.Paṭhamaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjitvāti ettha daharakumāro atthato evaṃ vadati nāma ‘‘passatha, bho, mayhampi tumhākaṃ viya hatthapādā atthi, sake panamhi muttakarīse palipanno, attano dhammatāya uṭṭhahitvā nhāyituṃ na sakkomi, ahaṃ kiliṭṭhagattomhi, nhāpetha manti vattumpi na sakkomi, jātitomhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi jātito aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākampi jāti āgamissati, iti tassā pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā’’ti. Tenesa devadūto nāma jāto, vacanattho pana maghadevasutte vuttova.

Dutiyaṃdevadūtanti etthāpi jarājiṇṇasatto atthato evaṃ vadati nāma – ‘‘passatha, bho, ahampi tumhe viya taruṇo ahosiṃ ūrubalabāhubalajavanasampanno, tassa me tā balajavanasampattiyo antarahitā, vijjamānāpi me hatthapādā hatthapādakiccaṃ na karonti, jarāyamhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi jarāya aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākampi jarā āgamissati, iti tassā pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā’’ti. Tenesa devadūto nāma jāto.

Dutiyaṃ devadūta

Tatiyaṃ devadūtanti etthāpi gilānasatto atthato eva vadati nāma – ‘‘passatha, bho, ahampi tumhe viya nirogo ahosiṃ, somhi etarahi byādhinā abhihato sake muttakarīse palipanno, uṭṭhātumpi na sakkomi, vijjamānāpi me hatthapādā hatthapādakiccaṃ na karonti, byādhitomhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi byādhito aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākaṃ byādhi āgamissati, iti tassa pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā’’ti. Tenesa devadūto nāma jāto.

Tatiyaṃ devadūta
commentary_english:
263. "**Having questioned the first divine messenger ( *devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjitvā*)**, the young boy spoke thus, in essence: 'Look, gentlemen (*bho*), I too have hands and feet (*hatthapādā atthi*) like you. I am lying in my own excrement (*sake panamhi muttakarīse palipanno*). I cannot even rise to bathe (*nhāyituṃ na sakkomi*) according to my nature (*attano dhammatāya*). I am soiled (*kiliṭṭhagattomhi*). I cannot even say, "Bathe me (*nhāpetha manti vattumpi na sakkomi*)". I am born thus (*ediso jāto*), because I have not been freed from birth (*jātitomhi aparimuttatāya*).
It is not just I (*na kho panāhameva*); you too have not been freed from birth (*tumhepi jātito aparimuttāva*).
Just as birth (*jāti*) will come to me (*mayhaṃ*), so too will it come to you (*evaṃ tumhākampi jāti āgamissati*). Therefore (*iti*), before it comes to you (*tassā pure āgamanāva*), do what is good (*kalyāṇaṃ karotha*).'
Therefore (*tenesa*), he is called a divine messenger (*devadūto nāma jāto*). The meaning of this speech (*vacanattho pana*) has already been stated in the Maghadeva Sūtra (*maghadevasutte vuttova*)."

"**The second** divine messenger (*devadūta*) also spoke thus, in essence: 'Look, gentlemen (*bho*), I too was young (*taruṇo ahosiṃ*), possessing strength in thighs and arms, and swiftness (*ūrubalabāhubalajavanasampanno*). But now (*tassa me tā*), those powers and swiftness (*balajavanasampattiyo*) have disappeared (*antarahitā*). Though my hands and feet (*hatthapādā*) still exist (*vijjamānāpi*), they do not perform the functions of hands and feet (*hatthapādakiccaṃ na karonti*). I am born thus (*ediso jāto*), because I have not been freed from old age (*jarāyamhi aparimuttatāya*).
It is not just I (*na kho panāhameva*); you too have not been freed from old age (*tumhepi jarāya aparimuttāva*).
Just as old age (*jarā*) will come to me (*mayhaṃ*), so too will it come to you (*evaṃ tumhākampi jarā āgamissati*). Therefore (*iti*), before it comes to you (*tassā pure āgamanāva*), do what is good (*kalyāṇaṃ karotha*).'
Therefore (*tenesa*), he is called a divine messenger (*devadūto nāma jāto*)."

 "**The third** divine messenger (*devadūta*) also spoke thus, in essence: 'Look, gentlemen (*bho*), I too was healthy (*nirogo ahosiṃ*), like you. But now (*etarahi*), I am afflicted by illness (*byādhinā abhihato*), lying in my own excrement (*sake muttakarīse palipanno*). I cannot even rise (*uṭṭhātumpi na sakkomi*). Though my hands and feet (*hatthapādā*) still exist (*vijjamānāpi*), they do not perform the functions of hands and feet (*hatthapādakiccaṃ na karonti*). I am born thus (*ediso jāto*), because I have not been freed from illness (*byādhitomhi aparimuttatāya*).
It is not just I (*na kho panāhameva*); you too have not been freed from illness (*tumhepi byādhito aparimuttāva*).
Just as illness (*byādhi*) will come to me (*mayhaṃ*), so too will it come to you (*evaṃ tumhākaṃ byādhi āgamissati*). Therefore (*iti*), before it comes to you (*tassā pure āgamanāva*), do what is good (*kalyāṇaṃ karotha*).'
Therefore (*tenesa*), he is called a divine messenger (*devadūto nāma jāto*)."

**The third divine messenger**

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, tassa te viññussa sato mahallakassa na etadahosi – ahampi khomhi byādhidhammo , byādhiṃ anatīto. Handāhaṃ kalyāṇaṃ karomi kāyena vācāya manasā’ti? So evamāha – ‘nāsakkhissaṃ, bhante, pamādassaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, pamādavatāya na kalyāṇamakāsi kāyena vācāya manasā. Taggha tvaṃ, ambho purisa, tathā karissanti yathā taṃ pamattaṃ. Taṃ kho pana te etaṃ pāpakammaṃ neva mātarā kataṃ na pitarā kataṃ na bhātarā kataṃ na bhaginiyā kataṃ na mittāmaccehi kataṃ na ñātisālohitehi kataṃ na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṃ na devatāhi kataṃ, tayāvetaṃ pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, tvaññevetassa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedissasī’’’ti.
mula_english:
264. Then, monks, King Yama, having questioned, examined, and addressed the second divine messenger, questions, examines, and addresses the third divine messenger: ‘Good man, have you not seen the third divine messenger appear among humans?’ He says, ‘I have not seen, venerable sir.’

Then, monks, King Yama says: ‘Good man, have you never seen in the world a woman or a man who is sick, suffering, seriously ill, lying fouled in his own excrement and urine, being lifted up by some and put to bed by others?’ He says, ‘I have seen, venerable sir.’

Then, monks, King Yama says: ‘Good man, did it never occur to you—an intelligent and mature man—"I too am subject to disease (*vyādhidharma*), I am not exempt from disease (*vyādhiṃ anatītaḥ*). Now let me do good with body, speech, and mind?"’ He says, ‘I was not able, venerable sir, I was negligent, venerable sir.’

Then, monks, King Yama says: ‘Good man, through negligence you have failed to do good by body, speech, and mind. Certainly, good man, they will deal with you according to your negligence. That evil action of yours was not done by mother, not done by father, not done by brother, not done by sister, not done by friends and companions, not done by relatives, not done by ascetics or Brahmins (*samaṇabrāhmaṇehi*), not done by gods (*devatāhi*); that evil action was done by you, and you alone will experience its result.’

mula_pali:
265. ‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā tatiyaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjitvā samanugāhitvā samanubhāsitvā catutthaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjati samanugāhati samanubhāsati – ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṃ addasa manussesu catutthaṃ devadūtaṃ pātubhūta’nti? So evamāha – ‘nāddasaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṃ addasa manussesu rājāno coraṃ āgucāriṃ gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārente – kasāhipi tāḷente vettehipi tāḷente addhadaṇḍakehipi tāḷente hatthampi chindante pādampi chindante hatthapādampi chindante kaṇṇampi chindante nāsampi chindante kaṇṇanāsampi chindante bilaṅgathālikampi karonte saṅkhamuṇḍikampi karonte rāhumukhampi karonte jotimālikampi karonte hatthapajjotikampi karonte erakavattikampi karonte cīrakavāsikampi karonte eṇeyyakampi karonte baḷisamaṃsikampi karonte kahāpaṇikampi karonte khārāpatacchikampi karonte palighaparivattikampi karonte palālapīṭhakampi karonte tattenapi telena osiñcante sunakhehipi khādāpente jīvantampi sūle uttāsente asināpi sīsaṃ chindante’ti? So evamāha – ‘addasaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, tassa te viññussa sato mahallakassa na etadahosi – ye kira, bho, pāpakāni kammāni karonti te diṭṭheva dhamme evarūpā vividhā kammakāraṇā karīyanti, kimaṅgaṃ kimaṅga (sī. pī.) pana parattha ! Handāhaṃ kalyāṇaṃ karomi kāyena vācāya manasā’ti? So evamāha – ‘nāsakkhissaṃ, bhante, pamādassaṃ, bhante’’’ti.

kimaṅga (sī. pī.)

‘‘Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā evamāha – ‘ambho purisa, pamādavatāya na kalyāṇamakāsi kāyena vācāya manasā. Taggha tvaṃ, ambho purisa, tathā karissanti yathā taṃ pamattaṃ. Taṃ kho pana te etaṃ pāpakammaṃ neva mātarā kataṃ na pitarā kataṃ na bhātarā kataṃ na bhaginiyā kataṃ na mittāmaccehi kataṃ na ñātisālohitehi kataṃ na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṃ na devatāhi kataṃ, tayāvetaṃ pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, tvaññevetassa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedissasī’’’ti.
mula_english:
“Then, monks, King Yama, having questioned, examined, and cross-examined the man about the third divine messenger, questions, examines, and cross-examines him about the fourth divine messenger, saying: ‘Good man, did you not see the fourth divine messenger appear among humankind?’ He says: ‘I did not see him, venerable sir.’”

“Then, monks, King Yama says to him: ‘Good man, did you never see in the world kings arresting a criminal caught in wrongdoing, inflicting various kinds of punishments – having them beaten with whips, having them beaten with canes, having them beaten with half-cudgels, even cutting off their hands, cutting off their feet, cutting off both hands and feet, cutting off their ears, <pb ed="m" n="3.
0220"/> cutting off their noses, cutting off both ears and noses, making *bilaṅgathālika* (a particular form of torture), making *saṅkhamuṇḍika* (another form of torture), making *rāhumukha* (yet another torture), making *jotimālika* (another torture), making *hatthapajjotika* (another torture), <pb ed="t" n="3.
0339"/> making *erakavattika* (another torture), making *cīrakavāsika* (another torture), making *eṇeyyaka* (another torture), making *baḷisamaṃsika* (another torture), making *kahāpaṇika* (another torture), making *khārāpatacchika* (another torture), making *palighaparivattika* (another torture), making *palālapīṭhaka* (another torture), even pouring hot oil over them, having them eaten by dogs, even impaling them alive on a stake, even cutting off their heads with a sword?’ He says: ‘I saw it, venerable sir.’”

“Then, monks, King Yama says to him: ‘Good man, did it never occur to you—an intelligent and mature man—"Those who do evil actions have such tortures of various kinds inflicted on them here and now; what to say of the hereafter!"? Surely I should do good with body, speech, and mind!’” He says: ‘I was not able, venerable sir; I was negligent, venerable sir.’”

“Then, monks, King Yama says to him: ‘Good man, through negligence you did not do good by body, speech, and mind.
Indeed, good man, they will do to you according to your negligence.
