Bhagavāpi taṃdivasaṃ paccūsakāle lokaṃ volokento pukkusātiṃ disvā cintesi – ‘‘ayaṃ kulaputto sahāyena pesitaṃ sāsanamattakaṃ vācetvā atirekatiyojanasatikaṃ mahārajjaṃ pahāya maṃ uddissa pabbajitvā aṭṭhahi ūnakāni dve yojanasatāni atikkamma rājagahaṃ pāpuṇissati, mayi agacchante pana tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni appaṭivijjhitvā ekarattivāsena anāthakālakiriyaṃ karissati, mayi pana gate tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni paṭivijjhissati. Janasaṅgahatthāyeva pana mayā satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni pāramiyo pūritā, karissāmi tassa saṅgaha’’nti pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā muhuttaṃ attadarathakilamathaṃ paṭipassambhetvā – ‘‘kulaputto mayi gāravena dukkaraṃ akāsi, atirekayojanasataṃ rajjaṃ pahāya antamaso mukhadhovanadāyakampi ceṭakaṃ aggahetvā ekakova nikkhanto’’ti sāriputtamahāmoggallānādīsu kañci anāmantetvā sayameva attano pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā ekakova nikkhanto. Gacchanto ca neva ākāse uppati, na pathaviṃ saṃkhipi, – ‘‘kulaputto mama lajjamāno hatthiassarathasuvaṇṇasivikādīsu ekayānepi anisīditvā antamaso ekapaṭalikaṃ upāhanampi anāruyha paṇṇacchattakampi aggahetvā nikkhanto, mayāpi padasāva gantuṃ vaṭṭatī’’ti pana cintetvā padasāva agamāsi.

So asīti anubyañjanāni byāmappabhā bāttiṃsa mahāpurisalakkhaṇānīti imaṃ buddhasiriṃ paṭicchādetvā valāhakapaṭicchanno puṇṇacando viya aññatarabhikkhuvesena gacchanto ekapacchābhatteneva pañcacattālīsa yojanāni atikkamma sūriyatthaṅgamalīvelāya kulaputte paviṭṭhamatteyeva taṃ kumbhakārasālaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – ‘‘tena kho pana samayena, pukkusāti, nāma kulaputto bhagavantaṃ uddissa saddhāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito, so tasmiṃ kumbhakārāvesane paṭhamaṃ vāsūpagato hotī’’ti.

Evaṃ gantvāpi pana bhagavā – ‘‘ahaṃ sammāsambuddho’’ti pasayha kumbhakārasālaṃ apavisitvā dvāre ṭhitova kulaputtaṃ okāsaṃ kārento sace te bhikkhūtiādimāha. Urundanti vivittaṃ asambādhaṃ. Viharatāyasmā yathāsukhanti yena yena iriyāpathena phāsu hoti, tena tena yathāsukhaṃ āyasmā viharatūti okāsaṃ akāsi. Atirekatiyojanasatañhi rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito kulaputto parassa chaḍḍitapatitaṃ kumbhakārasālaṃ kiṃ aññassa sabrahmacārino maccharāyissati. Ekacce pana moghapurisā sāsane pabbajitvā āvāsamacchariyādīhi abhibhūtā attano vasanaṭṭhāne mayhaṃ kuṭi mayhaṃ pariveṇanti aññesaṃ avāsāya parakkamanti. Nisīdīti accantasukhumālo lokanātho devavimānasadisaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pahāya tattha tattha vippakiṇṇachārikāya bhinnabhājanatiṇapalāsakukkuṭasūkaravaccādisaṃkiliṭṭhāya saṅkāraṭṭhānasadisāya kumbhakārasālāya tiṇasanthāraṃ santharitvā paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ paññapetvā devavimānasadisaṃ dibbagandhasugandhaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā nisīdanto viya nisīdi.

sace te bhikkhū Urunda Viharatāyasmā yathāsukha Nisīdī

Iti bhagavāpi asambhinnamahāsammatavaṃse uppanno, kulaputtopi khattiyagabbhe vaḍḍhito. Bhagavāpi abhinīhārasampanno, kulaputtopi abhinīhārasampanno. Bhagavāpi rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito, kulaputtopi. Bhagavāpi suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, kulaputtopi. Bhagavāpi samāpattilābhī, kulaputtopi. Iti dvepi khattiyā dvepi abhinīhārasampannā dvepi rājapabbajitā dvepi suvaṇṇavaṇṇā dvepi samāpattilābhino kumbhakārasālaṃ pavisitvā nisinnāti tehi kumbhakārasālā ativiya sobhati, dvīhi sīhādīhi paviṭṭhaguhādīhi āharitvā dīpetabbaṃ. Tesu pana dvīsu bhagavā – ‘‘sukhumālo ahaṃ paramasukhumālo ekapacchābhattena pañcacattālīsa yojanāni āgato, muhuttaṃ tāva sīhaseyyaṃ kappetvā maggadarathaṃ paṭipassambhemī’’ti cittampi anuppādetvā nisīdantova phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajji. Kulaputtopi – ‘‘dvānavutiyojanasataṃ āgatomhi, muhuttaṃ tāva nipajjitvā maggadarathaṃ vinodemī’’ti cittaṃ anuppādetvā nisīdamānova ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ samāpajji. Idaṃ sandhāya atha kho bhagavā bahudeva rattintiādi vuttaṃ.

atha kho bhagavā bahudeva ratti

Nanu ca bhagavā kulaputtassa dhammaṃ desessāmīti āgato, kasmā na desesīti? Kulaputtassa maggadaratho appaṭipassaddho, na sakkhissati dhammadesanaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ, so tāvassa paṭipassambhatūti na desesi. Apare – ‘‘rājagahaṃ nāma ākiṇṇamanussaṃ avivittaṃ dasahi saddehi, so saddo diyaḍḍhayāmamattena sannisīdati, taṃ āgamento na desesī’’ti vadanti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ, brahmalokappamāṇampi hi saddaṃ bhagavā attano ānubhāvena vūpasametuṃ sakkoti, maggadarathavūpasamaṃ āgamentoyeva pana na desesi.

Tattha bahudeva rattinti diyaḍḍhayāmamattaṃ. Etadahosīti bhagavā phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya suvaṇṇavimāne maṇisīhapañjaraṃ vivaranto viya pañcapasādappaṭimaṇḍitāni akkhīni ummīletvā olokesi, athassa hatthakukkuccapādakukkuccasīsakampanavirahitaṃ sunikhātaindakhīlaṃ viya niccalaṃ avibbhantaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭimaṃ viya nisinnaṃ kulaputtaṃ disvā etaṃ – ‘‘pāsādikaṃ kho’’tiādi ahosi. Tattha pāsādikanti pasādāvahaṃ. Bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ panetaṃ, pāsādikena iriyāpathena iriyati. Yathā iriyato iriyāpatho pāsādiko hoti, evaṃ iriyatīti ayamettha attho. Catūsu hi iriyāpathesu tayo iriyāpathā na sobhanti. Gacchantassa hi bhikkhuno hatthā calanti, pādā calanti, sīsaṃ calati, ṭhitassa kāyo thaddho hoti, nipannassāpi iriyāpatho amanāpo hoti, pacchābhatte pana divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā cammakhaṇḍaṃ paññapetvā sudhotahatthapādassa catusandhikapallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nipannasseva iriyāpatho sobhati. Ayañca kulaputto pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ appetvā nisīdi. Itissa iriyāpatheneva pasanno bhagavā – ‘‘pāsādikaṃ kho’’ti parivitakkesi.

bahudeva ratti Etadahosī pāsādika

Yaṃnūnāhaṃ puccheyyanti kasmā pucchati? Kiṃ bhagavā attānaṃ uddissa pabbajitabhāvaṃ na jānātīti? No na jānāti, apucchite pana kathā na patiṭṭhāti, apatiṭṭhitāya kathāya kathā na sañjāyatīti kathāpatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ pucchi.

Yaṃnūnāhaṃ puccheyya

Disvāca pana jāneyyāsīti tathāgataṃ buddhasiriyā virocantaṃ ayaṃ buddhoti sabbe jānanti. Anacchariyametaṃ jānanaṃ, buddhasiriṃ pana paṭicchādetvā aññatarapiṇḍapātikavesena caranto dujjāno hoti. Iccāyasmā, pukkusāti, ‘‘na jāneyya’’nti sabhāvameva katheti. Tathā hi naṃ ekakumbhakārasālāya nisinnampi na jānāti.

Disvā ca pana jāneyyāsī

Etadahosīti maggadarathassa vūpasamabhāvaṃ ñatvā ahosi. Evamāvusoti kulaputto sahāyena pesitaṃ sāsanamattaṃ vācetvā rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajamāno – ‘‘dasabalassa madhuradhammadesanaṃ sotuṃ labhissāmī’’ti. Pabbajito, pabbajitvā ettakaṃ addhānaṃ āgacchanto – ‘‘dhammaṃ te bhikkhu desessāmī’’ti padamattassa vattāraṃ nālattha, so ‘‘dhammaṃ te bhikkhu desessāmī’’ti vuttaṃ kiṃ sakkaccaṃ na suṇissati. Pipāsitasoṇḍo viya hi pipāsitahatthī viya cāyaṃ, tasmā sakkaccaṃ savanaṃ paṭijānanto ‘‘evamāvuso’’ti āha.

Etadahosī Evamāvuso
commentary_english:
342. It is thus that I have heard: the *dhātuvibhaṅgasutta*. There, *cārika* means a *cārika* of quick going. *Sace te bhaggava agarū* means if you, Bhaggava, have no ailment or discomfort. *Sace so anujānātī* means the following occurred to Bhaggava: “Those who have gone forth [as mendicants] have different intentions; one delights in company, another delights in solitude. If he is one who delights in solitude, he will say, ‘Friend, do not enter, the hall has been obtained by me.’ If this one is one who delights in solitude, he will say, ‘Friend, depart, the hall has been obtained by me.’ Thus, I will become a cause of dispute for both; what is given is indeed properly given, what is done is indeed properly done.” Therefore, he spoke thus. *Kulaputto* means both one who is well-born by birth and one who is well-born in conduct. *Vāsūpagato* means one who has approached a dwelling. From where have you come? From Takkasīla City. A *kulaputto*, one who has approached a dwelling. Here is a sequential account: It is said that in the central region, in the city of Rājagaha, while Bimbisāra was ruling, in the outlying area, in the city of Takkasīla, King Pukkusāti was ruling. Then, merchants from Takkasīla, taking merchandise, came to Rājagaha, and taking tribute, they saw the king. The king, having been worshiped by them and when they were standing, asked, “Where do you dwell?” "We are dwellers of Takkasīla, O deva." Then the king asked them about the prosperity, well-being, and abundance of the countryside and about the affairs of the city, and he asked, “What is the name of your king?” "Pukkusāti by name, O deva." "Is he righteous?" "Yes, deva, he is righteous. He benefits the people with the four bases of sympathy; he stands in the place of mother and father to the world, pleasing the people like an infant lying on his lap." “At what age does he live?” Then they told him his age. Even in age he was born as an equal to Bimbisāra. Then the king said to them, “Fathers, your king is righteous, and in age he is equal to me; could you make your king a friend to me?” “We are able, O deva.” The king, having dismissed the toll for them and having given them a house, said, “Go, sell the merchandise, and at the time of departure, having seen me, you may go.” Having done so, at the time of departure, they saw the king. “Go to your king, and with my words, having repeatedly asked about his health, say, ‘The king desires friendship with you’,” he said. Having agreed, “It is well,” they went, returned the merchandise, and after eating breakfast, they approached the king and paid homage. The king asked, “Why, sirs, have you not been seen for so many days?” They announced the whole matter. The king said, “Good, fathers, because of you, a king has been obtained by me as a friend in the central region,” he was delighted. On another occasion, merchants dwelling in Rājagaha also went to Takkasīla. When they came, taking tribute, King Pukkusāti asked, “From where have you come?” Having heard, “From Rājagaha,” [he said,] “You have come from the city of my friend.” “Yes, venerable sir.” Having asked about the health of his friend, [Bimbisāra] further proclaimed, "From today onwards, may all the merchants who come to my friend's city from the city, whether by foot-caravan or by cart-caravan, receive lodging and food from the royal storehouse, pay no customs duties, and suffer no harm." Bimbisāra also had the same proclamation made in his own city. Then, Bimbisāra sent a gift to Pukkusāti, saying: "In the borderlands, it is said that jewels such as gems and pearls arise. May my friend not be miserly towards me if any jewel, pleasing to see or hear, arises in his kingdom." Pukkusāti also sent a return gift, saying: "In the Middle Country, it is said that a great realm exists. May my friend not be miserly towards me if any such jewel arises there." Thus, as time went on, even without seeing one another, they became firm friends. Then, after they had made this agreement and were living [in their respective kingdoms], Pukkusāti's gift arrived first. The king had obtained eight priceless blankets of five different colors. He thought, "These blankets are very beautiful; I will send them to my friend." So, he had them wrapped in eight sturdy boxes the size of lac-balls. After placing the blankets in them, he sealed them with lac, wrapped them in white cloth, put them in a chest, wrapped the chest with cloth, and sealed it with the royal seal, saying to his ministers, "Give these to my friend." He also gave an order: "This gift is to be viewed in the middle of the city, surrounded by ministers and other officials." They went and gave it to Bimbisāra. Having heard the order, Bimbisāra had a drum beaten, [announcing] "The ministers and other officials are to assemble!" Then, surrounded by ministers and other officials in the middle of the city, seated on an excellent dais with a white parasol held above him, he broke the seal, removed the cloth, opened the chest, took out the bundle inside, saw the lac-balls, and thought: "My friend Pukkusāti, thinking 'Jutavittaka is my friend,' and believing [me to be poor], sent this gift." Taking one of the balls in his hand, turning it around and weighing it, he knew that there was cloth inside. Then, striking it against the foot of the dais, the lac immediately broke open. He opened the box with his fingernail, saw the jeweled blanket inside, and had the others opened as well; all were blankets. Then, he had them spread out. They were rich in color, pleasing to the touch, sixteen cubits long and eight cubits wide. The crowd, seeing them, snapped their fingers and tossed their garments in the air, [exclaiming] "Pukkusāti, our king's unseen friend, sent such a gift without even seeing [him]! It is fitting to make such a person a friend!" and was delighted. The king had each blanket appraised, and all were priceless. Of these, he sent four to the Sammāsambuddha, and kept four in his own palace. Then he thought: "It is proper for me, when sending [a gift] later, to send more than the gift sent first. And an invaluable gift was sent to me by my friend, what then should I send?" What jewel is there in Rājagaha that is superior to those? There is none. The king is of great merit. Moreover, since the time he became a *sotāpanna*, other than the Three Jewels, there is no other jewel capable of generating joy for him. He began to search for a jewel. A jewel, by name, is twofold: with consciousness and without consciousness. Of these, jewels without consciousness are gold, silver, and so on; those with consciousness are bound to the senses. A jewel without consciousness is used for enjoyment in the manner of ornaments and so forth by those with consciousness. Thus, of these two jewels, that with consciousness is superior. A jewel with consciousness is also twofold: animal jewels and human jewels. Among these, animal jewels are elephants and horses; but these too arise solely for the enjoyment of humans. Thus, of these two, the human jewel is superior. The human jewel is also twofold: woman-jewels and man-jewels. Among these, the woman-jewel born to a *cakravartin* king is also for the enjoyment of the man. Thus, of these two, the man-jewel is superior. The man-jewel is also twofold: householder jewels and homeless jewels. Among these, even a *cakravartin* king today reveres a *pabbajita sāmaṇera* with the fivefold prostration. Thus, of these two, the homeless jewel alone is 0208"/> is the best. Lay treasures are twofold: those of a trainee and those of one beyond training. Among these, even a hundred thousand trainees do not attain the place of one beyond training. Thus, among these two, the treasure of one beyond training is the best. Again, that is twofold: the treasure of the Buddha and the treasure of a disciple. Among these, even a hundred thousand treasures of disciples do not attain the place of the treasure of the Buddha. Thus, among these two, the treasure of the Buddha is the best.

Again, the treasure of the Buddha is twofold: the treasure of a solitary buddha and the treasure of an all-knowing buddha. Among these, even a hundred thousand solitary buddhas do not attain the place of an all-knowing buddha. Thus, among these two, the treasure of an all-knowing buddha is indeed the best. Indeed, in the world with its deities, there is no treasure equal to the treasure of the Buddha. Therefore, thinking, "I will send an unequaled treasure to my friend," he asked the residents of Takkasila, "Friends, in your country, are these three treasures, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, visible?" The sound of that, great king, is not there at all; how could there be a vision?"

"Excellent, friend!" the king, pleased, thought, "It would be possible to send the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, the dwelling place of my friend, for the sake of the welfare of the people. But Buddhas do not raise the dawn in border countries. Therefore, it is not possible for the Teacher to go. It would be possible to send Sariputta, Moggallana, and other great disciples. But by me it is fitting to send men, even having heard 'The elders are dwelling in the border region,' to bring them to my presence and attend to them. Therefore, it is not possible to go even for the elders. In whatever way the teaching is sent, the Teacher and the great disciples are as if gone; in that way, I will send the teaching." Having thought, having a golden plate made, four spans in length, a handbreadth wide, neither too thin nor too thick, "There today I will write the letters," he thought. Early in the morning, having bathed his head, having undertaken the observance day vows, having eaten breakfast, having removed perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, with a golden stylus, taking natural cinnabar, starting from below, closing the doors, ascending to the palace, opening the lion window facing the east, sitting on the surface of the sky, writing the letters on the golden plate – "Here the Tathagata arose in the world, a worthy one, a Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Well-gone One, Knower of the World, Unexcelled, Trainer of those to be tamed, Teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One." Thus far he wrote the virtues of the Buddha in part.

Then, "Thus, having fulfilled the ten perfections, having passed away from the Tusita heaven, he took rebirth in his mother's womb , thus the world was revealed; while dwelling in his mother's womb, this name he had; while dwelling in the midst of the house, this name he had; thus, having gone forth in the Great Renunciation, thus he made the Great Struggle. Having done such difficult deeds, having ascended the Great Bodhi-mandala, seated on the unconquered seat, he pierced the knowledge of omniscience; as he pierced the knowledge of omniscience, thus the world was revealed. In the world with its deities, there is no other treasure of such a kind."

Whatever wealth there is here or in the world beyond,

or whatever excellent treasure there is in the heavens,

there is nothing equal to the Tathagata;

in the Buddha, too, this excellent treasure is found;

by this truth, may there be well-being." (Khu. Pa. 6. 3; Su. Ni. 226) –

Thus, having written the virtues of the Buddha in part, praising the second, the Dharma Jewel – "Well proclaimed by the Blessed One is the Dharma…pe… to be known individually by the wise." "The four foundations of mindfulness…pe…the Noble Eightfold Path." "The Dharma taught by the Teacher is of such a kind and of such a kind," having written in part the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment –

Dharma Jewel

"Whatever 0199"/> the best of Buddhas praised purity,

0199"/>

they call concentration uninterrupted;

there is no concentration equal to that,

this too is a precious jewel in the Dhamma;

by this truth may there be well-being.’’

(khu. pā. 6. 5; su. ni. 228) –

Thus, having written about the qualities of the Dhamma in part, while praising the third *saṅgharatanaṃ* (Sangha Jewel) – ‘‘The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way…pe… field of merit for the world.’’ ‘‘Indeed, clansmen, having heard the Dhamma talk of the Teacher, thus go forth, some abandoning the white umbrella, some abandoning the office of sub-king, some abandoning the position of commander-in-chief, etc. And having gone forth, they fulfill this practice," having written about the Lesser Moral Habits, the Middle Moral Habits, the Great Moral Habits, etc., in part, the restraint of the six doors, mindfulness and clear comprehension, contentment with the four requisites, the nine kinds of forest dwelling, the abandonment of the hindrances, preliminary work, the knowledges of jhāna, the thirty-eight meditation subjects, up to the destruction of the āsavas, in part; having written about the sixteen kinds of mindfulness of breathing meditation subject in detail – ‘‘The Sangha of the Teacher’s disciples is endowed with such qualities.

**Saṅgharatanaṃ**

Those persons who are eight, the good ones,

these four pairs exist;

they are worthy of offerings, disciples of the Well-Gone One,

gifts given to them are of great fruit;

this too is a precious jewel in the Sangha,

by this truth may there be well-being.’’

(khu. pā. 6. 6; su. ni. 229) –

Thus, having written about the qualities of the Sangha in part – ‘‘The Blessed One’s Dispensation is well-proclaimed, leading out, if my friend is able, let him go forth into homelessness,’’ having rolled up the golden plate, having wrapped it in soft cloth, having placed it in a heartwood casket, he placed that casket – a golden one in a golden one, a silver one in a silver one, a jewel one in a jewel one, a coral one in a coral one, a ruby one in a ruby one, a sapphire one in a sapphire one, a crystal one in a crystal one, an ivory one in an ivory one, an all-jewel one in an all-jewel one, a wicker one in a wicker one – in a heartwood container.

Again, having taken the heartwood container to the golden container by the same method as before, he placed the all-jewel container in the wicker container. Then, having taken the wicker container to the heartwood box by the same method as before, having placed the all-jewel box in the wicker box, having wrapped it with outer cloth, having sealed it with the royal seal, he commanded the ministers – ‘‘In the place where my command is carried out, have the road decorated; may the road be eight *usabha*s wide, may the place for four *usabha*s be only swept, in the middle, prepare four *usabha*s with royal power.’’ Then, having had the auspicious elephant decorated, having placed a couch on top of it, having raised the white umbrella, having had the city streets sprinkled and swept, well-decorated with raised flags and banners, banana trees, full water pots, perfumes, incense, flowers, etc., having sent swift messengers to those within his jurisdiction, saying, ‘‘Let them make such offerings in their own territories,’’ having himself adorned himself with all ornaments – ‘‘Surrounded by an army mixed with all kinds of music, I will send a gift,’’ having gone to the border of his territory, he gave a verbal message to the minister – ‘‘Dear Pukkusāti, my friend, receiving this gift, without receiving it in the midst of the women’s quarters, let him ascend to the palace and receive it.’’ Having given this message, bowing with the five-point prostration, he turned back, thinking, ‘‘The Teacher is going to the border country.’’ Those within his jurisdiction, by that same method, having prepared the road, conveyed the gift.

Pukkusāti also, from the border of his own kingdom, by that same method, having prepared the road, having had the city decorated, went to meet the gift. The gift reached Takkasilā on the Uposatha day; the minister who had gone taking the gift also announced the message spoken by the king. Having heard that, having considered the tasks to be done for those who had come with the gift, having taken the gift, having ascended to the palace, having had guards placed at the door, saying, ‘‘Let no one enter here,’’ having opened the lion window, having placed the gift on a high seat, having himself sat on a low seat, having broken the seal, having removed the covering, opening in sequence from the wicker box, seeing the heartwood casket, he thought – ‘‘This great gift will not be for another jewel, truly, a jewel worthy to be heard of has arisen in the Middle Country.’’ Then, opening that casket, breaking the royal seal, having drawn out the soft cloth on both sides, he saw the golden plate.

He, having spread it out – ‘‘Pleasing indeed are the letters, even heads, even rows, square,’’ beginning from there, began to read. To him – while reading the Buddha’s qualities, ‘‘Here a Tathāgata has arisen in the world,’’ a strong gladness arose, ninety-nine thousand hair follicles became hairs standing on end. He does not know his standing state or his sitting state. Then it occurred to him: "By relying on a friend, I am able to hear this rare teaching, even after hundreds of thousands of aeons," and a stronger joy arose. Since he was unable to recite further, he sat down with the rapture of joy and tranquility, and then began with the qualities of the Dharma, "Well proclaimed is the Dharma by the Blessed One (svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo)." There, too, it happened just as before. Again, having sat down with the rapture of joy and tranquility, he began with the qualities of the Saṅgha, "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples (suppaṭipanno) is behaving well" There, too, it happened just as before. Then, at the end of everything, having recited the practice of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ), he developed the four and five jhānas, and he spent his time in the bliss of jhāna. No one else is allowed to see [him]; only the attendant Cūḷupaṭṭhāka enters. Thus, he spent about half a month. The townspeople, having gathered in the royal courtyard, raised an uproar, "From the day the gift was received onwards, there is no display of strength or display of drama, there is no giving of judgment, the king should show the gift sent by the friend to whomever he wishes; kings, by means of gifts, also try to deceive and make the kingdom their own. What indeed is our king doing (kiṃ nāma amhākaṃ rājā karotī)?" Having heard the uproar, the king thought, "Am I ruling the kingdom, or am I a teacher (satthāra)?". Then this occurred to him: "The state of having made the kingdom one's self (rajjakāritaattabhāvo) cannot be calculated by a calculator, nor by a great calculator minister. I will uphold the teacher's teaching (satthusāsanaṃ dhāressāmī)," having taken the sword placed on the bed, and having cut off his hair, and having opened the lion cage, he threw the lock of hair with the crest jewel in the middle of the assembly, "Having taken this, may you rule the kingdom (etaṃ gahetvā rajjaṃ kārethā)," the great crowd, having lifted it up, cried out, "Kings like you, gods, receive gifts from a friend (sahāyakasantikā laddhapaṇṇākārā nāma rājāno tumhādisā honti devā)!" with a single cry. The king also had hair and beard of two finger-widths in length (raññopi dvaṅgulamattaṃ kesamassu ahosi). It was just like the Bodhisattva's renunciation (pabbajjāsadisameva kira jātaṃ). Then, having sent the attendant Cūḷupaṭṭhāka, and having had two ochre robes and a clay bowl brought from the market, "To those who are arahants in the world (ye loke arahanto), to them I renounce (pabbajjā)," having put on one ochre robe, and having wrapped one, and having put the bowl on his left shoulder, and having taken the knife handle, "Is my renunciation suitable (sobhati nu kho me pabbajjā) or not (no vā)," having walked back and forth on the great floor a few times, "My renunciation is suitable (sobhati me pabbajjā)," having opened the door, he descended from the palace. However, even having seen the plays and so on standing at the three gates, they did not recognize him. "A Private Buddha (paccekabuddho) has come to speak Dharma to our king (eko paccekabuddho amhākaṃ rañño dhammakathaṃ kathetuṃ āgato)," they thought. However, having climbed to the upper palace, and having seen the king's standing and sitting places, and having known that the king had gone, they cried out with a single cry, like people on a ship sinking in the middle of the ocean. The eighteen armies, all the townspeople, and the force of soldiers, having surrounded the noble youth, cried out a great cry. The ministers also said this to him, "O King, the kings of the middle country (majjhimadesarājāno) are very deceitful, having sent a message, "Whether the jewel of the Buddha (buddharatanaṃ) has arisen in the world or not," you will go knowing (gamissatha), return (nivattatha), O King (devā)!" I trust my friend, there is no double talk between him and me (saddahāmahaṃ mayhaṃ sahāyakassa, tassa mayā saddhiṃ dvejjhavacanaṃ nāma natthi), stay here (tiṭṭhatha), you (tumheti). They followed right along. The noble youth, having made a mark with the knife handle, "Whose is this kingdom (idaṃ rajjaṃ kassā)," he said? Yours, O King (tumhākaṃ devāti). Whoever changes this mark, should be made to obey the king's command (rājāṇāya kāretabboti). In the Mahājanaka Jātaka, Sīvalidevī, unable to change the mark made by the Bodhisattva (bodhisattena katalekhaṃ sīvalidevī antaraṃ kātuṃ avisahantī), went away transformed. By the path she had gone, the great crowd went. But the great crowd did not dare to change that mark (taṃ pana lekhaṃ mahājano antaraṃ kātuṃ na visahi), having made the mark a headdress, they cried out transformed. A young man, thinking, "In the place I go, he will give me a tooth-stick or water for the mouth," departed without taking even a single servant. Thus it occurred to him: "My teacher, having gone forth in the great going-forth, is one who has gone forth alone," and he went forth alone. And, "I am ashamed before the teacher," and "My teacher, having gone forth, did not mount a vehicle," he did not mount even a single slipper, nor did he carry a leaf parasol. A great crowd, having climbed trees, ramparts, elevated platforms, and so on, looked, saying, "This is our king going." The young man, thinking, "A long distance must be gone; it is not possible to cross the road alone," followed a caravan. For the very delicate young man, because of the hardness of the earth, as he was walking, blisters arose on the soles of his feet and broke; painful feeling arose. When the caravan had made camp and settled down, the young man left the road and sat at the foot of a certain tree. In the place where he was sitting, there was no one to do foot-service or back-service; the young man, having attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, having calmed the burning pain of the journey and the chariot, passed the time in the pleasure of jhāna. The next day, when the sun had risen, having done the tending of the body, he again followed the caravan. At breakfast time, people took a bowl for the young man, and having put hard food and soft food into the bowl, they gave it to him. Even though it was unhulled rice, or stale, or mixed with gravel, or unsalted or oversalted, the young man, having reflected on the place of entering, ate it as if it were ambrosia, and by this method, he had gone two hundred yojanas, lacking eight. Even while going near the gate-chamber of Jetavana, he did not ask, "Where does the teacher dwell?" Why? Because of reverence for the teacher, and also because of the king's command that had been sent. For the king—thinking "Here, a *tathāgata* arises in the world," and having made the teacher seem as if he had arisen in Rajagaha, sent a command—therefore, without asking him, he had crossed a road of about forty-five yojanas. He, at sunset, having arrived at Rajagaha, asked, "Where does the teacher dwell?" "From where, *bhante*, have you come?" "From there, toward the north." "Teacher, on the road by which you have come, forty-five yojanas from here, there is a city named Savatthi; the teacher dwells there." The young man thought, "Now it is the wrong time; it is not possible to go. Today, having stayed right here, tomorrow I will go to the teacher's presence." Then he asked, "Where do those who have gone forth, who have arrived at the wrong time, dwell?" "In this potter's hall, *bhante*." Then he asked that potter for lodging there, and having entered, he sat down. The Blessed One also, on that day, at dawn, while looking over the world, saw Pukkusāti and thought, "This young man, having read a mere message sent by a friend, having abandoned a great kingdom of more than a hundred yojanas, having gone forth for my sake, having crossed two hundred yojanas lacking eight, will arrive at Rajagaha; if I do not go, without penetrating the three fruits of asceticism, by dwelling for a single night, he will make an end of his life without a protector; if I go, he will penetrate the three fruits of asceticism. Indeed, for the sake of helping people, I have fulfilled the perfections for more than a hundred thousand *kappas*, and four incalculable *asaṅkhyeyyas*; I will do help for him"—having done the tending of the body early in the morning, surrounded by the community of monks, having gone to Savatthi for alms, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, having entered the Perfumed Chamber, having for a moment calmed the weariness of his own journey and chariot—"This young man, out of reverence for me, has done what is difficult to do; having abandoned a kingdom of more than a hundred yojanas, without taking even a servant to give him water for his face, he has gone forth alone," without addressing anyone among Sariputta, Mahamoggallana, and so on, he himself, having taken his bowl and robe, went forth alone. And while going, he neither rose up into the sky nor compressed the earth,—"This young man, ashamed before me, not having sat down in any vehicle among elephants, horses, chariots, gold palanquins, and so on, without mounting even a single slipper, and without taking even a leaf parasol, has gone forth; it is fitting for me also to go on foot," thus thinking, he went on foot. He, concealing that glorious Buddhahood with its eighty secondary characteristics, its fathom-wide aura, and its thirty-two marks of a Great Man, going in the guise of another monk, having crossed forty-five yojanas in a single afternoon, just as the young man had entered that potter's hall at sunset, he arrived. With reference to that, it was said: "At that time, Pukkusāti, a young man, having gone forth from home into homelessness, out of faith, having aimed at the Blessed One, was the first to take up residence in that potter's workshop." 0047"/> Even after going there, the Blessed One, thinking, "I am the *sammāsambuddha*," confidently entered the potter's shed, and standing at the door, while making an opportunity for the clansman, he spoke beginning with "sace te bhikkhū." urunda means secluded, not crowded. "viharatāyasmā yathāsukha" means, 'In whatever posture (iriyapatha) it is comfortable, in that posture, may the venerable one live comfortably,' he made an opportunity. For the clansman, having given up a kingdom exceeding one hundred and thirty leagues, and having gone forth, why would he be jealous of a fellow member of the holy life regarding a discarded, fallen potter's shed? However, some foolish men, having gone forth in the Dispensation, overcome by jealousy of dwellings and so on, strive to prevent others from dwelling in their own dwelling place, saying, "My hut, my enclosure." nisīdī: the world-protector, being exceedingly delicate, having abandoned a scented chamber resembling a deva-mansion, spread out a grass mat in the potter's shed resembling a rubbish heap, soiled with scattered ashes, broken dishes, grass, leaves, chicken and pig excrement, and having laid out a robe collected from a dust heap, he sat down as if entering a scented chamber resembling a deva-mansion, fragrant with divine scents. sace te bhikkhū urunda viharatāyasmā yathāsukha nisīdī Thus, the Blessed One was born in an unbroken line of Mahāsammatas, and the clansman was raised in a noble khattiya (warrior) family. The Blessed One was accomplished in aspiration (abhinīhāra), and so was the clansman. The Blessed One gave up a kingdom and went forth, and so did the clansman. The Blessed One was golden-hued, and so was the clansman. The Blessed One was a gainer of attainments (samāpatti), and so was the clansman. Thus, both were khattiyas, both accomplished in aspiration, both royal renunciates, both golden-hued, both gainers of attainments; by their sitting down, having entered the potter's shed, the potter's shed shone exceedingly, it should be illuminated by bringing in the example of caves entered by two lions and so on. However, of those two, the Blessed One, without even producing the thought, "I am delicate, exceedingly delicate, I have come forty-five leagues on one meal, having taken a moment, I will arrange a lion's repose and calm the weariness of the journey", only sitting down, attained the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpattiṃ). The clansman also, without producing the thought, "I have come one hundred and ninety-two leagues, having lain down for a moment, I will dispel the weariness of the journey", only sitting down, attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). With reference to this, "atha kho bhagavā bahudeva ratti" and so on was said. atha kho bhagavā bahudeva ratti But surely, the Blessed One came to teach the Dharma to the clansman, why did he not teach? The clansman's weariness of the journey was not calmed, he would not be able to receive the Dharma-teaching, so that it might be calmed for him, he did not teach. Others say, "Rājagaha is crowded with people, not secluded, with ten sounds, that sound subsides in about two and a half hours, waiting for that he did not teach." That is without reason, for the Blessed One, by his own power, is able to calm even a sound the size of the Brahma-world, but he did not teach only waiting for the calming of the weariness of the journey. There, "bahudeva ratti" means about two and a half hours. "etadahosī": the Blessed One, rising from the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpattiṃ), as if opening a jeweled lion-window in a golden palace, having opened his eyes adorned with the five kinds of serenity (pasāda), he looked around, then seeing the clansman sitting without hand-worry, foot-worry, or head-shaking, motionless like a well-buried pillar of Indra, unwavering, like a golden statue, this occurred to him: "How pleasing!" and so on. There, "pāsādika" means inducing serenity. However, this is neuter in meaning, he comports himself with a serene posture. Just as the posture of one comporting himself is serene, thus he comports himself, this is the meaning here. For of the four postures, three postures do not shine. For when a bhikkhu is walking, his hands move, his feet move, his head moves, when standing, his body is stiff, and the posture of one lying down is also unpleasant, however, the posture of one who has washed his hands and feet well after the meal, and having swept the daytime dwelling, having laid down a piece of leather, having bent his four-jointed couch, only the posture of one lying down shines. And this clansman, having bent his couch, sat down without applying the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. Thus, pleased only with his posture, the Blessed One thought, "How pleasing!"

bahudeva ratti etadahosī pāsādika

yaṃnūnāhaṃ puccheyya: why does he ask? Does the Blessed One not know that he went forth aiming at himself? No, he knows, but when not asked, the talk does not become established, without the talk being established, talk does not arise, so he asked in order to establish the talk.

yaṃnūnāhaṃ puccheyya

disvāca pana jāneyyāsī: all know the Tathāgata, shining with the glory of the Buddha, "This is the Buddha." It is not so surprising to know [this], but a buddha, concealing his radiance and wandering in the guise of just any alms-seeker, is difficult to recognize. Thus spoke the venerable Pukkusāti, “I would not know,” stating simply the nature of things. For indeed, he does not even know him when he is sitting in a single potter's workshop. Having seen And if you should know, it was like this: having known the appeasement of the chariot of the path, it was like this. "Thus, friend," the clansman, having had the message sent by his friend read, renouncing the kingdom and going forth, [thinking] "I will obtain [the chance] to hear the sweet Dhamma-teaching of the Ten-Powered One (daśabala)." Having gone forth, having gone forth. Coming such a distance, he did not find anyone to utter even a word of "I will teach you the Dhamma, monk," so will he not attentively listen to that which was said, "I will teach you the Dhamma, monk"? Just as a thirsty trunk, just as a thirsty elephant, so is he; therefore, promising attentive listening, he said, "Yes, friend (evam āvuso)." It was like this. "Thus, friend."

mula_pali: 343. ‘‘‘Chadhāturo chaddhāturo (sī.) ayaṃ, bhikkhu, puriso chaphassāyatano aṭṭhārasamanopavicāro caturādhiṭṭhāno; yattha ṭhitaṃ maññassavā nappavattanti, maññassave kho pana nappavattamāne muni santoti vuccati. Paññaṃ nappamajjeyya, saccamanurakkheyya, cāgamanubrūheyya, santimeva so sikkheyyā’ti – ayamuddeso dhātuvibhaṅgassa chadhātuvibhaṅgassa (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.).
mula_english:
343.
"Bhikkhu, this person is composed of six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*), six bases of contact (*chaphassāyatana*), eighteen mental considerations (*aṣṭhārasamanopavicāra*), and four foundations (*caturādhiṣṭhāna*). Where, remaining, the currents of conceit (*maññassava*) do not proceed, and when the currents of conceit do not proceed, one is called a sage (*muni*) at peace (*santa*)."

One should not neglect wisdom (*prajñā*), one should protect truth (*satya*), one should cultivate generosity (*tyāga*), and one should train only for peace (*śānti*). This is the summary (*uddeśa*) of the exposition (*vibhaṅga*) of the elements (*dhātu*).
commentary_pali:
343.Chadhāturo ayanti bhagavā kulaputtassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ akathetvā āditova arahattassa padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ accantasuññataṃ vipassanālakkhaṇameva ācikkhituṃ āraddho. Yassa hi pubbabhāgapaṭipadā aparisuddhā hoti, tassa paṭhamameva sīlasaṃvaraṃ indriyesu guttadvārataṃ bhojane mattaññutaṃ jāgariyānuyogaṃ satta saddhamme cattāri jhānānīti imaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ ācikkhati. Yassa panesā parisuddhā, tassa taṃ akathetvā arahattassa padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ vipassanameva ācikkhati. Kulaputtassa ca pubbabhāgapaṭipadā parisuddhā. Tathā hi anena sāsanaṃ vācetvā pāsādavaragateneva ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattitaṃ, yadassa dvānavutiyojanasabhaṃ āgacchantassa yānakiccaṃ sādhesi, sāmaṇerasīlampissa paripuṇṇaṃ. Tasmā pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ akathetvā arahattassa padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ accantasuññataṃ vipassanālakkhaṇamevassa ācikkhituṃ āraddho.

Tattha chadhāturoti dhātuyo vijjamānā, puriso avijjamāno. Bhagavā hi katthaci vijjamānena avijjamānaṃ dasseti, katthaci avijjamānena vijjamānaṃ, katthaci vijjamānena vijjamānaṃ, katthaci avijjamānena avijjamānanti sabbāsave vuttanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Idha pana vijjamānena avijjamānaṃ dassento evamāha. Sace hi bhagavā purisoti paṇṇattiṃ vissajjetvā dhātuyo icceva vatvā cittaṃ upaṭṭhāpeyya, kulaputto sandehaṃ kareyya, sammohaṃ āpajjeyya, desanaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Tasmā tathāgato anupubbena purisoti paṇṇattiṃ pahāya ‘‘sattoti vā purisoti vā puggaloti vā paṇṇattimattameva, paramatthato satto nāma natthi, dhātumatteyeva cittaṃ ṭhapāpetvā tīṇi phalāni paṭivijjhāpessāmī’’ti anaṅgaṇasutte (ma. ni. 1.57 ādayo) vuttabhāsantarakusalo tāya tāya bhāsāya sippaṃ uggaṇhāpento ācariyo viya evamāha.

chadhāturo

Tattha cha dhātuyo assāti chadhāturo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ tvaṃ purisoti sañjānāsi, so chadhātuko, na cettha paramatthato puriso atthi, purisoti pana paṇṇattimattamevāti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Caturādhiṭṭhānoti ettha adhiṭṭhānaṃ vuccati patiṭṭhā, catupatiṭṭhānoti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – svāyaṃ bhikkhu puriso chadhāturo chaphassāyatano aṭṭhārasamanopavicāro, so ettova vivaṭṭitvā uttamasiddhibhūtaṃ arahattaṃ gaṇhamāno imesu catūsu ṭhānesu patiṭṭhāya gaṇhātīti caturādhiṭṭhānoti. Yattha ṭhitanti yesu adhiṭṭhānesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Maññassa vā nappavattantīti maññassa vā mānassa vā nappavattanti. Muni santoti vuccatīti khīṇāsavamuni upasanto nibbutoti vuccati. Paññaṃ nappamajjeyyāti arahattaphalapaññāya paṭivijjhanatthaṃ āditova samādhivipassanāpaññaṃ nappamajjeyya. Saccamanurakkheyyāti paramatthasaccassa nibbānassa sacchikiriyatthaṃ āditova vacīsaccaṃ rakkheyya. Cāgamanubrūheyyāti arahattamaggena sabbakilesapariccāgakaraṇatthaṃ āditova kilesapariccāgaṃ brūheyya. Santimeva so sikkheyyāti arahattamaggena sabbakilesavūpasamanatthaṃ āditova kilesavūpasamanaṃ sikkheyya. Iti paññādhiṭṭhānādīnaṃ adhigamatthāya imāni samathavipassanāpaññādīni pubbabhāgādhiṭṭhānāni vuttāni.

chadhāturo Caturādhiṭṭhāno Yattha ṭhita Maññassa vā nappavattantī Muni santoti vuccatī Paññaṃ nappamajjeyyā Saccamanurakkheyyā Cāgamanubrūheyyā Santimeva so sikkheyyā
commentary_english:
343. *Cha dhāturo aya*nti: The Bhagavān, without elaborating on the preliminary practice of a noble son, immediately commenced teaching the characteristic of insight (*vipaśyanā*), which is the ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) that serves as the foundation (*pada-sthāna-bhūta*) for *arhat*-ship.

If the preliminary practice is impure, he first teaches moral restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*), guarding the senses (*indriyesu guttadvārataṃ*), moderation in food (*bhojane mattaññutaṃ*), engagement in wakefulness (*jāgariyānuyogaṃ*), the seven good qualities (*satta saddhamme*), and the four *dhyānas*—thus, he teaches this preliminary practice.

But if that is pure, he does not elaborate on that; he teaches only insight (*vipaśyanā*) as the foundation (*pada-sthāna-bhūtaṃ*) for *arhat*-ship.

And the preliminary practice of the noble son is pure.

Thus, by causing him to recite the teaching (*śāsanaṃ vācetvā*) while remaining in the upper story of the palace (*pāsādavaragatena eva*), the fourth *jhāna* of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattitaṃ*) was produced; that which accomplished the task of travel (*yāna-kiccaṃ sādhesi*) for him who was coming a distance of ninety-two *yojanas*; his monastic precepts (*śrāmaṇera-śīlam*), too, were complete (*paripūrṇam*).

Therefore, without elaborating on the preliminary practice, he immediately commenced teaching the characteristic of insight (*vipaśyanā*), which is the ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) that serves as the foundation (*pada-sthāna-bhūta*) for *arhat*-ship.

There, *cha dhāturo*ti means that the elements (*dhātuyo*) are present, but the person (*puriso*) is not present.

The Bhagavān shows the non-existent (*avijjamānaṃ*) by means of the existent (*vijjamānena*), the existent (*vijjamānaṃ*) by means of the non-existent (*avijjamānena*), the existent (*vijjamānaṃ*) by means of the existent (*vijjamānena*), and the non-existent (*avijjamānaṃ*) by means of the non-existent (*avijjamānaṃ*). This should be expanded in accordance with the method stated in the discourse on all the defilements (*sabbāsave vuttanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ*).

Here, however, showing the non-existent (*avijjamānaṃ*) by means of the existent (*vijjamānena*), he speaks thus:

"If, indeed, the Bhagavān, having rejected the designation (*paṇṇattiṃ vissajjetvā*) 'person (*puriso*),' and saying only 'elements (*dhātuyo*)', were to establish the mind (*cittaṃ upaṭṭhāpeyya*), the noble son would be in doubt (*sandehaṃ kareyya*), would fall into confusion (*sammohaṃ āpajjeyya*), and would not be able to accept the teaching (*desanaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ na sakkuṇeyya*).

Therefore, the Tathāgata gradually abandoning the designation (*paṇṇattiṃ pahāya*) 'person (*puriso*)', [says:] 'A being (*satto*) or a person (*puriso*) or an individual (*puggalo*) is merely a designation (*paṇṇattimattameva*). In reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no such thing as a being (*satto nāma natthi*). Having established the mind (*cittaṃ ṭhapāpetvā*) in merely the elements (*dhātu-matteyeva*), I will cause [you] to penetrate the three fruits (*tīṇi phalāni paṭivijjhāpessāmī*)," as the teacher (*ācariyo*) who is skilled in other languages (*vuttabhāsāntara-kusalo*) in the Anaṅgaṇa-sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 1.57 ff.), teaching a craft (*sippaṃ uggaṇhāpento*) in this and that language (*tāya tāya bhāsāya*), speaks thus.

*Chadhāturo*

There, *cha dhātuyo assāti chadhāturo* means "because there are six elements, therefore, *chadhāturo*."

This means: "That which you recognize as a person (*puriso*), that is *cha-dhātuko*. But there is no person (*puriso*) in reality (*paramārthato*). A person (*puriso*), however, is merely a designation (*paṇṇattimattameva*)."

In the remaining passages, too, this is the method (*sesapadesupi eseva nayo*).

*Caturādhiṭṭhāno*ti: Here, *adhiṭṭhānaṃ* is said to be *patiṭṭhā*, meaning "four foundations (*catu-patiṭṭhāno*)".

This means: "This monk (*bhikkhu*) is a person (*puriso*) who is *cha-dhāturo*, who has six sense-spheres (*cha-phassāyatano*), and who has eighteen mental examinations (*aṭṭhārasa-manopavicāro*). Having turned away from this very thing (*so etto va vivaṭṭitvā*), while taking hold of *arhat*-ship (*arahattaṃ gaṇhamāno*), which is the supreme accomplishment (*uttama-siddhi-bhūtaṃ*), he takes hold by standing on these four grounds (*imesu catūsu ṭhānesu patiṭṭhāya gaṇhāti*)." Therefore, *caturādhiṭṭhāno*ti.

*Yattha ṭhita*nti means "that on which it stands (*patitṭhitaṃ*) in those foundations (*adhiṭṭhānesu*)."

*Maññassa vā nappavattantī*ti means "they do not proceed (*nappavattanti*) to conceit (*maññassa*) or to pride (*mānassa*)."

*Muni santoti vuccatī*ti means "*khīṇāsava* *muni* is said to be *upasanto* and *nibbuto*."

*Paññaṃ nappamajjeyyā*ti means "one should not neglect (*nappamajjeyyā*) the wisdom (*paññaṃ*) of insight (*samādhi-vipaśyanā-paññaṃ*) from the beginning (*ādito va*) for the sake of penetrating (*paṭivijjhana-atthaṃ*) the wisdom (*paññaṃ*) that is the fruit of *arhat*-ship (*arahatta-phala-paññaṃ*)."

*Saccamanurakkheyyā*ti means "from the beginning (*ādito va*) one should guard (*rakkheyya*) the truth of speech (*vacī-saccaṃ*) for the sake of realizing (*sacchikiriya-atthaṃ*) the ultimate truth (*paramattha-saccassa*) of *nirvāṇa* (*nibbānassa*)."

*Cāgamanubrūheyyā*ti means "from the beginning (*ādito va*) one should cultivate (*brūheyya*) renunciation of defilements (*kilesa-pariccāgaṃ*) for the sake of causing the renunciation of all defilements (*sabba-kilesa-pariccāga-karaṇa-atthaṃ*) by means of the path of *arhat*-ship (*arahatta-maggena*)."

*Santimeva so sikkheyyā*ti means "from the beginning (*ādito va*) one should train (*sikkheyya*) in the calming of defilements (*kilesa-vūpasamanaṃ*) for the sake of the calming of all defilements (*sabba-kilesa-vūpasamana-atthaṃ*) by means of the path of *arhat*-ship (*arahatta-maggena*)."

Thus, these foundations that are the preliminary part (*pubbabhāga-adhiṭṭhānāni*)—namely, serenity, insight, and wisdom (*samatha-vipaśyanā-paññā-ādīni*)—have been stated for the sake of attaining the foundations of wisdom and so forth (*paññādhiṭṭhāna-ādīnaṃ adhigama-atthaya*).

*Chadhāturo*
*Caturādhiṭṭhāno*
*Yattha ṭhita*
*Maññassa vā nappavattantī*
*Muni santoti vuccatī*
*Paññaṃ nappamajjeyyā*
*Saccamanurakkheyyā*
