“What is the reason for that?” “Because, venerable sir, while that oil-lamp is burning, its oil, wick, and flame are impermanent and subject to change, so its radiance must be impermanent and subject to change.”

“So too, sisters, would anyone be speaking rightly who spoke thus: ‘These six internal bases (*ajjhattikā āyatanā*) are impermanent; but the pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that one experiences in dependence upon the six internal bases is permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change’?” “No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?” “Because each feeling (*vedanā*) arises in dependence upon its corresponding condition (*paccayaṃ paṭicca*), venerable sir.

And with the cessation of its corresponding condition, the feeling ceases.”

“Good, good, sisters! So it is with a noble disciple who sees this as it actually is with proper wisdom.”
commentary_pali: 402.Pagevassa chāyāti mūlādīni nissāya nibbattā chāyā paṭhamataraṃyeva aniccā.
commentary_english: 402. *pagevassa chāyā*: the shadow that arises dependent on roots and so on is impermanent from the very beginning.

mula_pali: 403. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhaginiyo, mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato mūlampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, khandhopi anicco vipariṇāmadhammo, sākhāpalāsampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, chāyāpi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā. Yo nu kho, bhaginiyo, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘amussa mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato mūlampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, khandhopi anicco vipariṇāmadhammo, sākhāpalāsampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, yā ca khvāssa chāyā sā niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā’ti; sammā nu kho so, bhaginiyo, vadamāno vadeyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Amussa hi, bhante, mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato mūlampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, khandhopi anicco vipariṇāmadhammo, sākhāpalāsampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ; pagevassa chāyā aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā’’ti. ‘‘Evameva kho, bhaginiyo, yo nu kho evaṃ vadeyya – ‘cha khome bāhirā āyatanā aniccā aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā (sī. pī.). Yañca kho cha bāhire āyatane paṭicca paṭisaṃvedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā taṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhamma’nti; sammā nu kho so, bhaginiyo, vadamāno vadeyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Tajjaṃ tajjaṃ, bhante, paccayaṃ paṭicca tajjā tajjā vedanā uppajjanti. Tajjassa tajjassa paccayassa nirodhā tajjā tajjā vedanā nirujjhantī’’ti. ‘‘Sādhu, sādhu, bhaginiyo! Evañhetaṃ, bhaginiyo, hoti ariyasāvakassa yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato’’.
mula_english:
403. “Sisters, suppose a great tree is standing possessed of heartwood: its root (*mūla*) is impermanent and subject to change (*vipariṇāmadharma*), its trunk (*khandha*) is impermanent and subject to change, its branches and foliage are impermanent and subject to change, and its shadow (*chāyā*) is impermanent and subject to change.

Now would anyone be speaking rightly who spoke thus: ‘The root of this great tree standing possessed of heartwood is impermanent and subject to change, its trunk is impermanent and subject to change, its branches and foliage are impermanent and subject to change, but its shadow is permanent (*nitya*), everlasting (*dhruva*), eternal (*śāśvata*), not subject to change (*avipariṇāmadharma*)’?”

“No, indeed, Lord.”

“What is the reason for that?”

“Because, venerable sir, the root, trunk, branches, and foliage of this great tree standing possessed of heartwood are impermanent and subject to change, so its shadow must be impermanent and subject to change.”

“So too, sisters, would anyone be speaking rightly who spoke thus: ‘These six external bases (*bāhirā āyatanā*) are impermanent, but the pleasant (*sukha*), painful (*dukkha*), or neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukha*) feeling (*vedanā*) that one experiences in dependence upon the six external bases is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change’?”

“No, indeed, Lord.”

“What is the reason for that?”

“Because each feeling arises in dependence upon its corresponding condition (*pratyaya*), and with the cessation (*nirodha*) of its corresponding condition, the feeling ceases.”

“Good, good, sisters! So it is with a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) who sees this as it actually is with proper wisdom (*sammappaññā*).

mula_pali:
404. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhaginiyo, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā gāviṃ vadhitvā tiṇhena govikantanena gāviṃ saṅkanteyya anupahacca antaraṃ maṃsakāyaṃ anupahacca bāhiraṃ cammakāyaṃ. Yaṃ yadeva tattha antarā vilimaṃsaṃ vilimaṃ (sī. pī. ka.) antarā nhāru antarā bandhanaṃ taṃ tadeva tiṇhena govikantanena sañchindeyya saṅkanteyya sampakanteyya samparikanteyya. Sañchinditvā saṅkantitvā sampakantitvā samparikantitvā vidhunitvā bāhiraṃ cammakāyaṃ teneva cammena taṃ gāviṃ paṭicchādetvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathevāyaṃ gāvī saṃyuttā imināva cammenā’ti; sammā nu kho so, bhaginiyo, vadamāno vadeyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Amu hi, bhante, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā gāviṃ vadhitvā tiṇhena govikantanena gāviṃ saṅkanteyya anupahacca antaraṃ maṃsakāyaṃ anupahacca bāhiraṃ cammakāyaṃ. Yaṃ yadeva tattha antarā vilimaṃsaṃ antarā nhāru antarā bandhanaṃ taṃ tadeva tiṇhena govikantanena sañchindeyya saṅkanteyya sampakanteyya samparikanteyya. Sañchinditvā saṅkantitvā sampakantitvā samparikantitvā vidhunitvā bāhiraṃ cammakāyaṃ teneva cammena taṃ gāviṃ paṭicchādetvā kiñcāpi so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathevāyaṃ gāvī saṃyuttā imināva cammenā’ti; atha kho sā gāvī visaṃyuttā teneva cammenā’’ti.

‘‘Upamā kho me ayaṃ, bhaginiyo, katā atthassa viññāpanāya. Ayamevettha attho; ‘antarā maṃsakāyo’ti kho, bhaginiyo, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ; ‘bāhiro cammakāyo’ti kho bhaginiyo, channetaṃ bāhirānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ; ‘antarā vilimaṃsaṃ, antarā nhāru, antarā bandhana’nti kho, bhaginiyo, nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ; ‘tiṇhaṃ govikantana’nti kho, bhaginiyo, ariyāyetaṃ paññāya adhivacanaṃ; yāyaṃ ariyā paññā antarā kilesaṃ antarā saṃyojanaṃ antarā bandhanaṃ sañchindati saṅkantati sampakantati samparikantati.
mula_english:
“Sisters, suppose a skilled butcher or his apprentice were to kill a cow and carve it up with a sharp butcher’s knife. Without damaging the inner mass of flesh, without damaging the outer hide. Whatever inner flesh remains, whatever inner sinews, whatever inner ligaments, he would cut, sever, and carve away with the sharp butcher’s knife. Then, having cut, severed, carved, thoroughly carved and removed the outer hide, he would cover the cow with that same hide and say: ‘This cow is joined to this hide just as it was before.’ Sisters, would he be speaking rightly?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?”

“Because, venerable sir, if that skilled butcher or his apprentice were to kill a cow and carve it up with a sharp butcher’s knife, without damaging the inner mass of flesh, without damaging the outer hide, whatever inner flesh remains, whatever inner sinews, whatever inner ligaments, he would cut, sever, and carve away with the sharp butcher’s knife. Then, having cut, severed, carved, thoroughly carved and removed the outer hide, even if he covers the cow with that same hide and says: ‘This cow is joined to this hide just as it was before,’ that cow would still be disjoined from that hide.”

“Sisters, I have given this simile in order to convey a meaning. Here is the meaning: ‘The inner mass of flesh’ is a term for the six internal sense bases (ajjhattikāni āyatanāni). ‘The outer hide’ is a term for the six external sense bases (bāhirāni āyatanāni). ‘The inner tendons, sinews, and ligaments’ is a term for delight and lust (nandīrāga). ‘The sharp butcher’s knife’ is a term for noble wisdom (ariyā paññā) - the noble wisdom that cuts, severs, carves, and thoroughly carves away the inner defilements (kilesa), fetters (saṃyojana), and bonds (bandhana).”

mula_pali: 405. ‘‘Satta kho panime, bhaginiyo, bojjhaṅgā, yesaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Katame satta? Idha, bhaginiyo, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ, dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Ime kho, bhaginiyo, satta bojjhaṅgā, yesaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī’’ti.
mula_english:
“Sisters, there are these seven enlightenment factors through the development and cultivation of which a *bhikkhu*, by realising for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind (*ceto-vimutti*) and deliverance by wisdom (*paññā-vimutti*) that are taintless with the destruction of the taints (*āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ*).

Which seven? Here, sisters, a *bhikkhu* develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*sati-sambojjhaṅga*) which is supported by seclusion (*viveka-nissitaṃ*), dispassion (*virāga-nissitaṃ*), and cessation (*nirodha-nissitaṃ*), and ripens in relinquishment (*vossagga-pariṇāmiṃ*). He develops the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor (*dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅgaṃ*)…the energy enlightenment factor (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅgaṃ*)…the rapture enlightenment factor (*pīti-sambojjhaṅgaṃ*), the tranquility enlightenment factor (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅgaṃ*), the concentration enlightenment factor (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅgaṃ*), the equanimity enlightenment factor (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅgaṃ*) which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and ripens in relinquishment.

These are the seven enlightenment factors through the development and cultivation of which a *bhikkhu*, by realising for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints.”

mula_pali: 406. Atha kho āyasmā nandako tā bhikkhuniyo iminā ovādena ovaditvā uyyojesi – ‘‘gacchatha, bhaginiyo; kālo’’ti. Atha kho tā bhikkhuniyo āyasmato nandakassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā āyasmantaṃ nandakaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho tā bhikkhuniyo bhagavā etadavoca – ‘‘gacchatha, bhikkhuniyo; kālo’’ti. Atha kho tā bhikkhuniyo bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu. Atha kho bhagavā acirapakkantīsu tāsu bhikkhunīsu bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, tadahuposathe cātuddase na hoti bahunojanassa kaṅkhā vā vimati vā – ‘ūno nu kho cando, puṇṇo nu kho cando’ti, atha kho ūno candotveva hoti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, tā bhikkhuniyo nandakassa dhammadesanāya attamanā honti no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappā’’ti.
mula_english:
406.
Then the venerable Nandaka, having advised the nuns with this instruction, dismissed them, saying: “Go, sisters, it is time.”

Then the nuns, having delighted and rejoiced in the venerable Nandaka’s words, rose from their seats, and after paying homage to the venerable Nandaka, circumambulated him keeping him on their right. They went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, stood at one side.

Standing at one side, the Blessed One told the nuns: “Go, sisters, it is time.”

Then the nuns paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, circumambulating him keeping him on their right.

Then, soon after the nuns had left, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, just as on the Uposatha day of the fourteenth there is no doubt or perplexity for most people as to whether the moon is incomplete or full, since the moon is clearly incomplete.

Even so, monks, those nuns are pleased with Nandaka's teaching of the Dharma, but their intention has not yet been fulfilled.”

mula_pali: 407. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ nandakaṃ āmantesi – ‘‘tena hi tvaṃ, nandaka, svepi tā bhikkhuniyo tenevovādena ovadeyyāsī’’ti. ‘‘Evaṃ , bhante’’ti kho āyasmā nandako bhagavato paccassosi. Atha kho āyasmā nandako tassā rattiyā accayena pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto attadutiyo yena rājakārāmo tenupasaṅkami. Addasaṃsu kho tā bhikkhuniyo āyasmantaṃ nandakaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna āsanaṃ paññāpesuṃ, udakañca pādānaṃ upaṭṭhapesuṃ. Nisīdi kho āyasmā nandako paññatte āsane. Nisajja pāde pakkhālesi. Tāpi kho bhikkhuniyo āyasmantaṃ nandakaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho tā bhikkhuniyo āyasmā nandako etadavoca – ‘‘paṭipucchakathā kho, bhaginiyo, bhavissati. Tattha ājānantīhi ‘ājānāmā’ tissa vacanīyaṃ, na ājānantīhi ‘na ājānāmā’ tissa vacanīyaṃ. Yassā vā panassa kaṅkhā vā vimati vā, ahameva tattha paṭipucchitabbo – ‘idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ; imassa kvattho’’’ti. ‘‘Ettakenapi mayaṃ, bhante, ayyassa nandakassa attamanā abhiraddhā yaṃ no ayyo nandako pavāretī’’ti.
mula_english:
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Nandaka, "Then, Nandaka, tomorrow also you should advise those nuns with this same advice."

"Yes, venerable sir," the venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One.

Then, the venerable Nandaka, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, went to Śrāvastī for alms.

Having wandered for alms in Śrāvastī, and while returning from the alms-round after the meal, he went with a companion to the Rājaka Park.

The nuns saw the venerable Nandaka coming from afar.

Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet.

The venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat.

Having sat down, he washed his feet.

Then the nuns, having paid homage to the venerable Nandaka, sat down at one side.

When the nuns were seated to one side, the venerable Nandaka said this: “The talk will be in the form of questions, sisters.

There, those who understand should say, 'We understand'; those who do not understand should say, 'We do not understand.'

And if anyone has doubt or uncertainty, I myself should be asked there: ‘Venerable Sir, what is the meaning of this?’”

“Even with this, venerable sir, we are pleased and delighted that the venerable Nandaka gives us leave.”

mula_pali: 408. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhaginiyo, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ , bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhaginiyo, sotaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante…pe… ghānaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante… jivhā… kāyo… mano nicco vā anicco vā’’ti? ‘‘Anicco, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Pubbeva no etaṃ, bhante, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ – ‘itipime cha ajjhattikā āyatanā aniccā’’’ti. ‘‘Sādhu sādhu, bhaginiyo! Evañhetaṃ, bhaginiyo, hoti ariyasāvakassa yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato’’.
mula_english:
“What do you think of this, sisters, is the eye permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“But that which is impermanent, is it unpleasant or pleasant?” “Unpleasant, venerable sir.”

“And is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma) as: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?” “No, venerable sir.”

“What do you think of this, sisters, is the ear permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir…pe… Is the nose permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir… The tongue… The body… Is the mind permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.”

“And is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?” “Because previously, venerable sir, we have seen it well with proper wisdom (sammappaññā) as it actually is: ‘These six internal sense-bases (ajjhattikā āyatanā) are impermanent.’”

“Good, good, sisters! So it is, sisters, for a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) who sees it as it actually is with proper wisdom.”

mula_pali: 409. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhaginiyo, rūpā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhaginiyo, saddā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante…pe… gandhā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante… rasā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante… phoṭṭhabbā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti ? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante… dhammā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Pubbeva no etaṃ, bhante, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ – ‘itipime cha bāhirā āyatanā aniccā’’’ti. ‘‘Sādhu sādhu, bhaginiyo! Evañhetaṃ, bhaginiyo, hoti ariyasāvakassa yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato’’.
mula_english:
409. “What do you think of this, sisters, are forms permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“But that which is impermanent, unpleasant or pleasant?” “Unpleasant, venerable sir.”

“And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant, stressful, subject to change as: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?” “No, venerable sir.”

“What do you think of this, sisters, are sounds permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir…pe… Are smells permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir… Are tastes permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir… Are tangibles permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir… Are mind-objects permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“But that which is impermanent, unpleasant or pleasant?” “Unpleasant, venerable sir.”

“And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant, stressful, subject to change as: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?” “No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?” “Because previously, venerable sir, we have seen it well with proper wisdom as it actually is: ‘These six external sense bases are impermanent.’”

“Good, good, sisters! So it is, sisters, with a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) who sees this as it actually is with proper wisdom.”

mula_pali: 410. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhaginiyo, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante…pe… sotaviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante… ghānaviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante… jivhāviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante… kāyaviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante… manoviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Pubbeva no etaṃ, bhante, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ – ‘itipime cha viññāṇakāyā aniccā’’’ti. ‘‘Sādhu sādhu, bhaginiyo! Evañhetaṃ, bhaginiyo, hoti ariyasāvakassa yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato’’.
mula_english:
"What do you think of this, sisters, is eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir... is ear-consciousness permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir... is nose-consciousness permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir... is tongue-consciousness permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir... is body-consciousness permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir... is mind-consciousness permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir."

"But that which is impermanent, is that unpleasant or pleasant?" "Unpleasant, venerable sir."

"And is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir."

"Why is that?" "Because this has already been well seen by us with proper wisdom as it actually is: 'Thus, these six aggregates of consciousness are impermanent.'"

"Good, good, sisters! So it is, sisters, with a noble disciple who sees this as it actually is with proper wisdom."

mula_pali: 411. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhaginiyo, telappadīpassa jhāyato telampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, vaṭṭipi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā, accipi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā, ābhāpi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā. Yo nu kho, bhaginiyo, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘amussa telappadīpassa jhāyato telampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, vaṭṭipi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā, accipi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā; yā ca khvāssa ābhā sā niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā’ti; sammā nu kho so, bhaginiyo, vadamāno vadeyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Amussa hi, bhante, telappadīpassa jhāyato telampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, vaṭṭipi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā, accipi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā ; pagevassa ābhā aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā’’ti. ‘‘Evameva kho, bhaginiyo, yo nu kho evaṃ vadeyya – ‘cha khome ajjhattikā āyatanā aniccā. Yañca kho cha ajjhattike āyatane paṭicca paṭisaṃvedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā taṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhamma’nti; sammā nu kho so, bhaginiyo, vadamāno vadeyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Tajjaṃ tajjaṃ, bhante, paccayaṃ paṭicca tajjā tajjā vedanā uppajjanti. Tajjassa tajjassa paccayassa nirodhā tajjā tajjā vedanā nirujjhantī’’ti. ‘‘Sādhu sādhu, bhaginiyo! Evañhetaṃ, bhaginiyo, hoti ariyasāvakassa yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato’’.
mula_english:
“Sisters, suppose an oil-lamp is burning: its oil is impermanent and subject to change, its wick is impermanent and subject to change, its flame is impermanent and subject to change, and its radiance is impermanent and subject to change.

Now would anyone be speaking rightly who spoke thus: ‘While this oil-lamp is burning, its oil, wick, and flame are impermanent and subject to change, but its radiance is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change’?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?”

“Because, venerable sir, while that oil-lamp is burning, its oil, wick, and flame are impermanent and subject to change, then what to say of its radiance being impermanent and changeable?”

“So too, sisters, would anyone be speaking rightly who spoke thus: ‘These six internal bases (*ajjhattikā āyatanā*) are impermanent and subject to change, but the pleasant (*sukha*), painful (*dukkha*), or neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukhaṃ*) feeling that one experiences in dependence upon the six internal bases is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change’?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?”

“Because each feeling (*vedanā*) arises in dependence upon its corresponding condition (*paccaya*), and with the cessation of its corresponding condition, the feeling ceases.”

“Good, good, sisters! So it is with a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) who sees this as it actually is with proper wisdom (*sammappaññā*).”

mula_pali: 412. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhaginiyo, mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato mūlampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, khandhopi anicco vipariṇāmadhammo, sākhāpalāsampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, chāyāpi aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā. Yo nu kho, bhaginiyo, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘amussa mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato mūlampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, khandhopi anicco vipariṇāmadhammo, sākhāpalāsampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ; yā ca khvāssa chāyā sā niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā’ti; sammā nu kho so bhaginiyo, vadamāno vadeyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Amussa hi, bhante, mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato mūlampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, khandhopi anicco vipariṇāmadhammo, sākhāpalāsampi aniccaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ; pagevassa chāyā aniccā vipariṇāmadhammā’’ti. ‘‘Evameva kho, bhaginiyo, yo nu kho evaṃ vadeyya – ‘cha khome bāhirā āyatanā aniccā. Yañca kho bāhire āyatane paṭicca paṭisaṃvedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā taṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ avipariṇāmadhamma’nti; sammā nu kho so, bhaginiyo, vadamāno vadeyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Tajjaṃ tajjaṃ, bhante, paccayaṃ paṭicca tajjā tajjā vedanā uppajjanti. Tajjassa tajjassa paccayassa nirodhā tajjā tajjā vedanā nirujjhantī’’ti. ‘‘Sādhu sādhu, bhaginiyo! Evañhetaṃ, bhaginiyo, hoti ariyasāvakassa yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato’’.
mula_english:
Sisters, suppose a great tree is standing possessed of heartwood: its root is impermanent and subject to change, its trunk is impermanent and subject to change, its branches and foliage are impermanent and subject to change, and its shadow is impermanent and subject to change.

Now would anyone be speaking rightly who spoke thus: ‘The root, trunk, branches, and foliage of this great tree standing possessed of heartwood are impermanent and subject to change, but its shadow is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change’?” “No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?” “Because, venerable sir, the root, trunk, branches, and foliage of this great tree standing possessed of heartwood are impermanent and subject to change, so its shadow must be impermanent and subject to change.”

“Just so, sisters, now would anyone be speaking rightly who spoke thus: ‘These six external sense-spheres are impermanent, but the pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that one experiences in dependence upon the six external bases is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change’?” “No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?” “Because each feeling (*vedanā*) arises in dependence upon its corresponding condition, and with the cessation of its corresponding condition, the feeling ceases.”

“Good, good, sisters! So it is with a noble disciple who sees this as it actually is with proper wisdom.”

mula_pali:
413. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhaginiyo, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā gāviṃ vadhitvā tiṇhena govikantanena gāviṃ saṅkanteyya anupahacca antaraṃ maṃsakāyaṃ anupahacca bāhiraṃ cammakāyaṃ. Yaṃ yadeva tattha antarā vilimaṃsaṃ antarā nhāru antarā bandhanaṃ taṃ tadeva tiṇhena govikantanena sañchindeyya saṅkanteyya sampakanteyya samparikanteyya. Sañchinditvā saṅkantitvā sampakantitvā samparikantitvā vidhunitvā bāhiraṃ cammakāyaṃ teneva cammena taṃ gāviṃ paṭicchādetvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathevāyaṃ gāvī saṃyuttā imināva cammenā’ti; sammā nu kho so, bhaginiyo, vadamāno vadeyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kissa hetu’’? ‘‘Amu hi, bhante, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā gāviṃ vadhitvā tiṇhena govikantanena gāviṃ saṅkanteyya anupahacca antaraṃ maṃsakāyaṃ anupahacca bāhiraṃ cammakāyaṃ. Yaṃ yadeva tattha antarā vilimaṃsaṃ antarā nhāru antarā bandhanaṃ taṃ tadeva tiṇhena govikantanena sañchindeyya saṅkanteyya sampakanteyya samparikanteyya. Sañchinditvā saṅkantitvā sampakantitvā samparikantitvā vidhunitvā bāhiraṃ cammakāyaṃ teneva cammena taṃ gāviṃ paṭicchādetvā kiñcāpi so evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathevāyaṃ gāvī saṃyuttā imināva cammenā’ti; atha kho sā gāvī visaṃyuttā teneva cammenā’’ti.

‘‘Upamā kho me ayaṃ, bhaginiyo, katā atthassa viññāpanāya ayamevettha attho. ‘Antarā maṃsakāyo’ti kho, bhaginiyo, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ; ‘bāhiro cammakāyo’ti kho, bhaginiyo, channetaṃ bāhirānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ; ‘antarā vilimaṃsaṃ antarā nhāru antarā bandhana’nti kho, bhaginiyo, nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ; ‘tiṇhaṃ govikantana’nti kho, bhaginiyo, ariyāyetaṃ paññāya adhivacanaṃ; yāyaṃ ariyā paññā antarā kilesaṃ antarā saṃyojanaṃ antarā bandhanaṃ sañchindati saṅkantati sampakantati samparikantati.
mula_english:
413.
"Just as, sisters, a skilled butcher or a butcher's apprentice, having killed a cow, would dissect the cow with a sharp butcher's knife, without damaging the inner flesh (*māṃsakāya*) and without damaging the outer hide (*cammakāya*), and whatever was on the inside—the flesh that clings, the sinews (*nhāru*), the ligaments (*bandhana*)—that he would cut, sever, carve, and completely carve away with a sharp butcher’s knife.

Having cut, severed, carved, and completely carved away, and having removed the outer hide (*cammakāya*), he would cover the cow with that same hide and say: ‘This cow is joined to this hide just as it was before.’ Would he be speaking rightly if he were to say that?” “No, venerable sir.”

“What is the reason for that?” “Because, venerable sir, a skilled butcher or a butcher's apprentice, having killed a cow, would dissect the cow with a sharp butcher's knife, without damaging the inner flesh (*māṃsakāya*) and without damaging the outer hide (*cammakāya*), and whatever was on the inside—the flesh that clings, the sinews (*nhāru*), the ligaments (*bandhana*)—that he would cut, sever, carve, and completely carve away with a sharp butcher’s knife.

Having cut, severed, carved, and completely carved away, and having removed the outer hide (*cammakāya*), even if he covers the cow with that same hide and says: ‘This cow is joined to this hide just as it was before,’ that cow would still be disjoined from that hide.”

“Sisters, I have given this simile in order to convey a meaning. This is the meaning here: ‘The inner flesh (*māṃsakāya*)’ is a designation for the six internal sense bases (*adhyātmikāni āyatanāni*); ‘the outer hide (*cammakāya*)’ is a designation for the six external sense bases (*bāhirāni āyatanāni*); ‘the flesh that clings, the sinews (*nhāru*), the ligaments (*bandhana*)’ is a designation for delight and lust (*nandīrāga*); ‘the sharp butcher’s knife (*tikhṇaṃ govikantana*)’ is a designation for noble wisdom (*āryā paññā*), which cuts, severs, carves, and completely carves away the inner defilements (*kleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and bonds (*bandhana*).
commentary_pali: 413.Anupahaccāti anupahanitvā. Tattha maṃsaṃ piṇḍaṃ piṇḍaṃ katvā cammaṃ alliyāpento maṃsakāyaṃ upahanati nāma. Cammaṃ baddhaṃ baddhaṃ katvā maṃse alliyāpento maṃsakāyaṃ upahanati nāma. Evaṃ akatvā. Vilimaṃsaṃ nhārubandhananti sabbacamme laggavilīpanamaṃsameva. Antarākilesasaṃyojanabandhananti sabbaṃ antarakilesameva sandhāya vuttaṃ.
commentary_english:
413. *Anupahaccā* means without striking.

There, having made a lump, a lump of flesh, sticking the skin, he injures the flesh-body, it is said.

Having bound the skin, bound, sticking [it] on the flesh, he injures the flesh-body, it is said.

Without doing this.

*Vilimaṃsaṃ nhārubandhana* means only the flesh that dissolves, sticks, and smears on all the skin.

*Antarākilesasaṃyojanabandhana* means all that is said referring to the internal affliction.

mula_pali: 414. ‘‘Satta kho panime, bhaginiyo, bojjhaṅgā, yesaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Katame satta? Idha, bhaginiyo, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti…pe… vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Ime kho, bhaginiyo, satta bojjhaṅgā yesaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharatī’’ti.
mula_english:
“Sisters, there are these seven factors of enlightenment through the development and cultivation of which a *bhikkhu*, by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind (*ceto-vimutti*) and deliverance by wisdom (*paññā-vimutti*) that are taintless with the destruction of the taints (*āsavānaṃ khayā*).

Which seven? Here, sisters, a *bhikkhu* develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*sati-sambojjhaṅgaṃ*), which is supported by seclusion (*viveka-nissitaṃ*), dispassion (*virāga-nissitaṃ*), and cessation (*nirodha-nissitaṃ*), and ripens in relinquishment (*vossagga-pariṇāmiṃ*). He develops the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor…the energy enlightenment factor…the rapture enlightenment factor, the tranquility enlightenment factor, the concentration enlightenment factor, the equanimity enlightenment factor, which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and ripens in relinquishment.

These are the seven enlightenment factors through the development and cultivation of which a *bhikkhu*, by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints.”
commentary_pali: 414.Satta kho panimeti kasmā āhāti? Yā hi esā paññā kilese chindatīti vuttā, sā na ekikāva attano dhammatāya chindituṃ sakkoti. Yathā pana kuṭhārī na attano dhammatāya chejjaṃ chindati, purisassa tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ paṭicceva chindati, evaṃ na vinā chahi bojjhaṅgehi paññā kilese chindituṃ sakkoti. Tasmā evamāha. Tena hīti yena kāraṇena tayā cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, cha bāhirāni , cha viññāṇakāye, dīpopamaṃ, rukkhopamaṃ, gāvūpamañca dassetvā sattahi bojjhaṅgehi āsavakkhayena desanā niṭṭhapitā, tena kāraṇena tvaṃ svepi tā bhikkhuniyo teneva ovādena ovadeyyāsīti.
commentary_english:
414. Why does he say, "satta kho panime" (these seven)? Because the wisdom (paññā) that is said to cut off defilements (kilese), is not able to cut them off by itself, according to its own nature (dhammatāya).

Just as an axe does not cut what is to be cut (chejjaṃ) by its own nature (dhammatāya), but cuts it only by relying on the effort (vāyāmaṃ) of a person (purisassa tajjaṃ paṭicceva), so too, wisdom (paññā) is not able to cut off defilements (kilese) without the six factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).

Therefore, he said thus.

Because by you, through that cause (yena kāraṇena), the six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāni āyatanāni*), the six external sense bases (*bāhirāni*), the six bodies of consciousness (*viññāṇakāye*), having shown the simile of the lamp (*dīpopamaṃ*), the simile of the tree (*rukkopamaṃ*), and the simile of the cow (*gāvūpamañca*), the teaching (desanā) was completed (niṭṭhapitā) by the seven factors of enlightenment (*sattahi bojjhaṅgehi*) through the destruction of the influxes (*āsavakkhayena*), therefore, you should advise those nuns (bhikkhuniyo) tomorrow as well with that same advice (ovādena ovadeyyāsīti).

mula_pali:
415. Atha kho āyasmā nandako tā bhikkhuniyo iminā ovādena ovaditvā uyyojesi – ‘‘gacchatha, bhaginiyo; kālo’’ti. Atha kho tā bhikkhuniyo āyasmato nandakassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā āyasmantaṃ nandakaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho tā bhikkhuniyo bhagavā etadavoca –‘‘gacchatha, bhikkhuniyo; kālo’’ti. Atha kho tā bhikkhuniyo bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu. Atha kho bhagavā acirapakkantīsu tāsu bhikkhunīsu bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, tadahuposathe pannarase na hoti bahuno janassa kaṅkhā vā vimati vā – ‘ūno nu kho cando, puṇṇo nu kho cando’ti, atha kho puṇṇo candotveva hoti; evameva kho, bhikkhave, tā bhikkhuniyo nandakassa dhammadesanāya attamanā ceva paripuṇṇasaṅkappā ca. Tāsaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ bhikkhunisatānaṃ yā pacchimitā bhikkhunī sā yā pacchimā bhikkhunī, sā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), yā pacchimikā, tā bhikkhuniyo (ka.) sotāpannā avinipātadhammā niyatā sambodhiparāyanā’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Nandakovādasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.
mula_english:
415. Then venerable Nandaka, having advised the nuns with this advice, sent them off, saying: “Go, sisters, it is time.”

Then the bhikkhunis, having delighted and rejoiced in the venerable Nandaka’s words, rose from their seats, and after paying homage to the venerable Nandaka, circumambulated him keeping him on their right. They went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, stood at one side.

Standing at one side, the Blessed One told them: “Go, sisters, it is time.”

Then the bhikkhunis paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him on their right, and departed.

Then, soon after they had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, just as on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth people are not doubtful or perplexed as to whether the moon is incomplete or full, since then the moon is clearly full, so too, those bhikkhunis are satisfied with Nandaka’s teaching of the *dharma* and their intention has been fulfilled.

Of those five hundred nuns, the last nun was a *srotāpanna* (stream enterer), no longer subject to falling (into the lower realms), with a fixed destiny, and bound for complete awakening."

The Blessed One spoke thus. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s statement.

The Nandakovada Sutra, the fourth, is finished.
commentary_pali:
415.Sā sotāpannāti yā sā guṇehi sabbapacchimikā, sā sotāpannā. Sesā pana sakadāgāmianāgāminiyo ca khīṇāsavā ca. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ paripuṇṇasaṅkappāti. Ajjhāsayapāripūriyā. Yassā hi bhikkhuniyā evamahosi – ‘‘kadā nu kho ahaṃ ayyassa nandakassa dhammadesanaṃ suṇantī tasmiṃyeva āsane sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchikareyya’’nti, sā sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchākāsi. Yassā ahosi ‘‘sakadāgāmiphalaṃ anāgāmiphalaṃ arahatta’’nti, sā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tenāha bhagavā ‘‘attamanā ceva paripuṇṇasaṅkappā cā’’ti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Nandakovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
415. ‘A Stream-Enterer’ (sotāpanna), the quality of the very least of all is a Stream-Enterer (sotāpanna).

The rest are Once-Returners (sakadāgāmi), Non-Returners (anāgāmin) and those who Destroyed the Pollutants (khīṇāsava).

How are their aspirations said to be fulfilled (paripuṇṇasaṅkappa)?

Through the fulfilment of their intentions (ajjhāsayapāripūriyā).

For that nun, it occurred thus: “When will I, while listening to the Dharma teaching of the venerable Nandaka, realize the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) in this very seat?” She realized the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

For her, it occurred thus: “Once-returner fruit (sakadāgāmiphala), non-returner fruit (anāgāmiphala), Arahatship (arahatta)!” She realized Arahatship (arahattaṃ).

Therefore the Fortunate One (bhagavā) said: “(They) were uplifted and their aspirations were fulfilled (paripuṇṇasaṅkappā).”

The Papancasudani, commentary to the Majjhima Nikaya.

The Nandakovadasutta Commentary is finished.

mula_pali:
416. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho bhagavato rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘‘paripakkā kho rāhulassa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ rāhulaṃ uttariṃ āsavānaṃ khaye vineyya’’nti. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ āmantesi – ‘‘gaṇhāhi, rāhula, nisīdanaṃ; yena andhavanaṃ tenupasaṅkamissāma divāvihārāyā’’ti . ‘‘Evaṃ, bhante’’ti kho āyasmā rāhulo bhagavato paṭissutvā nisīdanaṃ ādāya bhagavantaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhi.

Tena kho pana samayena anekāni devatāsahassāni bhagavantaṃ anubandhāni honti – ‘‘ajja bhagavā āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ uttariṃ āsavānaṃ khaye vinessatī’’ti. Atha kho bhagavā andhavanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle paññatte āsane nisīdi. Āyasmāpi kho rāhulo bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ bhagavā etadavoca –
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Wood, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

Then, when the Blessed One was alone and secluded, this thought arose in his mind: “The qualities conducive to the liberation (*vimutti*) of Rāhula are ripe. Suppose I were to further train Rāhula in the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).”

Then, early in the morning, the Blessed One, having dressed and taking his bowl and robe, went into Sāvatthī for alms. After wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, returning from his alms round, he addressed the venerable Rāhula, “Take, Rāhula, a sitting cloth; we will go to the Blind Men’s Grove (*andhavana*) for the day’s abiding.”

“So be it, Lord,” replied the venerable Rāhula. And taking a mat, he followed behind the Blessed One, step by step.

Then on that occasion, many thousands of deities followed the Blessed One, thinking: “Today the Blessed One will lead the venerable Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints (*āsava*)."

Then the Blessed One went into the Blind Men’s Grove (*andhavana*) and sat down at the root of a certain tree on a seat made ready. The venerable Rāhula also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side.

When the venerable Rāhula was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him:
commentary_pali:
416.Evaṃme sutanti rāhulovādasuttaṃ. Tattha vimuttiparipācanīyāti vimuttiṃ paripācentīti vimuttiparipācanīyā. Dhammāti pannarasa dhammā. Te saddhindriyādīnaṃ visuddhikāraṇavasena veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘‘Assaddhe puggale parivajjayato, saddhe puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato pasādanīye suttante paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi saddhindriyaṃ visujjhati. Kusīte puggale parivajjayato āraddhavīriye puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato sammappadhāne paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi vīriyindriyaṃ visujjhati. Muṭṭhassatī puggale parivajjayato upaṭṭhitassatī puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato satipaṭṭhāne paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi satindriyaṃ visujjhati . Asamāhite puggale parivajjayato samāhite puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato jhānavimokkhe paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi samādhindriyaṃ visujjhati. Duppaññe puggale parivajjayato paññavante puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato gambhīrañāṇacariyaṃ paccavekkhato imehi tīhākārehi paññindriyaṃ visujjhati. Iti ime pañca puggale parivajjayato pañca puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato pañca suttantakkhandhe paccavekkhato imehi pannarasahi ākārehi imāni pañcindriyāni visujjhantī’’ti (paṭi. ma. 1.185).

Aparepi pannarasa dhammā vimuttiparipācanīyā – saddhādīni pañcimāni indriyāni, aniccasaññā, anicce dukkhasaññā, dukkhe anattasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññāti, imā pañca nibbedhabhāgiyā saññā, meghiyattherassa kathitā kalyāṇamittatādayo pañcadhammāti. Kāya pana velāya bhagavato etadahosīti. Paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokentassa.
commentary_english:
416. Thus have I heard: the Rāhulovāda Sutta.

There, *vimuttiparipācanīyā* means that which ripens liberation; therefore, *vimuttiparipācanīyā*.

*Dhammā* means fifteen things.

These should be understood in terms of being the cause of purification of the faith faculty, and so forth.

Thus it was said:

"By avoiding a person without faith, by associating with, honoring, and attending upon a person with faith, by reflecting on inspiring discourses, the faith faculty is purified by these three aspects.

By avoiding a lazy person, by associating with, honoring, and attending upon a person who has aroused energy, by reflecting on right effort, the energy faculty is purified by these three aspects.

By avoiding a person with a confused mind, by associating with, honoring, and attending upon a person with an established mind, by reflecting on mindfulness meditation, the mindfulness faculty is purified by these three aspects.

By avoiding a person who is not concentrated, by associating with, honoring, and attending upon a concentrated person, by reflecting on absorption and liberation, the concentration faculty is purified by these three aspects.

By avoiding a person who is unwise, by associating with, honoring, and attending upon a wise person, by reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge, the wisdom faculty is purified by these three aspects.

Thus, by avoiding these five types of person, by associating with, honoring, and attending upon these five types of person, by reflecting on the five aggregates of discourses, by these fifteen aspects these five faculties are purified" (Paṭi. Ma. 1. 185).

Moreover, there are fifteen things that ripen liberation: these five faculties beginning with faith, the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), the perception of suffering in impermanence (*anicce dukkhasaññā*), the perception of non-self in suffering (*dukkhe anattasaññā*), the perception of abandonment (*pahānasaññā*), the perception of detachment (*virāgasaññā*); these five perceptions pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiyā saññā*), and the five qualities such as good friendship spoken by the Elder Meghiya.

But at what periods did the Blessed One speak thus?

Towards the time of dawn he was looking around the world.

mula_pali: 417. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rāhula, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante ’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rāhula, rūpā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rāhula, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rāhula, cakkhusamphasso nicco vā anicco vā’’ti? ‘‘Anicco, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rāhula, yamidaṃ yampidaṃ (sī. ka.) cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ tampi niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti ? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’.
mula_english:
417. “Rahula, what do you think? Is the eye permanent (nityaṃ) or impermanent (aniccaṃ)?” “Impermanent, venerable sir (bhante).”
“But that which is impermanent (aniccaṃ), (is) that unpleasant (duḥkhaṃ) or pleasant (sukhaṃ)?” “Unpleasant, venerable sir (bhante).”
“And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant (aniccaṃ), stressful (duḥkhaṃ), subject to change (vipariṇāmadhammaṃ) as: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?” “No, venerable sir (bhante).”
“Rahula, what do you think? Are forms (rūpā) permanent (niccā) or impermanent (aniccā)?” “Impermanent, venerable sir (bhante).”
“But that which is impermanent (aniccaṃ), (is) that unpleasant (duḥkhaṃ) or pleasant (sukhaṃ)?” “Unpleasant, venerable sir (bhante).”
“And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant (aniccaṃ), stressful (duḥkhaṃ), subject to change (vipariṇāmadhammaṃ) as: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?” “No, venerable sir (bhante).”
“Rahula, what do you think? Is eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇaṃ) permanent (niccaṃ) or impermanent (aniccaṃ)?” “Impermanent, venerable sir (bhante).”
“But that which is impermanent (aniccaṃ), (is) that unpleasant (duḥkhaṃ) or pleasant (sukhaṃ)?” “Unpleasant, venerable sir (bhante).”
“And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant (aniccaṃ), stressful (duḥkhaṃ), subject to change (vipariṇāmadhammaṃ) as: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?” “No, venerable sir (bhante).”
“Rahula, what do you think? Is eye-contact (cakkhusamphasso) permanent (nicco) or impermanent (anicco)?” “Impermanent, venerable sir (bhante).”
“But that which is impermanent (aniccaṃ), (is) that unpleasant (dukkhaṃ) or pleasant (sukhaṃ)?” “Unpleasant, venerable sir (bhante).”
“And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant (aniccaṃ), stressful (duḥkhaṃ), subject to change (vipariṇāmadhammaṃ) as: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?” “No, venerable sir (bhante).”
“Rahula, what do you think? Are any feeling (vedanāgataṃ), any perception (saññāgataṃ), any formations (saṅkhāragataṃ), any consciousness (viññāṇagataṃ) that arise with eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa) as condition per-manent (niccaṃ) or impermanent (aniccaṃ)?” “Impermanent, venerable sir (bhante).”
“But that which is impermanent (aniccaṃ), (is) that unpleasant (dukkhaṃ) or pleasant (sukhaṃ)?” “Unpleasant, venerable sir (bhante).”
“And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant (aniccaṃ), stressful (duḥkhaṃ), subject to change (vipariṇāmadhammaṃ) as: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?” “No, venerable sir (bhante).”

mula_pali: 418. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi rāhula, sotaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante…pe… ghānaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante…pe… jivhā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante…pe… kāyo nicco vā anicco vā’’ti? ‘‘Anicco, bhante…pe… mano nicco vā anicco vā’’ti? ‘‘Anicco, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ –‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi rāhula, dhammā niccā vā aniccā vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccā, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi rāhula, manoviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi rāhula, manosamphasso nicco vā anicco vā’’ti? ‘‘Anicco, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rāhula, yamidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ, tampi niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Aniccaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā’’ti? ‘‘Dukkhaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’.
mula_english:
418.
"What do you think, Rahula? Is the ear permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir…pe… Is the nose permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir…pe… Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir…pe… Is the body permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir…pe… Is the mind permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir."

"But that which is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, venerable sir."

"And is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir."

"What do you think, Rahula? Are things permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir."

"But that which is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, venerable sir."

"And is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir."

"What do you think, Rahula, is mind-consciousness permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir."

"But that which is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, venerable sir."

"And is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir."

"What do you think, Rahula, is mind-contact permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir."

"But that which is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, venerable sir."

"And is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir."

"What do you think, Rahula, are any feeling (vedanāgataṃ), any perception (saññāgataṃ), any formations (saṅkhāragataṃ), any consciousness (viññāṇagataṃ) that arise with mind-contact as condition permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, venerable sir."

"But that which is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, venerable sir."

"And is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, venerable sir."

mula_pali:
419. ‘‘Evaṃ passaṃ, rāhula, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmiṃ cakkhusmimpi (syā. kaṃ.) evamitaresupi nibbindati, rūpesu nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇe nibbindati, cakkhusamphasse nibbindati, yamidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ tasmimpi nibbindati. Sotasmiṃ nibbindati, saddesu nibbindati…pe… , ghānasmiṃ nibbindati, gandhesu nibbindati… jivhāya nibbindati, rasesu nibbindati… kāyasmiṃ nibbindati, phoṭṭhabbesu nibbindati… manasmiṃ nibbindati, dhammesu nibbindati, manoviññāṇe nibbindati, manosamphasse nibbindati, yamidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ tasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā rāhulo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti. Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ bhaññamāne āyasmato rāhulassa anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci. Tāsañca anekānaṃ devatāsahassānaṃ virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādi – ‘yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma’’nti.

Cūḷarāhulovādasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.
mula_english:
419. Seeing thus, Rāhula, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye (*cakṣusmiṃ*)... he becomes disenchanted with forms (*rūpesu*), disenchanted with eye-consciousness (*cakṣuviññāṇe*), disenchanted with eye-contact (*cakṣusamphassa*), and disenchanted with any feeling (*vedanāgataṃ*), any perception (*saññāgataṃ*), any formations (*saṅkhāragataṃ*), any consciousness (*viññāṇagataṃ*) that arise with eye-contact as condition. He becomes disenchanted with that as well.

He becomes disenchanted with the ear (*sotasmiṃ*), he becomes disenchanted with sounds (*saddesu*) ... He becomes disenchanted with the nose (*ghānasmiṃ*), he becomes disenchanted with odors (*gandhesu*)… He becomes disenchanted with the tongue (*jivhāya*), he becomes disenchanted with tastes (*rasesu*)… He becomes disenchanted with the body (*kāyasmiṃ*), he becomes disenchanted with tangibles (*phoṭṭhabbesu*)… He becomes disenchanted with the mind (*manasmiṃ*), he becomes disenchanted with mind-objects (*dhammesu*), he becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇe*), he becomes disenchanted with mind-contact (*manosamphassa*), and he becomes disenchanted with any feeling (*vedanāgataṃ*), any perception (*saññāgataṃ*), any formations (*saṅkhāragataṃ*), any consciousness (*viññāṇagataṃ*) that arise with mind-contact as condition. He becomes disenchanted with that as well.

Being disenchanted (*nibbindaṃ*), he becomes dispassionate (*virajjati*); through dispassion (*virāgā*) he is liberated (*vimuccati*). With release (*vimuttasmiṃ*), there is the knowledge (*ñāṇaṃ*) "It is liberated (*vimuttamiti*)."

‘Destroyed is birth (*khīṇā jāti*), the holy life has been lived (*vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ*), what had to be done has been done (*kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ*), there is no more coming to any state of being (*nāparaṃ itthattāyā*)’ he understands.

The Blessed One spoke thus (*idamavoca bhagavā*). The venerable Rāhula was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words (*attamano āyasmā rāhulo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti*). Now while this discourse was being spoken, through non-clinging (*anupādāya*) the venerable Rāhula’s mind (*cittaṃ*) was liberated (*vimucci*) from the taints (*āsavehi*). And in those many thousands of deities (*devatāsahassānaṃ*) there arose the stainless (*virajaṃ*), immaculate (*vītamalaṃ*) vision of the Dhamma (*dhammacakkhuṃ*): “All that is subject to arising (*samudayadhammaṃ*), is all subject to cessation (*nirodhadhammaṃ*).”

The Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, the fifth, is finished (*cūḷarāhulovādasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ*).
commentary_pali:
419.Anekānaṃ devatāsahassānanti āyasmatā rāhulena padumuttarassa bhagavato pādamūle pālitanāgarājakāle patthanaṃ paṭṭhapentena saddhiṃ patthanaṃ paṭṭhapitadevatāyeva. Tāsu pana kāci bhūmaṭṭhakā devatā, kāci antalikkhakā, kāci cātumahārājikā, kāci devaloke, kāci brahmaloke nibbattā. Imasmiṃ pana divase sabbā ekaṭṭhāne andhavanasmiṃyeva sannipatitā. Dhammacakkhunti upāliovāda- (ma. ni. 2.69) dīghanakhasuttesu (ma. ni. 2.206) paṭhamamaggo dhammacakkhunti vutto, brahmāyusutte (ma. ni. 2.395) tīṇi phalāni, imasmiṃ sutte cattāro maggā, cattāri ca phalāni dhammacakkhunti veditabbāni. Tattha hi kāci devatā sotāpannā ahesuṃ, kāci sakadāgāmī, anāgāmī, khīṇāsavā. Tāsañca pana devatānaṃ ettakāti gaṇanavasena paricchedo natthi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Rāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
419. Āyasmā Rāhula made the following prayer at the foot of the Blessed Padumuttara, during the time of Pālitanāga, the king, saying, "Of the thousands of gods (anekānaṃ devatāsahassāna)," and he established the prayer together with the established deity.

Moreover, some of those deities were earth-dwelling (bhūmaṭṭhakā devatā), some were in the sky (antalikkhakā), some were of the realm of the Four Great Kings (cātumahārājikā), some were born in the heaven of the gods (devaloke), and some were born in the Brahma-world (brahmaloke nibbattā).

On this day, all of them gathered in one place, in the Blind Grove (andhavanasmiṃyeva sannipatitā).

*Dhammacakkhu* [is explained] in the Upāli instruction (M.N. 2.69), in the Dīghanakha Sutta (M.N. 2.206), the first path (paṭhamamaggo) is called *dhammacakkhu*, in the Brahmāyu Sutta (M.N. 2.395), there are three fruits (tīṇi phalāni), in this sutta, there are four paths (cattāro maggā), and four fruits (cattāri ca phalāni) should be understood as *dhammacakkhu*.

There, some deities were stream-enterers (sotāpannā ahesuṃ), some were once-returners (sakadāgāmī), non-returners (anāgāmī), [and] arahants with taints destroyed (khīṇāsavā).

And there is no determination of the number of those deities as being so many (ettakāti gaṇanavasena paricchedo natthi).

The rest is clear throughout (sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti).

The Rāhulovāda Sutta Commentary of the Papañcasūdanī, commentary to the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.

mula_pali:
420. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘bhikkhavo’’ti. ‘‘Bhadante’’ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – ‘‘dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsessāmi, yadidaṃ – cha chakkāni. Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha; bhāsissāmī’’ti. ‘‘Evaṃ, bhante’’ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

‘‘Cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni veditabbāni, cha bāhirāni āyatanāni veditabbāni, cha viññāṇakāyā veditabbā, cha phassakāyā veditabbā, cha vedanākāyā veditabbā, cha taṇhākāyā veditabbā.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard: On one occasion the Blessed One (bhagavā) was dwelling near Sāavatthī (sāvatthiyaṃ) in Jeta’s Grove (jetavane), Anāthapindika’s Park (anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme).
There the Fortunate One (bhagavā) addressed the monks (bhikkhū), saying: “Monks (bhikkhavo)!”
“Venerable sir (bhadante),” those monks (bhikkhū) replied to the Fortunate One (bhagavato).
The Blessed One (bhagavā) said this: “Monks (bhikkhave), I will teach you the Dhamma (dhammaṃ) admirable in the beginning (ādikalyāṇaṃ), admirable in the middle (majjhekalyāṇaṃ), admirable in the end (pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ), with its meaning (sātthaṃ) and with its expression (sabyañjanaṃ), entirely complete (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ), surpassingly pure (parisuddhaṃ); I will expound the holy life (brahmacariyaṃ), in other words, the six sextets (cha chakkāni).
Listen to that (taṃ), pay close attention (sādhukaṃ manasi karotha); I will speak (bhāsissāmīti).”
“As you say, lord (evaṃ bhante),” those monks (bhikkhū) replied to the Blessed One (bhagavato).
The Blessed One (bhagavā) said this:

“The six internal sense bases (cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni) should be known (veditabbāni), the six external sense bases (cha bāhirāni āyatanāni) should be known (veditabbāni), the six classes of consciousness (cha viññāṇakāyā) should be known (veditabbā), the six classes of contact (cha phassakāyā) should be known (veditabbā), the six classes of feeling (cha vedanākāyā) should be known (veditabbā), the six classes of craving (cha taṇhākāyā) should be known (veditabbā).
commentary_pali:
420.Evaṃme sutanti chachakkasuttaṃ. Tattha ādikalyāṇantiādimhi kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ niddosaṃ katvā desessāmi. Majjhapariyosānesupi eseva nayo. Iti bhagavā ariyavaṃsaṃ navahi, mahāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ sattahi, mahāassapuraṃ sattahiyeva padehi thomesi. Idaṃ pana suttaṃ navahi padehi thomesi.

Veditabbānīti sahavipassanena maggena jānitabbāni. Manāyatanena tebhūmakacittameva kathitaṃ, dhammāyatanena bahiddhā tebhūmakadhammā ca, manoviññāṇena ṭhapetvā dve pañcaviññāṇāni sesaṃ bāvīsatividhaṃ lokiyavipākacittaṃ. Phassavedanā yathāvuttavipākaviññāṇasampayuttāva. Taṇhāti vipākavedanāpaccayā javanakkhaṇe uppannataṇhā.

Veditabbānī Taṇhā
commentary_english:
420. evaṃ me suta, the Chachakkasutta.

There, ādikalyāṇa means: I will teach [the Dhamma] making the beginning good, auspicious, and without fault. The same method applies to the middle and the end. Thus, the Blessed One praised the Ariyavaṃsa with nine, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna with seven, the Mahāassapura with seven words. But he praised this sutta with nine words.

veditabbānī means: they should be known with the path together with insight. With manāyatana, only the three-plane consciousness is spoken of; with dhammāyatana, the external three-plane *dhamma*s as well; with manoviññāṇa, leaving aside the two five consciousnesses, the remaining twenty-two kinds of mundane resultant consciousness. Contact and feeling are only associated with the aforementioned resultant consciousness. taṇhā means: craving that has arisen in the moment of impulsion due to resultant feeling.

veditabbānī, taṇhā

mula_pali:
421. ‘‘‘Cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni veditabbānī’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Cakkhāyatanaṃ, sotāyatanaṃ, ghānāyatanaṃ, jivhāyatanaṃ , kāyāyatanaṃ, manāyatanaṃ. ‘Cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni veditabbānī’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ chakkaṃ.

‘‘‘Cha bāhirāni āyatanāni veditabbānī’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ . Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Rūpāyatanaṃ, saddāyatanaṃ, gandhāyatanaṃ, rasāyatanaṃ, phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ, dhammāyatanaṃ. ‘Cha bāhirāni āyatanāni veditabbānī’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ chakkaṃ.

‘‘‘Cha viññāṇakāyā veditabbā’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sotañca paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati sotaviññāṇaṃ, ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca uppajjati ghānaviññāṇaṃ, jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ, kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca uppajjati kāyaviññāṇaṃ, manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. ‘Cha viññāṇakāyā veditabbā’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ chakkaṃ.

‘‘‘Cha phassakāyā veditabbā’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso; sotañca paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati sotaviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso; ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca uppajjati ghānaviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso; jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso; kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca uppajjati kāyaviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso; manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. ‘Cha phassakāyā veditabbā’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idaṃ catutthaṃ chakkaṃ.

‘‘‘Cha vedanākāyā veditabbā’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā; sotañca paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati sotaviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā; ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca uppajjati ghānaviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā; jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā; kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca uppajjati kāyaviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā; manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā. ‘Cha vedanākāyā veditabbā’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ chakkaṃ.

‘‘‘Cha taṇhākāyā veditabbā’ti – iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā; sotañca paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati sotaviññāṇaṃ…pe… ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca uppajjati ghānaviññāṇaṃ… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ… kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca uppajjati kāyaviññāṇaṃ… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. ‘Cha taṇhākāyā veditabbā’ti – iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ. Idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ chakkaṃ.
mula_english: 421. “‘The six internal sense-spheres (*ajjhattikāni āyatanāni*) should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to what was it said? The eye sense-sphere (*cakkhāyatanaṃ*), the ear sense-sphere (*sotāyatanaṃ*), the nose sense-sphere (*ghānāyatanaṃ*), the tongue sense-sphere (*jivhāyatanaṃ*), the body sense-sphere (*kāyāyatanaṃ*), and the mind sense-sphere (*manāyatanaṃ*). ‘The six internal sense-spheres should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said. This is the first sextet. ‘‘‘The six external sense-spheres (*bāhirāni āyatanāni*) should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to what was it said? The form sense-sphere (*rūpāyatanaṃ*), the sound sense-sphere (*saddāyatanaṃ*), the smell sense-sphere (*gandhāyatanaṃ*), the taste sense-sphere (*rasāyatanaṃ*), the touch sense-sphere (*phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ*), and the mental object sense-sphere (*dhammāyatanaṃ*). ‘The six external sense-spheres should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said. This is the second sextet. ‘‘‘The six aggregates of consciousness (*viññāṇakāyā*) should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to what was it said? Dependent on the eye (*cakkhu*) and forms (*rūpe*), eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) arises; dependent on the ear (*sota*) and sounds (*sadde*), ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇaṃ*) arises; dependent on the nose (*ghāna*) and smells (*gandhe*), nose-consciousness (*ghānaviññāṇaṃ*) arises; dependent on the tongue (*jivha*) and tastes (*rase*), tongue-consciousness (*jivhāviññāṇaṃ*) arises; dependent on the body (*kāya*) and tactile objects (*phoṭṭhabbe*), body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇaṃ*) arises; dependent on the mind (*mana*) and mental objects (*dhamme*), mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇaṃ*) arises. ‘The six aggregates of consciousness should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said. This is the third sextet. ‘‘‘The six aggregates of contact (*phassakāyā*) should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to what was it said? Dependent on the eye (*cakkhu*) and forms (*rūpe*), eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact (*phasso*); dependent on the ear (*sota*) and sounds (*sadde*), ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact; dependent on the nose (*ghāna*) and smells (*gandhe*), nose-consciousness (*ghānaviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact; dependent on the tongue (*jivha*) and tastes (*rase*), tongue-consciousness (*jivhāviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact; dependent on the body (*kāya*) and tactile objects (*phoṭṭhabbe*), body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact; dependent on the mind (*mana*) and mental objects (*dhamme*), mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact. ‘The six aggregates of contact should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said. This is the fourth sextet. ‘‘‘The six aggregates of feeling (*vedanākāyā*) should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to what was it said? Dependent on the eye (*cakkhu*) and forms (*rūpe*), eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact (*phasso*), with contact as condition there is feeling (*vedanā*); dependent on the ear (*sota*) and sounds (*sadde*), ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact, with contact as condition there is feeling; dependent on the nose (*ghāna*) and smells (*gandhe*), nose-consciousness (*ghānaviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact, with contact as condition there is feeling; dependent on the tongue (*jivha*) and tastes (*rase*), tongue-consciousness (*jivhāviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact, with contact as condition there is feeling; dependent on the body (*kāya*) and tactile objects (*phoṭṭhabbe*), body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact, with contact as condition there is feeling; dependent on the mind (*mana*) and mental objects (*dhamme*), mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact, with contact as condition there is feeling. ‘The six aggregates of feeling should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said. This is the fifth sextet. ‘‘‘The six aggregates of craving (*taṇhākāyā*) should be known.’ Thus was it said. And in reference to what was it said? Dependent on the eye (*cakkhu*) and forms (*rūpe*), eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact (*phasso*), with contact as condition there is feeling (*vedanā*), with feeling as condition there is craving (*taṇhā*); dependent on the ear (*sota*) and sounds (*sadde*), ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇaṃ*) arises…pe… dependent on the nose (*ghāna*) and smells (*gandhe*), nose-consciousness (*ghānaviññāṇaṃ*) arises… dependent on the tongue (*jivha*) and tastes (*rase*), tongue-consciousness (*jivhāviññāṇaṃ*) arises… dependent on the body (*kāya*) and tactile objects (*phoṭṭhabbe*), body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇaṃ*) arises… dependent on the mind (*mana*) and mental objects (*dhamme*), mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇaṃ*) arises, the meeting of the three is contact, with contact as condition there is feeling, with feeling as condition there is craving. ‘The six aggregates of craving should be known.’ Thus was it said. This is the sixth sextet.

mula_pali:
422. ‘‘‘Cakkhu attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Cakkhussa uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘cakkhu attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti cakkhu anattā.

‘‘‘Rūpā attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Rūpānaṃ uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘rūpā attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti cakkhu anattā, rūpā anattā.

‘‘‘Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Cakkhuviññāṇassa uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘cakkhuviññāṇaṃ attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti cakkhu anattā, rūpā anattā, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anattā.

‘‘‘Cakkhusamphasso attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Cakkhusamphassassa uppādopi vayopi paññāyati . Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘cakkhusamphasso attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti cakkhu anattā, rūpā anattā, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anattā, cakkhusamphasso anattā.

‘‘‘Vedanā attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Vedanāya uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘vedanā attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti cakkhu anattā, rūpā anattā, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anattā, cakkhusamphasso anattā, vedanā anattā.

‘‘‘Taṇhā attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Taṇhāya uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘taṇhā attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti cakkhu anattā, rūpā anattā, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anattā, cakkhusamphasso anattā, vedanā anattā, taṇhā anattā.
mula_english:
422. “If anyone were to say, ‘The eye (*cakkhu*) is the self (*attā*)’, that wouldn’t be tenable. The arising and falling away of the eye (*cakkhussa*) are discerned. And when its arising and falling away are discerned, it would follow that ‘My self (*attā*) arises and falls away.’ That’s why it wouldn’t be tenable if anyone were to say, ‘The eye (*cakkhu*) is the self (*attā*)’. Thus, the eye (*cakkhu*) is not-self (*anattā*).

“If anyone were to say, ‘Forms (*rūpā*) are the self (*attā*)’, that wouldn’t be tenable. The arising and falling away of forms (*rūpānaṃ*) are discerned. And when its arising and falling away are discerned, it would follow that ‘My self (*attā*) arises and falls away.’ That’s why it wouldn’t be tenable if anyone were to say, ‘Forms (*rūpā*) are the self (*attā*)’. Thus, the eye (*cakkhu*) is not-self (*anattā*) and forms (*rūpā*) are not-self (*anattā*).

“If anyone were to say, ‘Consciousness at the eye (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) is the self (*attā*)’, that wouldn’t be tenable. The arising and falling away of consciousness at the eye (*cakkhuviññāṇassa*) are discerned. And when its arising and falling away are discerned, it would follow that ‘My self (*attā*) arises and falls away.’ That’s why it wouldn’t be tenable if anyone were to say, ‘Consciousness at the eye (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) is the self (*attā*)’. Thus, the eye (*cakkhu*) is not-self (*anattā*), forms (*rūpā*) are not-self (*anattā*), and consciousness at the eye (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) is not-self (*anattā*).

“If anyone were to say, ‘Contact at the eye (*cakkhusamphasso*) is the self (*attā*)’, that wouldn’t be tenable. The arising and falling away of contact at the eye (*cakkhusamphassassa*) are discerned.
And when its arising and falling away are discerned, it would follow that ‘My self (*attā*) arises and falls away.’ That’s why it wouldn’t be tenable if anyone were to say, ‘Contact at the eye (*cakkhusamphasso*) is the self (*attā*)’. Thus, the eye (*cakkhu*) is not-self (*anattā*), forms (*rūpā*) are not-self (*anattā*), consciousness at the eye (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) is not-self (*anattā*), and contact at the eye (*cakkhusamphasso*) is not-self (*anattā*).

“If anyone were to say, ‘Feeling (*vedanā*) is the self (*attā*)’, that wouldn’t be tenable. The arising and falling away of feeling (*vedanāya*) are discerned. And when its arising and falling away are discerned, it would follow that ‘My self (*attā*) arises and falls away.’ That’s why it wouldn’t be tenable if anyone were to say, ‘Feeling (*vedanā*) is the self (*attā*)’. Thus, the eye (*cakkhu*) is not-self (*anattā*), forms (*rūpā*) are not-self (*anattā*), consciousness at the eye (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) is not-self (*anattā*), contact at the eye (*cakkhusamphasso*) is not-self (*anattā*), and feeling (*vedanā*) is not-self (*anattā*).

“If anyone were to say, ‘Craving (*taṇhā*) is the self (*attā*)’, that wouldn’t be tenable. The arising and falling away of craving (*taṇhāya*) are discerned. And when its arising and falling away are discerned, it would follow that ‘My self (*attā*) arises and falls away.’ That’s why it wouldn’t be tenable if anyone were to say, ‘Craving (*taṇhā*) is the self (*attā*)’. Thus, the eye (*cakkhu*) is not-self (*anattā*), forms (*rūpā*) are not-self (*anattā*), consciousness at the eye (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*) is not-self (*anattā*), contact at the eye (*cakkhusamphasso*) is not-self (*anattā*), feeling (*vedanā*) is not-self (*anattā*), and craving (*taṇhā*) is not-self (*anattā*).
commentary_pali: 422.Cakkhu attāti pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Heṭṭhā kathitānañhi dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ anattabhāvadassanatthaṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhā. Tattha na upapajjatīti na yujjati. Vetīti vigacchati nirujjhati.
commentary_english: 422. “*Cakkhu attā*” is a distinct connection. Indeed, this teaching was begun in order to show the non-self nature of the two truths spoken of below. There, "*na upapajjati*" means it is not appropriate. "*Vetī*" means it departs, ceases.

mula_pali:
423. ‘‘‘Sotaṃ attā’ti yo vadeyya…pe… ‘ghānaṃ attā’ti yo vadeyya… ‘jivhā attā’ti yo vadeyya… ‘kāyo attā’ti yo vadeyya… ‘mano attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Manassa uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘mano attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti mano anattā.

‘‘‘Dhammā attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Dhammānaṃ uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘dhammā attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti mano anattā, dhammā anattā.

‘‘‘Manoviññāṇaṃ attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Manoviññāṇassa uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘manoviññāṇaṃ attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti mano anattā, dhammā anattā, manoviññāṇaṃ anattā.

‘‘‘Manosamphasso attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Manosamphassassa uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘manosamphasso attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti mano anattā, dhammā anattā, manoviññāṇaṃ anattā, manosamphasso anattā.

‘‘‘Vedanā attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Vedanāya uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘vedanā attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti mano anattā, dhammā anattā, manoviññāṇaṃ anattā, manosamphasso anattā, vedanā anattā.

‘‘‘Taṇhā attā’ti yo vadeyya taṃ na upapajjati. Taṇhāya uppādopi vayopi paññāyati. Yassa kho pana uppādopi vayopi paññāyati, ‘attā me uppajjati ca veti cā’ti iccassa evamāgataṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ na upapajjati – ‘taṇhā attā’ti yo vadeyya. Iti mano anattā, dhammā anattā, manoviññāṇaṃ anattā, manosamphasso anattā, vedanā anattā, taṇhā anattā.
mula_english:
423. If anyone were to say, “The ear is the self,” …pe… If anyone were to say, “The nose is the self,” … If anyone were to say, “The tongue is the self,” … If anyone were to say, “The body is the self,” … If anyone were to say, “The mind is the self,” that wouldn’t be tenable.
The arising & falling away of the intellect are discerned.
